whyPoints.description: Al Ain sits in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so private schools here answer to ADEK rather than to Dubai's KHDA. Writing that correctly is a small thing that tells a parent whether the rest of the page was written for their city or for a search engine.

faqs.question: Is Analysis and Approaches SL the right maths course for my child, or should they be in Applications and Interpretation?
faqs.answer: Watch them work through a past Paper 1 for forty minutes. A student suited to Analysis and Approaches starts each question, sets up a method and sometimes loses the thread in the algebra. A student better suited to Applications and Interpretation often does not start, because the opening move is an algebraic manipulation they were never fluent in, yet comes alive in front of a data set or a model. The content lists differ concretely too: Analysis and Approaches carries the binomial theorem, logarithms and real calculus, while Applications and Interpretation adds the chi-squared test, financial mathematics and Voronoi diagrams. In Al Ain the deciding factor is often whether the school timetables both routes at all.

faqs.question: Why is Paper 1 so much harder for my child than Paper 2 when the topics are the same?
faqs.answer: Because Paper 1 permits no calculator of any kind and Paper 2 requires one throughout. In Paper 2 a student who understands the shape of a problem can reach the answer by solving numerically, finding an intersection or reading an inverse normal value. In Paper 1 that same understanding earns nothing unless exact values, surd and index laws, log rules and clean factorising are available from memory at speed. A large gap between the two papers almost always means an unfinished IGCSE or MYP algebra habit that a calculator has been concealing, not a problem with Diploma mathematics itself. It responds to short, frequent, unassisted practice rather than to more content teaching.

faqs.question: How are the two papers and the exploration combined into a Standard Level maths grade?
faqs.answer: Analysis and Approaches SL has three assessed components. Paper 1 runs 1 hour 30 minutes for 80 marks and carries 40 per cent of the grade. Paper 2 runs 1 hour 30 minutes for 80 marks and carries another 40 per cent. The mathematical exploration carries the remaining 20 per cent and is marked out of 20. Both papers are divided into a short-response Section A and an extended-response Section B, and the formula booklet is supplied in both. The practical consequence is that a fifth of the grade is decided before the examination room, on work a student does over several months, which is the part of the course most families underestimate.

faqs.question: My daughter is in DP1 and wants to move up to Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level. Is that realistic in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: It depends far more on the timetable than on her ability. Higher Level adds ninety guided hours, proof by induction, complex numbers, three-dimensional vectors and differential equations, plus a one-hour Paper 3 worth a fifth of the grade. Al Ain Diploma cohorts are small, and many schools cannot run Analysis and Approaches at both levels in the same option block, so the move may require a timetable change rather than a class change. Raise it with the Diploma coordinator in DP1 while options are still movable. A specialist can tell you from a script whether the content step is manageable; only the school can tell you whether the slot exists.

faqs.question: What should a Standard Level maths exploration actually be about?
faqs.answer: Something the student can carry with mathematics at the level of their own course. The commonest cause of a low mark at Standard Level is topic choice, not writing. A topic that needs techniques above the syllabus forces the student to explain mathematics they do not control, which costs marks under use of mathematics and under communication at the same time. A topic that only needs GCSE-level work caps the same criterion from below. Good Standard Level topics usually start from something the student measures, models or already argues about, and the viability check belongs at the start, before weeks of work, rather than after a draft exists.

faqs.question: How many marks is each exploration criterion worth?
faqs.answer: Twenty marks in total across five criteria. Presentation carries four, mathematical communication carries four, personal engagement carries three, reflection carries three and use of mathematics carries six. The allocation should change how a student spends their time: the single largest block sits on the mathematics itself, while formatting, which absorbs the most anxiety, is worth four. Reflection is the criterion that cannot be added at the end, because the marks go to critical reflection developed through the work rather than to a closing paragraph about what was enjoyable. Ask your child which criterion they think is weakest; if they cannot name one, nobody has explained the rubric to them.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the exploration without putting my son at risk?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a firm boundary. A tutor may teach the mathematics needed to attempt the topic, check at the outset whether the topic can carry Standard Level mathematics, explain the criteria with their mark allocations, and read a draft and respond with questions about notation, assumptions, structure and missing reflection. A tutor may not supply paragraphs, hand back rewritten mathematics, perform calculations that then appear in the document, or deliver anything resembling finished coursework. The work has to be the student's own, and a malpractice finding falls on him rather than on anyone else. One test for any tutor: ask to see what they returned on the last draft they read.

faqs.question: We have ten weeks until the mock exams. What is the best use of them for Standard Level maths?
faqs.answer: Protecting reachable marks rather than attempting a rebuild. Content can be compressed into ten weeks; fluency cannot, so a student who still hesitates over index laws will hesitate over them in the examination. A realistic ten-week plan does three things: it fixes the cheap recurring faults, such as radians left off in Paper 2 and missing constants of integration, it drills the specific topics that appear reliably in Section A, and it installs the habit of writing enough method that correct answers attract their method marks. A tutor taking a late booking should tell you which plan they are selling, because the honest one is narrower than the hopeful one.

faqs.question: Do universities in the UAE and abroad insist on Analysis and Approaches rather than Applications and Interpretation?
faqs.answer: Published entry requirements name Analysis and Approaches more often for mathematics-facing degrees such as engineering, physics, mathematics and some economics programmes. It is a pattern rather than a rule: it varies between institutions, between courses within one institution, and between admissions cycles. Business, psychology, design, architecture and most social science routes commonly accept either course. The only safe method is to read the requirement on the specific programme's own admissions page for the year of entry, including for Al Ain's own institutions, and to do it before the DP1 option form goes back rather than in DP2. Do not take a route requirement from any tutoring site, this one included.

faqs.question: Which body regulates private schools in Al Ain, and does it decide which maths courses are offered?
faqs.answer: Al Ain is part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so its private schools come under ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. Dubai's KHDA has no role here, and pages that tell an Al Ain family otherwise were not written for them. Which Diploma maths courses a school offers is a school decision shaped by cohort size and staffing rather than a regulator instruction, which is why a small Al Ain Diploma cohort often runs one Standard Level route rather than two. The regulator governs licensing, inspection and curriculum approval, not your child's option block.

faqs.question: Does a private maths tutor in Al Ain need a permit, and can we ask to see it?
faqs.answer: Yes, and yes. Private tuition in the UAE runs on a MoHRE private tutor work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone offering private tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule has been published, so treat any specific amount you read with caution. Asking a tutor directly about their permit is reasonable and normal. Abu Dhabi's ethics rules also bar school staff from tutoring students enrolled at their own school.

faqs.question: Is online maths tuition genuinely as useful as someone sitting at the table?
faqs.answer: For this course, the format that matters is a shared writing surface, and online lessons have one. Standard Level maths teaching is watching a student attempt a manipulation and intervening at the exact moment the method goes wrong, which works on a shared whiteboard where both people write and the script stays afterwards for the student to revisit. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; every UAE lesson is one-to-one teaching over live video on Gulf Standard Time. What a family in Al Ain gains in exchange is a tutor chosen for knowing where Paper 1 marks go, instead of whoever could reach the house by five o'clock on a school day.

faqs.question: What do private maths tutors charge in this market, and what should we expect to pay?
faqs.answer: Published figures read in October 2026 give a usable range. Provider rate cards advertise budget online tuition from roughly AED 45 to 65 an hour, qualified subject tutors sit around AED 150 to 300, IB and IGCSE specialists around AED 200 to 450 and above, and premium named tutors have been quoted as high as AED 650. In-home visits carry a travel premium on top, which is why monthly in-home packages in this market run well above online ones. Those are market figures from providers' own pages and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table, not our price list. Ask any provider for the rate in AED per 60 minutes and whether it includes marking.

faqs.question: Can lessons move during Ramadan and the mock season without losing the plan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the shift should be planned rather than improvised. School hours shorten during Ramadan and afternoon energy drops, so the sessions that work are the ones moved to after iftar. We reschedule rather than pause, because a six-week break in unassisted arithmetic shows up afterwards in a way that a break in content teaching does not. The mock season is the opposite problem: families want to double the session count in the busiest month. The better answer is usually two shorter sessions a week rather than one long one, with timed sections marked against the published mark scheme wording instead of a tick for the right answer.

faqs.question: What happens if there is no Analysis and Approaches specialist free at the time we need?
faqs.answer: You get one of three honest answers. A different hour with the right specialist, which is the commonest fix and usually a question of moving by ninety minutes. A short wait with an actual date attached. Or a tutor based outside the UAE who teaches the same syllabus on Gulf Standard Time, which is how most niche Diploma requests are covered anywhere in this country. You are entitled to be told which of those three applies before you book, rather than finding out in the first lesson. What does not happen is a booking accepted and then filled with whoever happened to be available that week.

faqs.question: My son came through Cambridge IGCSE with a grade 8 in maths. Why is Standard Level going badly?
faqs.answer: Because IGCSE permits a calculator in the papers that matter and Analysis and Approaches SL Paper 1 does not. A strong IGCSE grade can be built while leaning on a calculator for arithmetic, taking partial credit on algebraic fractions and avoiding questions that need completing the square. Paper 1 removes all three shelters at once, often in the first DP1 mock. The gap is usually fluency rather than understanding: expanding and factorising on sight, index and surd laws in both directions, rearranging a formula where the subject appears twice. It is fixable with short, frequent, unassisted practice, but it takes months rather than weeks, which is why it is worth starting in DP1.

al-ain/ib-dp-math-aa-sl-tutor.closingHeading: Start with the question that decides everything else
al-ain/ib-dp-math-aa-sl-tutor.closingBody: Before buying any hours, settle whether your child is in the right Standard Level maths course. Send a marked Paper 1 or mock script and take the free diagnostic session with the tutor who would actually teach the course. You will get a short written answer the same day: the topic to work on, how long it should take, and whether a conversation with the Diploma coordinator in Al Ain matters more right now than a weekly slot. If the honest answer is that tuition is not what this student needs, we will tell you that. Lessons for UAE families run one to one online over live video, on Gulf Standard Time.

al-ain/ib-dp-math-ai-hl-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation at Higher Level for Al Ain Diploma students. Matching is by topic and by the nearest deadline - Paper 3 technique, the exploration, or the statistics and modelling content that HL goes much further into than SL does.

intro.heading: Three dates decide what the next six months should contain
paragraphs: Almost every Al Ain family who searches for Higher Level Applications and Interpretation help is holding the same three facts without having written them down. There is a grade on the last report. There is a grade the student needs - for a degree route, a university offer, or simply to keep the diploma total intact. And there is a number of weeks until the May examination session. The distance between the first two, divided by the third, is the whole of the planning problem, and it is nearly always possible to answer it in one session rather than in one term.

What makes AI HL distinctive is how much of the course sits outside the content most students expect from a mathematics class. Standard Level runs to 150 teaching hours; Higher Level runs to 240, and the extra time is not simply more of the same topics. It goes into matrices and their eigenvalues, graph theory and the route-finding problems built on it, complex numbers in polar and exponential form, differential equations approached numerically through Euler's method, coupled systems and their phase portraits, and formal hypothesis testing with chi-squared and t-tests. A student who was comfortable with the Standard Level version of statistics meets a different animal at Higher Level.

The assessment is also structured differently from Analysis and Approaches, which is the course most Al Ain parents have heard about. There is no non-calculator paper. Paper 1 and Paper 2 each run two hours for 110 marks and thirty per cent of the grade, with a graphic display calculator required throughout. Paper 3 runs one hour for 55 marks and twenty per cent, and consists of two compulsory extended-response investigations - the component that exists only at Higher Level and the one most likely to be discovered in March. The mathematical exploration carries the remaining twenty per cent.

Al Ain changes the arithmetic of the plan in one specific way. The city sits around 130 kilometres inland from Abu Dhabi, is part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi and is therefore regulated by ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. Its private-school set is much smaller than Abu Dhabi island's, so Higher Level mathematics is often taught in a cohort of a handful of students, sometimes in a shared class with Analysis and Approaches, and sometimes by a teacher whose Higher Level experience is in the other course. None of that is a failing of the school; it is a reason to know early where the gaps will be.

So this page is organised as a timeline rather than as a syllabus tour. Where a student usually is when a parent starts looking. How to measure that in one session. What thirty weeks of work actually contains, week block by week block. Where Paper 3 and the exploration sit in that calendar. What it costs by the month. And what a tutor may and may not do with assessed work, stated before anyone is asked for money.

al-ain/ib-dp-math-ai-hl-tutor.programmesIntro: Where a student entered the mathematics pathway predicts which part of Higher Level will hurt and when. The four stages below are described in terms of the gap each one leaves, because closing that gap is what the early weeks of a plan are for.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Applications and Interpretation at Higher Level is one of four mathematics routes a Diploma student can take, and the one aimed at modelling, data and applied problem solving rather than at abstract proof. Across the two years a student meets five topics - number and algebra, functions, geometry and trigonometry, statistics and probability, calculus - at a depth that assumes constant calculator use, and produces one piece of coursework, the mathematical exploration.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Ain the limiting factor is usually the option block rather than the student. With small Diploma cohorts, a school may timetable Higher Level mathematics against a Higher Level science, so a student wanting both finds the timetable has already decided. Knowing that in DP1 is worth more than discovering it in DP2.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP mathematics in extended form is the smoothest entry to this course, because its criteria already ask students to investigate patterns and to communicate reasoning - the two things the exploration is marked on. What MYP does not build is calculator fluency at the level AI HL assumes, since much of MYP is deliberately done by hand.
programmes.countryNote: Only a minority of Al Ain schools run MYP all the way to Year 11; most switch to IGCSE for the two preceding years. Students from the MYP route usually start the exploration with more confidence and the papers with less.

programmes.name: IGCSE Mathematics and Additional Mathematics
programmes.description: The most common route into Higher Level in Al Ain's British-curriculum schools. Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 at Extended tier builds the algebra this course needs; Additional Mathematics 0606 adds the calculus foundation and is the better predictor of a comfortable DP1. A student arriving from Core tier 0580 will need algebraic repair before the Higher Level content can land at all.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge runs IGCSE in a June series and a November series, and Al Ain students sit in both. The November cohort arrives in DP1 straight out of examinations, which tends to mask an algebra gap for a term because recall is still fresh.

programmes.name: The exploration and the diploma core
programmes.description: The mathematical exploration is coursework worth twenty per cent of the grade, marked out of twenty across five criteria, and it sits in the calendar next to Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay. Three independent written pieces competing for the same months is the single most common reason a Higher Level mathematics plan falls apart in the second year.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain schools set their own internal exploration deadlines and they vary widely between campuses. Ask for the date in the first term of DP2 and build the mathematics plan around it rather than hoping it lands in a quiet month.

al-ain/ib-dp-math-ai-hl-tutor.subjectsIntro: Students on this course rarely need only mathematics, and the subjects they pair it with change where the pressure lands. Each note below says what the subject demands of the same weeks the mathematics plan is trying to use.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, data and applied problem solving with a calculator throughout. Higher Level adds matrices and eigenvalues, graph theory, complex numbers in polar form, numerical solutions to differential equations and formal hypothesis testing, plus Paper 3.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The algebraic and proof-based route, with a non-calculator Paper 1. Relevant here mainly as the comparison: a student who finds abstract manipulation easier than interpreting a dataset may be in the wrong course, and that question is worth settling early in DP1.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The most common pairing with AI HL in Al Ain and the one that competes hardest for the same hours. Physics internal assessment and the mathematics exploration are frequently due within the same month, which is a calendar problem rather than a mathematics problem.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Pairs naturally with the statistics and modelling half of this course, and the Higher Level policy paper rewards the same comfort with quantitative evidence. Students strong in AI HL statistics usually find the Economics data-response paper easier than their classmates do.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Financial mathematics appears in both, and students taking the pair can often reuse the same understanding of compound growth and amortisation. The business internal assessment lands in DP2 and should be sequenced against the exploration deadline, not alongside it.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Graph theory, matrices and algorithmic thinking overlap directly with the Higher Level content here, which makes this a genuinely efficient pairing. The solution requirement in the computer science assessment is a large time commitment in DP2 and needs to be on the same calendar.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Quantitative chemistry leans on the same algebraic fluency, and students who struggle with rearrangement in one subject usually struggle in both. Useful signal: fixing the algebra once tends to move two grades rather than one.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Fieldwork statistics and the interpretation of spatial data overlap with the statistics topic, and Voronoi diagrams make more sense to a geography student than to anyone else in the room. The fieldwork write-up is another DP1 or DP2 deadline for the calendar.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Two written pieces that share the exploration's months. Mathematics explorations are also a legitimate Extended Essay subject, and a student attempting both in the same area needs the two questions separated clearly to avoid overlapping work.

sections.heading: Where an AI HL student usually is when a parent starts searching
paragraphs: There are four arrival points and they need different first months. The first is the DP1 student eight weeks into the course who has gone from comfortable at IGCSE to lost, usually because the pace assumed algebraic fluency that was never quite there. The second is the DP2 student whose grades have been stable at a 4 or 5 all year and who needs a 6 for a specific offer. The third is the student who has just sat a mock, met Paper 3 for the first time, and discovered that twenty per cent of the grade is a component nobody had practised. The fourth is the student with an exploration deadline inside a month and nothing written.

Those four are not variations of one problem. The first needs foundation repair before any Higher Level content can stick, and six weeks of that will feel like going backwards while being the only thing that works. The second needs a targeted hunt for the marks that are being left on the table, which is usually a handful of recurring faults rather than a knowledge gap. The third needs technique on an unfamiliar question format, which is fast to teach and almost never taught. The fourth needs the calendar managed, not mathematics.

The reason to name these clearly is that families usually describe the symptom - "he is struggling with maths" - and buy whatever is offered. A student in the second group given foundation work will be bored and will not improve. A student in the first group given Paper 3 technique will produce nothing, because the technique has nothing to stand on. The first session's only job is to establish which of the four you are in, and that can be done from two worked questions and the school's calendar.

Al Ain adds a fifth possibility worth mentioning: the student who is in AI HL because it was the only Higher Level mathematics the school could timetable that year. That is a real situation in a small cohort, and it deserves an honest conversation about whether Standard Level is the better route, which has to happen early enough for the school to act on it.

sections.heading: Measuring where they actually are, in one session
paragraphs: A baseline has to be made of work, not of conversation. A student can explain a method clearly and still lose eleven marks on it under time pressure, and only one of those facts is visible in a discussion. So the first session is a short set of questions chosen to separate the possible causes, and the result is written down so that everything afterwards can be compared against it.

The questions are chosen for diagnostic value rather than for coverage. One algebraic rearrangement with no context tells you whether the foundation is intact. One modelling question with a dataset tells you whether the student can choose a function rather than apply a given one. One statistics item requiring a hypothesis test tells you whether the Higher Level statistical content has landed or whether the student is pattern-matching from Standard Level work. One calculator-heavy item tells you whether the machine is being used fluently or fought with. And one unstructured, open item tells you how the student behaves when the route is not signposted, which is exactly what Paper 3 asks.

What comes out of that is a statement with weeks attached, not a grade prediction. An algebra gap is usually four to six weeks of work that will not show up in school tests for the first three. A model-selection weakness is a term of exposure to varied scenarios. A calculator-fluency problem is often two sessions. Paper 3 behaviour is four to six sessions. Those timescales are the useful output, because they are what turn a plan into something a family can check.

We send the baseline in writing afterwards, including the questions used, so that a second opinion is possible. A diagnosis that cannot be checked by anyone else is an assertion, and this course is expensive enough to deserve better.

sections.heading: Thirty weeks, counted forwards from today
paragraphs: A plan a family can hold is a plan with weeks in it. The block below is the shape we use for a student starting at the beginning of DP2 with roughly thirty usable weeks before the May session, allowing for school examinations, holidays and Ramadan. The content order is deliberate: foundations before new Higher Level material, the exploration cleared before the final term, and Paper 3 technique placed after the mocks when the student has enough content to investigate with.

Two things in this sequence are counter-intuitive and both are deliberate. The exploration is finished early, in weeks nine to fourteen, rather than being allowed to drift towards its deadline - because twenty per cent of the grade written under panic is a predictable loss, and because clearing it frees the final term entirely for papers. And Paper 3 work is left until week nineteen rather than started early, because investigation technique needs content to investigate; a student who meets Paper 3 in October simply fails at it more slowly.

The right-hand column matters as much as the others. A plan that says what should be measurable at each stage is a plan that can be falsified, which is the only kind worth paying for. If the student has not moved on calculator fluency by week six, the sessions are doing the wrong thing and the plan changes. We put that test in writing precisely so that it cannot quietly be skipped.

Where the student starts later than DP2's first week, the blocks compress from the front rather than the back: the final-term paper work and the Paper 3 block hold their place, and the foundation and content weeks shorten. A plan with eleven weeks in it is a different plan, not a shorter version of this one, and we say which items have been dropped rather than pretending everything still fits.

sections.heading: Paper 3 is the component the timeline usually forgets
paragraphs: Paper 3 exists only at Higher Level. It runs one hour, carries 55 marks and twenty per cent of the final grade, and contains two compulsory extended-response problems. Each one is an investigation: a scenario, a sequence of parts that build on one another, and a requirement to keep going when an early part has not gone perfectly. It looks nothing like Paper 1 or Paper 2, and most students meet it for the first time in a mock examination in the second year.

The marks are lost in three predictable places. The first is scoping: a student who begins calculating before understanding what the scenario is asking will produce correct mathematics aimed at the wrong question. The second is the chain structure - because the parts build, a wrong answer in part b can carry through, and students who do not know that examiners allow follow-through often abandon the question instead of continuing. The third is time: one hour for two extended problems gives roughly half an hour each, and a student who spends forty minutes on the first has thrown away a quarter of the paper's marks.

All three are trainable, which is why this is high-value tutoring late in the course. We work backwards from the behaviour: read the whole question before touching the calculator, write one sentence saying what the scenario is modelling, identify which topic is being tested, then begin. Then the clock is enforced strictly, because a student who has never been stopped at thirty minutes will not stop in the examination either.

Scheduling matters here as much as content. Paper 3 work placed too early is wasted because the student lacks the content to investigate with; placed too late it competes with whole-paper revision. After the mocks and before the final six weeks is usually right, which in a thirty-week plan puts it around week nineteen. Confirm the component durations, mark totals and weightings against the subject guide your child's school is teaching, since these are revised between cohorts.

sections.heading: The exploration slot, and what happens when it slips
paragraphs: The mathematical exploration is coursework worth twenty per cent of the grade and marked out of twenty across five criteria: presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and the use of mathematics. Only the last of those is about mathematical difficulty, and it carries six of the twenty marks. The other fourteen are awarded for how the work is framed, explained, owned and reflected upon - which is why strong mathematicians routinely score in the middle of the range and why the fix is rarely harder mathematics.

The slippage pattern is consistent. A student picks a topic in DP2's first term, does nothing for ten weeks because papers feel more urgent, then writes the exploration in the fortnight before the school's internal deadline, in the same fortnight as a Theory of Knowledge draft and a science internal assessment. The mathematics in it is usually fine. The reflection is thin, the personal engagement is asserted rather than evident, and four or five marks have been given away for reasons that have nothing to do with ability.

Putting the exploration early in the plan solves two problems at once. It protects those fourteen non-mathematical marks, and it clears the final term for paper work. In the thirty-week plan above it occupies weeks nine to fourteen, running alongside the statistics teaching rather than instead of it - which also means the student's statistical topic choice is informed by content they have just learned rather than guessed at in September.

At Higher Level the exploration should use Higher Level mathematics, and students often aim too low out of caution, then lose marks under the use-of-mathematics criterion for work that is correct but slight. A topic that invites a matrix model, a graph-theoretic treatment or a differential equation does more for the mark than a longer piece of Standard Level statistics. Confirm the criteria and mark allocations against your cohort's subject guide.

sections.heading: Al Ain's small Diploma cohorts and what they do to a plan
paragraphs: Al Ain is the Garden City, part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, roughly 130 kilometres inland from the capital, and regulated by ADEK, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. Its private-school set is considerably smaller than Abu Dhabi island's, and for Higher Level mathematics that has three concrete consequences a plan has to account for.

The first is cohort size. A Higher Level Applications and Interpretation group in an Al Ain school may be three or four students, sometimes taught in the same room as the Analysis and Approaches group, sometimes by a teacher whose own Higher Level experience is in the other course. That is not neglect; it is arithmetic. But it means the Higher Level-only content - matrices and eigenvalues, graph theory, coupled differential equations - may be covered quickly or late, and a tutor should ask which topics have actually been taught rather than assuming the published order.

The second is the option block. With few students, a school timetables what it can, so Higher Level mathematics and a Higher Level science frequently clash and a student is choosing between them rather than selecting both. Families who learn this in DP1 can sometimes negotiate; families who learn it in DP2 cannot. ADEK governs licensing and accreditation of the school, not its timetable, so this is a conversation with the Diploma coordinator rather than with the regulator.

The third is availability of local help. The pool of people in Al Ain who can teach Paper 3 investigation technique on this specific course is very small, and the distance to Abu Dhabi makes a weekly in-person arrangement with a capital-based tutor impractical for most families. That is the honest argument for online delivery on this page: not that it is more convenient, but that it is how a specialist on this course becomes reachable at all.

sections.heading: Online delivery against a visiting tutor for an Al Ain address
paragraphs: Parents in Al Ain searching for Higher Level mathematics help often want somebody at the dining table, so here is the position without hedging. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Al Ain families are taught one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with a shared whiteboard, screen-shared calculator work and marked scripts returned in writing.

For this particular course the trade-off is unusually favourable. The pool of tutors who can drive to an Al Ain address on a Tuesday evening and who have taught Paper 3 on Applications and Interpretation at Higher Level is extremely small - the city's inland position is exactly why. Online, the constraint disappears and the match is made on the course rather than on the commute. A family in Zakher gets a tutor who has marked dozens of these explorations rather than the nearest available mathematics graduate.

There are mechanical advantages too, specific to a calculator-led course. A graphic display calculator emulator can be shared on screen so the student watches the exact keystrokes rather than a description of them. A worked solution can be saved and re-watched when the method is forgotten in week nine. Timed Paper 3 attempts can be run with the clock visible to both people. And nobody loses forty minutes a session to the drive.

What online does not change is the need for the student to work between sessions. We ask for the last two marked scripts before the trial lesson, we return marked work every week, and if the pattern after six weeks is that nothing has been attempted in between, we say so plainly rather than selling another term.

sections.heading: What a tutor may do with the exploration, and what nobody should offer
paragraphs: The exploration is produced at home over weeks and carries a fifth of the grade, which makes it the place where the line between teaching and substitution gets crossed. The IB's academic-honesty rules require the work to be the student's own, and a diploma can be withheld where it is not. So the boundary is set out before any work on it begins.

A tutor may teach the mathematics a topic needs, question whether a chosen model is appropriate, explain what each of the five criteria rewards, read a draft and comment on it against those criteria, point out that notation is undefined or that a graph has no axis labels, and ask what the reflection is actually claiming. A tutor may not write the exploration, may not choose the topic for the student, may not produce the data, and may not rewrite the student's prose into their own. No tutor should offer to draft the exploration or to supply a finished piece.

The practical reason to hold that line is not only compliance. Fourteen of the twenty marks are awarded for presentation, communication, engagement and reflection - all of which are about a particular student's relationship with their own work. An adult's exploration handed to a student scores badly on exactly those criteria, because the engagement is not there to be found. The honest version is also the higher-scoring one, which is a rare piece of good luck in this subject.

There are providers in this market advertising completed internal assessments at a stated price. That is an academic-integrity breach rather than a shortcut, and for a component inside a diploma it risks the whole qualification. If a page offers to produce your child's assessed work, close it.

faqs.question: My son is eight weeks into DP1 in Al Ain and already lost in Higher Level AI. Is that recoverable?
faqs.answer: Usually, and the fix is almost never the Higher Level content itself. Eight weeks in, the common cause is algebraic fluency that was adequate at IGCSE and is not adequate here, so every new topic lands on unstable ground. Four to six weeks of deliberate foundation work normally settles it, with the warning that the first three of those weeks will feel like no progress because school tests still cover the new material. Starting this in DP1 is far cheaper than starting it in DP2, when there is no spare time to go backwards.

faqs.question: What is Paper 3 in Applications and Interpretation HL and how long is it?
faqs.answer: One hour, 55 marks, twenty per cent of the final grade, and Higher Level only - Standard Level students never sit it. It contains two compulsory extended-response problems, each an investigation built in linked parts, where a scenario is given and the student has to decide what mathematics applies. It behaves nothing like Papers 1 and 2, which is why most students meet it first in a mock. Four to six sessions of technique work usually changes performance on it substantially. Confirm the duration and weighting against your cohort's subject guide.

faqs.question: How many weeks before the May session should we start if we need a grade to move?
faqs.answer: Thirty usable weeks is a comfortable plan and roughly what starting at the beginning of DP2 gives you. Twenty is workable with the content narrowed. Eleven is a triage plan: Paper 3 technique, the recurring faults that cost most marks, and timed whole papers, with no attempt at breadth. Below eight weeks we would normally say what is reachable is exam technique rather than a grade, and we would rather say that than sell a plan that cannot land. Send the dates and we will tell you which of those you are looking at.

faqs.question: What does Higher Level AI contain that Standard Level does not?
faqs.answer: Standard Level runs to 150 teaching hours, Higher Level to 240, and the extra time goes into genuinely new material rather than more practice. Matrices with eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Graph theory and the route-finding problems built on adjacency matrices. Complex numbers in polar and exponential form. Differential equations approached numerically, including coupled systems and their phase portraits. Formal hypothesis testing with chi-squared and t-tests. Plus Paper 3. A student comfortable with Standard Level statistics should not assume the Higher Level treatment is an extension of it.

faqs.question: Is there a non-calculator paper in this course?
faqs.answer: No. Both Paper 1 and Paper 2 in Applications and Interpretation assume a graphic display calculator throughout, which is one of the clearest differences from Analysis and Approaches, where Paper 1 is sat without one. The practical consequence is that calculator fluency is a marked skill rather than a convenience: a student who hunts through menus for a regression or a distribution loses minutes they needed for reasoning. It is also one of the fastest things to fix, usually in one or two sessions of drilled routines.

faqs.question: When should the mathematical exploration be written if the school's deadline is in DP2?
faqs.answer: Earlier than the deadline, which sounds obvious and almost never happens. We place it in weeks nine to fourteen of a thirty-week plan, alongside the statistics teaching, for two reasons. Fourteen of its twenty marks are for presentation, communication, engagement and reflection, and those are the marks panic destroys. And clearing it early frees the final term entirely for paper work. A student writing the exploration in the fortnight before submission, next to a Theory of Knowledge draft, is giving away marks that have nothing to do with mathematical ability.

faqs.question: How is the exploration marked, and how many marks is the mathematics itself worth?
faqs.answer: Twenty marks across five criteria: presentation carries four, mathematical communication four, personal engagement three, reflection three, and use of mathematics six. So the mathematical content accounts for under a third of the total. Strong mathematicians routinely land mid-range because their notation is undefined, their graphs are unlabelled or their reflection is a closing sentence saying the topic was interesting. At Higher Level the mathematics should also be commensurate with Higher Level - cautious Standard Level work done at length loses marks on that criterion. Check the allocations against your cohort's guide.

faqs.question: Our Al Ain school teaches both maths courses in one room. Does that matter?
faqs.answer: It matters for what has actually been covered, not for the school's quality. In a small cohort a combined class is simple arithmetic, but it means the Higher Level-only topics - eigenvalues, graph theory, coupled differential equations - may be taught quickly, late, or in catch-up sessions. Before building any plan we ask which of those topics the student has genuinely met, rather than assuming the published teaching order. That question alone has changed the shape of the first month for several Al Ain families.

faqs.question: Would my daughter be better off moving to Standard Level AI?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and the decision belongs to the school rather than to a tutor. The honest test is whether the grade she needs is reachable at Higher Level in the weeks remaining, and whether any university route she is pursuing actually requires Higher Level - many do not, and the requirement should be read on the programme's own admissions page rather than assumed. If the answer is that a secure Standard Level grade serves her better than a struggling Higher Level one, we will say so, and say it early enough for the Diploma coordinator to act.

faqs.question: How much does Higher Level AI tutoring cost per month in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: By published market figures, Bestimate's Dubai table puts monthly spend for weekly one-hour sessions at roughly AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support. Advertised packages in this market include AED 799 monthly for eight online sessions. A ninety-minute weekly slot with a specialist, which is the usual shape for this course, sits above those bands. Those are other providers' published figures, read in October 2026. We quote after a free trial lesson and a baseline.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a maths tutor to our house in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Al Ain sessions are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, with a shared whiteboard, a shared calculator view and marked scripts returned in writing. For this course that is the stronger option rather than a compromise: the number of people in Al Ain who have taught Paper 3 on Applications and Interpretation at Higher Level is very small, and online delivery is what makes a specialist reachable at all.

faqs.question: How quickly should we expect to see the grade move?
faqs.answer: It depends which weakness is being repaired, and the plan should say so before you start. Calculator fluency shows up in one or two weeks. Paper 3 performance moves inside four to six sessions because it is technique. Model selection takes a term, because it needs exposure to many scenarios. An algebra gap takes four to six weeks and shows up in school tests later than that, because the tests are on new content. A tutor who promises movement without naming which weakness is being treated is guessing, and no honest plan includes a guaranteed grade.

faqs.question: Can we fit sessions around Ramadan and the Al Ain summer?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the plan should assume it rather than discover it. During Ramadan most Al Ain families move to post-iftar slots and we shorten sessions while keeping the weekly rhythm, since a four-week gap in the middle of a content block costs more than it saves. Across the long inland summer, families travelling abroad usually keep a reduced schedule across time zones, which works because nothing about a video session requires either person to be in the city. What we ask for is the schedule agreed in advance so the week blocks move together.

faqs.question: Does ADEK decide which maths course my child's Al Ain school offers?
faqs.answer: No. ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, which includes Al Ain. Which Diploma courses a school timetables, and at which levels, is the school's own decision within its licensed curriculum, driven mainly by cohort size and staffing. So a question about whether Higher Level Applications and Interpretation can be offered next year belongs with the Diploma coordinator. ADEK's role is relevant to inspection, licensing and accreditation rather than to the option block.

faqs.question: Is the person teaching our daughter Higher Level maths legally permitted to charge us for it?
faqs.answer: Individuals giving private lessons in the UAE need the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Those operating without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. Asking any prospective tutor about their permit is reasonable, and MoHRE's own service page sets out the application route.

faqs.question: What happens if no Higher Level AI specialist is free at the slot we need?
faqs.answer: We tell you rather than substituting a general mathematics tutor. This is a narrower specialism than it sounds: Paper 3 technique and the Higher Level-only content need someone who has taught them, and in peak season the early-evening Gulf Standard Time slots fill. In that case we offer the nearest available times, a different weekday, or a start a fortnight out with the week blocks recalculated. If the timeline cannot survive that delay, we say so, because a plan that cannot reach the examination date is not worth selling.

al-ain/ib-dp-math-ai-sl-tutor.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation at Standard Level for Al Ain students. Matching is by topic and by the school's own position in the year - whether the next deadline is the exploration, an internal examination or the May session itself.

intro.heading: Al Ain is not a smaller Abu Dhabi, and the plan should know it
paragraphs: Most pages about tutoring in the UAE are written about Dubai and then have the city name swapped. That is a problem in Al Ain specifically, because almost every operational fact changes. The regulator is different: Al Ain is part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so its private schools fall under ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. KHDA, whose announcements fill most UAE education coverage, has no authority here at all.

The school set is different too. Al Ain is the Garden City, roughly 130 kilometres inland from the capital, and its private-school population is far smaller than Abu Dhabi island's. Diploma cohorts are correspondingly small, which affects which courses are timetabled, who teaches them and how many internal assessment deadlines land in the same fortnight. For Standard Level Applications and Interpretation that usually means the course is taught well but thinly, with little room for a student who needs a topic revisited.

The week is different again. Across UAE private schools, Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies run alongside whichever international curriculum the school is licensed to teach - private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond those subjects, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. Those hours are fixed. A revision plan that treats the Diploma as the whole timetable will not survive the second term, and no amount of enthusiasm about mathematics changes the number of evenings available.

And the calendar is genuinely complicated. An Al Ain family may be holding a Cambridge IGCSE timetable for a younger child, a Pearson Edexcel one for another, and an IB session for the Diploma student, with entry deadlines months before the papers and results arriving in three different windows. Cambridge even allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and warns that using the wrong zone's timetable is the centre's own risk. A plan built on the wrong date is not a small error. Entry windows close months before the papers are sat, results arrive in three different months, and an Al Ain family holding two or three of those calendars at once has a scheduling problem long before anyone opens a textbook.

So this page is organised around the system rather than around the subject. Who regulates what. What the federal and emirate rules put in the week. How the examination calendar actually runs, with sources. What Standard Level Applications and Interpretation contains and where its marks go. What a UAE university file needs from the Ministry of Education. Who is legally permitted to teach your child privately. And what the market charges, with the travel premium separated out so you can see what it buys.

al-ain/ib-dp-math-ai-sl-tutor.programmesIntro: Al Ain campuses run several curricula under the same regulator, and students move between them more often than in larger cities because the choice of schools is narrow. Each stage below is described by what it leaves a Standard Level mathematics student carrying into the next one.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Applications and Interpretation at Standard Level is the modelling and data route through Diploma mathematics: 150 teaching hours across number and algebra, functions, geometry and trigonometry, statistics and probability, and introductory calculus. Both papers assume a graphic display calculator throughout, and the mathematical exploration carries twenty per cent of the grade as the course's only piece of coursework.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Ain the Standard Level group is often the larger of the two mathematics classes and the Higher Level group the small one, so this course is usually taught by a teacher who teaches it every year. The constraint is time rather than expertise: with few free periods there is limited scope to revisit a topic a student missed.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP mathematics in its standard form feeds this course well, because the criteria already expect students to investigate, model and communicate rather than only to calculate. Students arriving from MYP are generally comfortable with the exploration and less comfortable with the volume of calculator technique the Diploma papers assume.
programmes.countryNote: Few Al Ain campuses run MYP through to Year 11, so this is the minority route locally. Where it exists it tends to produce students who write a better exploration than their IGCSE-route classmates and who need more help with timed paper technique.

programmes.name: IGCSE Mathematics
programmes.description: The dominant route into this course in Al Ain's British-curriculum schools. Extended-tier Cambridge 0580 or Pearson 4MA1 at Higher tier gives the algebra and the statistical vocabulary Standard Level assumes. Core-tier students can succeed here but arrive without the algebraic rearrangement the functions topic depends on, and that gap is worth closing in DP1 rather than in the final term.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge runs IGCSE in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October, and Pearson runs International GCSE in May/June and November. Al Ain centres sit across these, so sibling examination seasons frequently overlap a Diploma student's revision weeks.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Relevant here as the feeder decision rather than as a course: families who choose a PYP primary in Al Ain are usually choosing the continuum, and the number of campuses offering it inland is small. A student who has come up through PYP and MYP in the same school meets the Diploma with far fewer transition gaps than one who arrives at DP1 from elsewhere.
programmes.countryNote: The practical Al Ain reality is that families sometimes move campus for reasons of location rather than curriculum, because the alternative is a long daily drive. Each move creates a syllabus gap that a tutor should map explicitly rather than assume away.

al-ain/ib-dp-math-ai-sl-tutor.subjectsIntro: Standard Level Applications and Interpretation shares skills with several other Diploma subjects, and in a small Al Ain cohort students often take combinations driven by the timetable rather than by preference. Each note says where the overlap actually is.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: At Standard Level: financial mathematics, modelling with functions, three-dimensional geometry and Voronoi diagrams, correlation and regression, the chi-squared test for independence, the normal distribution, and introductory differentiation with optimisation and the trapezoidal rule.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The algebraic alternative, with a non-calculator Paper 1. Useful here as the comparison a student should settle in DP1: if manipulating expressions is easier than interpreting a dataset, the other route may suit better, and the school needs to know early.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Shares the financial mathematics directly - compound growth, loan repayment, investment appraisal. Students taking both can revise the same arithmetic twice, and the business internal assessment competes with the mathematics exploration for DP2 weeks.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: The data-response paper rewards exactly the statistical reading this course teaches, including correlation and the limits of it. Students who understand why a regression line is not a causal claim write better economics answers than classmates who have only met the diagrams.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Fieldwork statistics overlap heavily: sampling design, correlation, chi-squared tests on categorical data. Voronoi diagrams also make immediate sense to a geography student, since the nearest-facility problem is a geography question before it is a mathematics one.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: A frequent choice in Al Ain, where water, agriculture and desert ecology are live local topics. The quantitative sections draw on the same statistical handling, and students often find their best exploration topic in data they collected for this course instead.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Research methods and the evaluation of statistical claims, which is the other half of the statistics topic. A psychology student who can explain what a significance test does has most of the reasoning the chi-squared question asks for.

subjects.name: Arabic and the mandatory UAE subjects
subjects.description: Arabic language, Islamic Education and social studies sit in the week under the federal regulations for private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum. Not IB-assessed, but they occupy fixed hours, and any honest mathematics plan puts them in the calendar before the tutoring.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Two written core components sharing the exploration's months. Mathematics is a legitimate Extended Essay subject, and in a small cohort the same teacher may supervise several of these, which affects how quickly draft feedback comes back.

regions.note: Central residential streets feeding several of the city's private campuses within a short drive, so the 4.30pm to 6pm window is usable most weekdays. Short journeys here also make a twice-weekly short session practical in the final term.

regions.name: Hili
regions.note: Northern districts with a mixed curriculum intake and a number of families whose children changed campus rather than city. Mapping the syllabus gap left by a transfer is the usual first job for a Standard Level student from this area.

regions.name: Al Foah
regions.note: Towards the northern edge of the city, with longer runs in both directions and students at campuses on the far side of town. Later weekday slots from 6.30pm are standard, and weekend blocks carry the heavier timed work.

regions.name: Al Maqam
regions.note: Established residential areas near the centre with reliable mid-evening availability. Families here are often running two or three children through different boards at once, which is why the examination calendar conversation matters more than the mathematics one at first.

regions.name: Al Jimi
regions.note: One of the densest school clusters in the city, so journeys are short and the school's own after-hours clinics are genuinely accessible. For students here we often recommend using the school's support first and buying tutoring only for what it does not cover.

regions.name: Asharej
regions.note: The university district, where households are used to academic calendars and tend to want the dated plan in writing. Standard Level students from this area more often ask about university entry requirements than about grades.

regions.name: Zakher
regions.note: Southern villa plots with longer drives and fewer nearby options of any kind. For a thinly supplied subject this is where online delivery changes what is reachable rather than merely what is convenient.

regions.name: Al Mutaredh
regions.note: Settled central neighbourhoods close to the main campuses, with predictable evenings. A useful district for fixed term-long slots, which matter because moving a weekly session repeatedly is how a plan quietly dies.

sections.heading: Which authority stands behind your child's Al Ain school
paragraphs: Al Ain is part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so its private schools come under ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. That single fact is missing from almost every tutoring page aimed at UAE families, most of which are written about Dubai and mention KHDA as though it covered the country. It does not. KHDA is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in Dubai, and its announcements - fee decisions, inspection frameworks, mandatory-subject guidance - apply there.

What ADEK's role means practically for a family planning tutoring is narrower than parents often assume. Licensing and accreditation govern whether a school may operate and which curricula it may teach. They do not govern which Diploma subjects a campus timetables, which is a staffing and cohort-size decision made by the school, and they do not govern private tutoring, which is a MoHRE matter. So a question about whether Standard Level and Higher Level mathematics can both run next year belongs with the Diploma coordinator rather than with the regulator.

Inspection outcomes are worth reading with the same care. A published rating is a judgement about a whole school across many measures, and a strong overall rating is entirely compatible with a thin Diploma mathematics provision in a cohort of six. When families ask us whether a rating predicts whether their child needs tutoring, the honest answer is that it does not, and that the more useful questions are how many students are in the mathematics group, who teaches it, and when the exploration deadline falls.

One more reason to get the regulator right: it determines whose published guidance applies to your child's week. A family in Al Ain reading KHDA's mandatory-subject requirements is reading a document for a different emirate. The federal position - that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, while adhering to the Ministry's general regulations - applies everywhere, and the emirate's own authority fills in the detail.
bullets: ADEK supervises licensing and accreditation of private schools across the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, including Al Ain
KHDA's remit is Dubai; its fee and mandatory-subject announcements do not apply here
Which Diploma courses run is the school's decision, not the regulator's

sections.heading: The regulator map across the seven emirates, and what each one does not control
paragraphs: Families move between emirates more often than between countries, and the rules change at the border. Five bodies cover private schools across the UAE. ADEK handles Abu Dhabi, which includes Al Ain. KHDA handles Dubai. The Sharjah Private Education Authority regulates private education in Sharjah. Ras Al Khaimah's Department of Knowledge regulates private education in that emirate. And the Ministry of Education plays a pivotal role in supervising private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah. That is the complete map, taken from the UAE government's own private-schools page.

The powers are not identical. Sharjah's and Ras Al Khaimah's authorities approve tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods, so curriculum and fee approval sits with the emirate regulator rather than only inspection. That difference matters to a family comparing schools across emirate lines, because the same curriculum can sit inside different approval regimes depending on where the campus is.

The right-hand column of the table below is the one families usually need and never see. No education regulator in the UAE sets what a private tutor may charge, approves tutoring providers, or licenses tutors - private tutoring runs through a MoHRE work permit instead. Any provider describing itself as approved, accredited or licensed by an education regulator is making a claim that should be checked against the regulator's own published register before a dirham changes hands.

IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and does not claim one. We name these bodies because understanding them helps a family plan, not because any of them endorses us.

sections.heading: What the federal rule puts in an Al Ain week before mathematics gets a look in
paragraphs: The federal baseline for curriculum is short and consequential: private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. Every emirate's requirements sit on top of that. So an Al Ain Diploma student is carrying their six Diploma subjects, the core, and a set of mandatory subjects assessed by the school rather than by the IB.

For a mathematics plan this is simple arithmetic rather than a policy question. Those lessons occupy periods, and the homework attached to them occupies evenings. A student with a Standard Level mathematics tutoring slot, an Arabic assessment, a social studies project and a Theory of Knowledge draft in the same week has one of those four things that can move, and it is the tutoring. Which is exactly why the tutoring is the thing that gets cancelled, and why the plan should be written with those fixtures already on it.

In practice we ask three questions before setting a slot. Which afternoons carry mandatory-subject homework. When the school's internal assessment calendar puts its heaviest fortnight. And whether the student is also sitting board examinations for a different qualification, which happens in Al Ain more than people expect, because families sometimes keep a sibling's board or add an external qualification. Only then does a day and a time get fixed, and it is fixed for the term rather than negotiated weekly.

The same logic applies to Ramadan and the inland summer. Ramadan moves the evening: most of our Al Ain families switch to post-iftar slots and keep sessions shorter. The summer in Al Ain is long and hot enough that families travel, so a reduced cross-time-zone schedule is normal rather than exceptional. Both are predictable, and a plan that pretends they will not happen is a plan with two holes in it.
bullets: Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies are the federal baseline in all private schools
Those subjects are school-assessed, not IB-assessed, and still occupy real hours
Fix the weekly slot around the school's heaviest assessment fortnight, not around a preference
Ramadan moves sessions post-iftar; the long summer runs on a reduced cross-time-zone schedule

sections.heading: The examination calendar an Al Ain family actually has to manage
paragraphs: Three awarding bodies, three sets of dates, and entry deadlines that sit months before the papers. This is the section competitors leave empty - across the pages researched for this project, no competitor named an examination session, a registration deadline or a results date at all - and it is the one that changes behaviour, because almost every planning mistake we see is a date mistake rather than a mathematics mistake.

Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. Every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for the zone and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong one. The gap between an entry deadline and a first paper is the part families underestimate. For a June sitting, entries close in the spring - months before the examination period, which itself runs across May and June on the zone timetable - and the binding date is printed on the centre's statement of entry rather than guessed from a tutoring page. Forecast grades are collected before the papers, results reach the centre on Cambridge Direct in the summer, and certificates follow some weeks later. The November series repeats the same shape half a year out and is the route a candidate uses to resit, with its own earlier deadline in the autumn term.

Pearson Edexcel International GCSE examinations are available in May/June and November each year, with the November 2026 final timetable running from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson also publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, which is why any table like this should link the live official timetable rather than freeze a date that can be revised.

For the IB itself we publish no session or results dates on this page, and that is deliberate. The IB's own site blocks automated checking, so nothing in this project's research is confirmed from the IB directly. UAE schools sit the May session as the main one, and your child's Diploma coordinator holds the exact windows, internal deadlines and upload dates. Ask the school and cite the school. A tutoring plan built on a date nobody verified is the one failure mode in this section that cannot be recovered.

sections.heading: What Standard Level Applications and Interpretation actually contains
paragraphs: One hundred and fifty teaching hours, five topics, two papers and one piece of coursework. The topics are number and algebra, functions, geometry and trigonometry, statistics and probability, and calculus, and the Standard Level treatment leans deliberately towards application: compound growth and loan repayment rather than abstract series, modelling a dataset with a sinusoidal function rather than proving trigonometric identities, the trapezoidal rule rather than formal integration techniques.

Both papers run ninety minutes for eighty marks and each carries forty per cent of the final grade, with a graphic display calculator required throughout. There is no non-calculator paper in this course, which is the clearest structural difference from Analysis and Approaches and the reason calculator fluency is a marked skill here rather than a convenience. The mathematical exploration carries the remaining twenty per cent and is marked out of twenty across five criteria, only six of which are for the mathematics itself.

Two topics in the Standard Level content are distinctive enough to name. Financial mathematics - compound interest, amortisation, annuities, percentage error - appears in no other Diploma mathematics course at this level and is usually the easiest place for a mid-range student to collect marks, because the methods are mechanical once the calculator routines are learned. And Voronoi diagrams, which sit in the geometry topic and solve nearest-facility problems, which students find either immediately obvious or completely opaque with very little in between.

Component durations, mark totals and weightings are published in the subject guide your child's school is teaching from and are revised between cohorts. Confirm them with the school before using them to prioritise revision, and treat the table below as the shape rather than the final word.

sections.heading: Where Standard Level marks go missing: the three recurring faults
paragraphs: After enough marked scripts the same three faults account for most of the gap between a 4 and a 6. The first is financial mathematics done by reasoning instead of by routine. A student who tries to think their way through an amortisation question will usually get an answer that is nearly right, and nearly right scores nothing. The calculator has a finance application designed for exactly this, and five minutes spent learning it reliably returns marks for the rest of the course.

The second is the chi-squared conclusion. Students learn to compute the statistic, read the critical value and stop - or write a conclusion that overstates what the test shows. The test for independence tells you whether there is evidence of association at a stated significance level, in the context of the data given. Marks are awarded for the conclusion being stated in that context, with the hypotheses named, and they are withheld for a bare verdict. This is one of the cheapest sets of marks in the whole course and one of the most commonly dropped.

The third is the modelling question that asks for a choice. Paper 2 frequently gives data and asks which function models it, and a student trained to apply a given function will apply the first one they recognise. The marks are in the justification: why exponential rather than quadratic, what the parameters mean in the context, and whether the model is reasonable outside the data range. Teaching this takes a term of exposure to varied scenarios, because it is a habit rather than a technique.

There is a fourth worth a sentence: calculator misuse under time. Not ignorance of the machine, but hunting through menus and typing values in the wrong order. It costs minutes rather than method marks, and minutes in a ninety-minute paper are marks. We drill the routines - regression, distributions, solvers, finance - until they stop requiring thought.
bullets: Financial mathematics belongs to a calculator routine, not to reasoning from first principles
A chi-squared conclusion must name the hypotheses, the significance level and the context
Modelling questions pay for the justification of the choice, not just the fitted curve
Calculator routines are drilled so the time goes on thinking rather than searching

sections.heading: What a UAE university file needs: Ministry of Education equivalency
paragraphs: Families in Al Ain applying to UAE universities meet a process almost no tutoring page mentions: equivalency of the secondary certificate through the Ministry of Education. It is a separate exercise from the school's own paperwork and from the awarding board's certificate, and it has published requirements that differ by curriculum.

For the British track, students must submit proof of one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level with the same grade, and must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. That five-subject rule is worth stating precisely, because at least one competitor page ranking in this market publishes a six-subject requirement, which is wrong.

For the American track, English proficiency requires a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying. For the IB we publish no points threshold, because none has been read on the Ministry's own site for this project and an unsourced figure on a page like this is worse than silence. Verify it on moe.gov.ae or with the attestation authority directly.

Two things to be clear about. IB Gram does not perform, expedite or guarantee equivalency or attestation for anybody - it is the Ministry's process and the family's application, and we describe it only so that nobody discovers it in August. And tutoring is not required for it. Equivalency is a documentary process about grades already achieved, and no provider should suggest otherwise.

sections.heading: Is the person teaching your child legally permitted to do it?
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE runs on a permit. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 on private tuition work permits, and individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so no amount should be quoted to you by anyone, including us.

The permit is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students. MoHRE's own service page for it is titled Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, lists no fees and a two-working-day completion time, and is applied for through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system. That page is the right thing to check rather than any provider's description of it.

There is an Abu Dhabi-specific point that applies in Al Ain. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff have been reported as prohibiting teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, with teachers tutoring outside school hours required to hold the MoHRE permit, whose code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. That is press-reported rather than quoted from the current policy document, so verify it against ADEK's own published policy before relying on it - but it is a good reason not to arrange tutoring with your child's own classroom teacher, however convenient that looks.

Finally, a line about ourselves, because this is where providers overreach. IB Gram is not approved, accredited, licensed or endorsed by ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, MoHRE, the Ministry of Education, the IB, Cambridge or Pearson, and we have no office, centre or branch in the UAE. Any page telling you its tutors are regulator-approved is making a claim you should ask it to evidence.
