sections.heading: What tuition for two children actually costs in this market
paragraphs: Published rates for the UAE tutoring market vary by a factor of ten, and almost no competing page in this search prints a single AED figure. The bands below are market rates collected from providers' own published pricing and from Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table. They are not IB Gram's price list. They are there so that a quote you receive in Al Ain can be judged against something, which is the part of the market that is currently opaque.

At the bottom of the market, budget online tutoring from university students runs from roughly AED 45 to 150 an hour, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from roughly AED 33 to 52. A qualified subject tutor working online sits in the AED 150 to 300 band, where Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. An in-home one-to-one visit, travel included, runs roughly AED 180 to 500, with Bestimate quoting 180 to 350 and independent home tutors 200 to 500. Specialist IB, IGCSE and A Level tutors sit at AED 200 to 450 and above, with TutorChase at AED 270. Premium named or examiner-track tutoring reaches AED 650, as BartyED publishes.

The arithmetic that matters to a two-curriculum household is the monthly one. Bestimate's monthly estimates for weekly one-hour sessions are AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist examination-year support. Monthly packages in the market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. Two children at specialist examination-year level is therefore a materially different commitment from one, and the honest planning move is to stagger intensity rather than run both at full rate all year.

Context helps as well. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that there would be no increase in school fees for private schools in Dubai for the 2026-27 academic year, under an economic incentives package. That is a Dubai measure rather than an Abu Dhabi one, so it does not apply to Al Ain fees, but it is a reminder that school fees are the dominant household education cost and tuition is the smaller variable line. IB Gram does not publish a rate card on this page. The sensible next step is a free trial lesson, which is a single introductory session at no charge once a tutor has been matched, and then a quote against the actual subject and level.

sections.heading: Proximity, coverage and what happens when nobody local covers a subject
paragraphs: The phrase in this search contains the word near, so it deserves a direct answer. For lessons delivered over live video, the tutor's distance from your villa has no effect on the lesson. What distance does affect is availability: the number of qualified specialists inside a twenty-minute drive of Al Jimi or Zakher is small, and for a subject like Higher Level Computer Science or Arabic as a first language at Diploma level it may be nought. A household that insists on a local tutor for those subjects is often choosing between a non-specialist nearby and nobody.

IB Gram's position on this is stated rather than concealed. Tutoring for UAE families is delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; home visits are an India-only service. Where a UAE-based tutor covers the subject, that is the first match offered, because the overlap of school context and time zone is genuinely useful. Where no UAE-based specialist is available for a subject at the level needed, the match comes from the wider tutor pool, teaching at Gulf Standard Time, and that is disclosed before any lesson is booked rather than after.

This is the disclosure that competing pages in this search do not make. Several route UAE parents to a non-UAE telephone number while implying local delivery; one shows a Dubai address on an Abu Dhabi page. Saying plainly which subjects are thinly covered in Al Ain, and what happens when they are, is more useful to a parent than a claim of complete coverage that falls apart at the first booking. sections.heading: The lines this page does not cross
paragraphs: A search for tuition in the UAE returns a number of providers offering things they should not. The most serious is completed coursework. Internal assessments, Extended Essays and Theory of Knowledge essays are assessed work that must be the student's own, and a provider that supplies finished pieces is exposing the student to a malpractice finding that can cost the Diploma entirely. A tutor's role is to teach, to question a method, to read a student's own draft and point at the criterion it is being marked against, and to stop there. No part of an assessed piece is ever authored by an IB Gram tutor.

The second is claimed status. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, the International Baccalaureate, Cambridge International or Pearson. Those bodies are named on this page because explaining what they do is useful to a parent, not because any of them endorses this platform. There is no IB Gram office, centre or branch anywhere in the UAE.

The third is the permit question, which affects any tutor you hire in Al Ain, from us or from anyone else. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated: the private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and is open to teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students. The Ministry's service page is Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, listing no fees and a two-working-day completion time, applied for through the Ministry's smart app, website and e-services system. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount is quoted here.

The fourth is a point specific to Abu Dhabi, and therefore to Al Ain. Press reporting of ADEK's professional-ethics rules indicates that private and charter school staff are barred from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and that teachers tutoring outside school hours must hold the private tuition work permit, whose code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. Verify the current wording against ADEK's own policy document before relying on it. Either way, asking your child's own subject teacher to tutor them privately is not a route this page will suggest.

process.title: Tell us what both children are sitting
process.description: Name the boards and the syllabus codes from each child's own specification sheets, the levels or tiers, and the next assessment date each one faces. Two children on two curricula need two different conversations, and the codes are what prevent a mismatch between a Cambridge student and a tutor who has only taught Pearson papers.

process.title: Send the last report and one marked paper each
process.description: A report gives the school's view; a marked script shows where the marks actually went. For the Diploma child, the most useful document is a marked internal assessment draft with the criterion feedback attached, because that identifies which criterion is costing marks rather than which topic looks weak.

process.title: Meet a matched tutor for a trial lesson at no charge
process.description: One introductory session per child, once a tutor has been matched to the named syllabus. There is no charge for it and no card is required to book it. Watch for whether the tutor asks diagnostic questions in the first ten minutes or starts teaching immediately; the first is the better sign.

process.title: Fix the two slots and the feedback rhythm
process.description: Agree a fixed weekly time for each child, usually back to back on one evening so the household loses one evening rather than two, and agree what arrives after each lesson in writing. Changing the slot every week is the commonest reason a tuition arrangement quietly stops working by November.

process.title: Review against the calendar, not the clock
process.description: Check progress at the points the boards and the school have set: before entries close, after the mock window, before each internal assessment deadline. Reviewing on a fixed monthly cycle instead means the review lands at a moment when nothing has been assessed and there is nothing to judge.

whyPoints.title: Two curricula planned as one household
whyPoints.description: The IGCSE child's heaviest weeks and the Diploma child's heaviest weeks rarely coincide, which is usable if someone maps them in September. Planning child by child instead produces the February collision that most two-curriculum families describe after the fact.

whyPoints.title: Syllabus codes, not year groups
whyPoints.description: A tutor is matched to 0580 or 4MA1 or Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, not to a year. Boards set different papers, tier differently and write different mark schemes, and a tutor who knows one board's scheme will misread the other's.

whyPoints.title: Al Ain's regulator, not Dubai's
whyPoints.description: Al Ain schools answer to ADEK. Most online tutoring content is written about KHDA and Dubai, and a parent following it checks the wrong database and reads the wrong inspection framework. This page follows the authority that actually applies.

whyPoints.title: Rates with sources attached
whyPoints.description: Every AED band here is attributed to the provider or rate table that published it, with the market framing kept separate from anything IB Gram charges. Three of the six competing pages in this search publish no price at all, and two quote in a currency UAE families do not transact in.

whyPoints.title: Coverage stated before you book
whyPoints.description: Where Al Ain has no specialist for a subject at the level needed, that is said before a lesson is booked and the match comes from the wider pool at Gulf Standard Time. No competing page in this cluster discloses a coverage limit at all.

whyPoints.title: A hard line on assessed work
whyPoints.description: Tutors teach, question and give feedback on the student's own drafts. No internal assessment, Extended Essay or Theory of Knowledge essay is authored, finished or edited to completion by a tutor, because that route costs the student the qualification.

faqs.question: Our two children are on different curricula - can one tuition plan cover both?
faqs.answer: One plan, two tutors. The plan is the household calendar: which weeks carry the IGCSE mocks, which carry the Diploma internal assessment deadlines, and which evening holds both slots. The teaching has to be separate, because Extended IGCSE Chemistry and Higher Level Diploma Chemistry are different courses with different mark schemes, and a tutor strong in one is not automatically useful in the other. In practice most Al Ain families we work with run back-to-back slots on a single evening, with the older child's session placed second and longer.

faqs.question: What does a search for IB IGCSE tuition near me actually return in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Three things, mixed together: tuition centres advertising group classes, individual tutors listing a district, and platforms that will match you with someone online. Google's local results rank partly on proximity, which means a listing can appear first because it is close rather than because it covers your child's syllabus. The city's specialist pool is small, so for Higher Level sciences or Arabic at Diploma level the nearest qualified person may be some distance away or not in Al Ain at all. Checking the syllabus a tutor has actually taught is more informative than checking the district.

faqs.question: Does ADEK inspect an IB school and an IGCSE school against the same framework?
faqs.answer: Yes. The u.ae government portal states that ADEK supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, which includes Al Ain, and its inspection framework applies to the school rather than to the curriculum it licenses. That makes two Al Ain schools on different curricula comparable on teaching quality and leadership. What it cannot tell you is whether a particular Higher Level subject is taught strongly this year, because inspection samples across a school rather than auditing a cohort of nine candidates in one subject.

faqs.question: Which Al Ain schools run the Diploma and which run Cambridge IGCSE?
faqs.answer: The split changes, so check each school's current listing rather than a tutoring page. Broadly, Al Ain's longer-established British-curriculum schools run IGCSE followed by A Levels, while a smaller number of IB World Schools in the city run the Middle Years Programme and the Diploma. Some schools run IGCSE and then offer the Diploma afterwards. Because the sixth-form offer differs between campuses, the Year 11 decision in Al Ain is often a decision between two schools as well as two qualifications, and it is worth asking each one how many candidates sat each Higher Level subject last year.

faqs.question: How do the IGCSE and IB exam windows overlap in one household calendar?
faqs.answer: The examination windows themselves usually do not collide badly. The collisions happen earlier. Cambridge final entries for the June series fall back in the spring, and for the November series in the autumn term; Pearson publishes its November timetable with entries well ahead of the late-October start. School mock windows sit three to four months before each series, and Diploma internal deadlines cluster in the same months. A family can therefore face an IGCSE mock fortnight, a Diploma internal assessment deadline and an Extended Essay checkpoint inside three weeks. Mapping that in September is the point of planning at household level.

faqs.question: Is my Year 11 child better off moving to the Diploma or staying on A Levels in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: It depends on the subject spread and on how the student handles a compulsory second language. The Diploma requires six subjects across groups plus Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay, which suits a broad student and penalises one with a single weak area that cannot be dropped. A Levels allow three or four subjects and no core. The Ministry's British-track equivalency route is written around A Levels and AS Levels. In Al Ain the choice also involves changing campus for several families, so drive time is a real factor alongside the academic one.

faqs.question: How much does tuition for two children on two curricula cost in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Judge it against published market bands rather than a single number. A qualified subject tutor working online is advertised in the UAE market at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200, while specialist IB and IGCSE tutoring runs AED 200 to 450 and above, with TutorChase at AED 270. Bestimate's monthly estimates for weekly one-hour sessions are AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist examination-year work. Two children at examination-year intensity is a materially larger commitment, so staggering intensity usually makes more sense than running both at full rate.

faqs.question: Do we need separate tutors for IGCSE Maths and Diploma Maths?
faqs.answer: Almost always, yes. Extended IGCSE Mathematics contains no calculus, while Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level uses differentiation inside the first term and assumes fast algebraic manipulation. The mark schemes reward different things: unshown method lines at IGCSE, and unjustified steps or missing units at Diploma level. A tutor who teaches both well exists, but matching on the specific syllabus is more reliable than hoping for the overlap. If one tutor does cover both, ask which Diploma mathematics course and which board's IGCSE they last taught, and when.

faqs.question: What does the Ministry of Education require from an IGCSE leaver and from a Diploma leaver?
faqs.answer: For the British track, as reported when the UAE clarified its equivalency requirements, a student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than grade E or 3, plus one accredited Advanced Level subject at no less than E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five. No International Baccalaureate points threshold appears in that source, so none is published here. Confirm the current rules on the Ministry's own site or with the emirate attestation authority before relying on them.

faqs.question: How close does a tutor need to be if the lessons happen on screen?
faqs.answer: Distance makes no difference to a lesson delivered over live video, which is how IB Gram teaches UAE families. What distance affects is availability. The number of qualified specialists within a short drive of Al Jimi or Zakher is small, and for Higher Level Computer Science or Diploma Arabic as a first language it may be none. Insisting on a local tutor for those subjects often means choosing a non-specialist nearby over a specialist on screen. For common IGCSE subjects the local pool is deeper and the question matters less.

faqs.question: Can lessons for both children run back to back on the same evening?
faqs.answer: Yes, and most two-curriculum households in Al Ain prefer it. Two consecutive slots mean the family loses one evening a week rather than two, and the household routine only has to accommodate a single fixed commitment. The usual arrangement puts the IGCSE child first in a shorter session and the Diploma child second in a longer one, because coursework feedback benefits from an unbroken block. Where the school run from Zakher or Al Yahar lands late, the pair of slots moves later rather than being split across two nights.

faqs.question: What happens to our tuition schedule during Ramadan in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: School hours shorten and the usable part of the evening moves, so the weekly slot moves with it. Families typically choose one of three patterns: an early-afternoon session straight after the shortened school day, a post-Iftar session, or a pause for the month with the hours made up afterwards. Because lessons are delivered over live video there is no travel to work around, which makes the post-Iftar option far easier to run than a visiting arrangement would be. Agree the pattern before the month starts rather than rescheduling week by week.

faqs.question: Which subjects do Al Ain families most often ask for at both levels?
faqs.answer: Mathematics first, by a wide margin, usually Extended IGCSE for the younger child and Analysis and Approaches for the older one. Chemistry and Physics follow, then Economics and Business at Diploma level. Arabic as a first language is heavily requested here specifically, because Al Ain's Emirati and Arabic-speaking population is proportionally larger than in some coastal cities and the mandatory subject stream sits alongside the international curriculum. English First Language to Language A is a common pairing that families underestimate, because the task type changes completely.

faqs.question: If no Al Ain tutor covers a subject, what do you do?
faqs.answer: We say so before a lesson is booked, and offer a match from the wider tutor pool teaching at Gulf Standard Time. For some Diploma Higher Level subjects the number of candidates in the whole city is small enough that no local specialist exists, which is a fact about Al Ain rather than about any platform. The alternative, which several providers in this market take, is to imply local coverage and then substitute someone remote after payment. Disclosure before booking is the better arrangement, even when the answer is less convenient.

faqs.question: Is the first lesson really at no charge, and what are the conditions?
faqs.answer: The trial is one introductory session, booked after a tutor has been matched to your child's named syllabus and level, and nothing is charged for it. No card is required to book it and there is no obligation afterwards. It exists so that the match can be judged on a real lesson rather than a profile, so use it to watch how the tutor diagnoses: a tutor who spends the first ten minutes asking what the student can already do is reading the problem, while one who starts teaching immediately is guessing.

al-ain/ib-igcse-tuition-near-me.closingHeading: Start with the two calendars, then the two tutors
al-ain/ib-igcse-tuition-near-me.closingBody: If you take one thing from this page, make it the September mapping exercise. Put both children's assessment years on one sheet: entry deadlines, mock windows, internal assessment dates, examination windows. The collisions become obvious, and they are nearly always earlier than families expect. Then match each child to a tutor by syllabus code rather than by year group or postcode, run the two trial lessons at no charge, and fix a single evening that carries both slots. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time; home visits are an India-only service and are not offered anywhere in the UAE. Tell us the boards, the levels and the next date each child faces, and we will start from there.

intro.heading: Al Ain is in Abu Dhabi's regulatory system and nowhere near its school market
paragraphs: Al Ain sits roughly 130 kilometres inland from Abu Dhabi city, and that geography produces the single most important fact about tutoring here: the emirate's rules apply in full, and the emirate's supply of specialist teachers does not. Private schools in Al Ain are regulated by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. The same authority, the same policies and the same professional-conduct rules as a campus on Abu Dhabi island. A much shorter list of schools, and a correspondingly shorter list of teachers.

A parent searching for an IB MYP Mathematics Tutor in Al Ain therefore meets two constraints at once. The first is availability: the inland private-school set is far smaller than the island's, and within it the number of teachers trained in Middle Years mathematics assessment rather than in general secondary maths is smaller still. The second is regulatory: the most obvious local option, your child's own maths teacher, is the one that the emirate's professional-ethics rules are reported to close off.

This page is organised around the local system rather than around the course, because the course is identical everywhere and the system is not. It covers what the regulator actually decides and what it leaves to the school; what the smaller inland school set does to maths staffing; what the mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies hours do to a week; and how an Al Ain academic year, with its long summer and its moving Ramadan, shapes when a maths plan can realistically run.

It also deals with the question most families here eventually ask, which is whether it is worth driving to Abu Dhabi for a specialist. The answer in dirhams is unambiguous once the road is priced in, and it is set out with published rates further down. In-home visits in this market are quoted at AED 180 to 350 by Bestimate and AED 200 to 500 by independent home tutors, and a two-hour round trip from the island is bought with that premium rather than better teaching.

One operational statement before the detail. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE, and home visits in Al Ain are not a service we sell at all; our in-home offering exists only in India. For Al Ain the delivery is one-to-one over live video, scheduled on Gulf Standard Time around the school run and, in Ramadan, around Iftar rather than through it. That is a deliberate model for an inland city, not a limitation we are apologising for.

Nothing on this page quotes a price of ours or predicts how fast a grade moves. Every dirham figure below is a published market rate with its source named, so an Al Ain parent can check it independently before speaking to any provider, us included.

al-ain/ib-myp-mathematics-tutor.programmesIntro: The notes below place each IB stage in the Al Ain context specifically, because the inland school set does not offer every stage on every campus and families here move between systems more than island families do.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each assessed against four criteria out of 8, summed and converted through published boundaries into a grade from 1 to 7. Mathematics splits into a standard and an extended route from MYP 4, and the final year can be certified by on-screen examination. Interdisciplinary units and the Personal Project sit alongside the subject work.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain's Middle Years provision is concentrated in a small number of campuses around Al Jimi, Al Khabisi, Asharej and Zakher, with most of the city's private schools running British, Indian or American curricula instead. A student arriving at MYP 3 from one of those routes has usually never been assessed against criterion B at all, and that gap is visible in the first investigation task rather than in their arithmetic.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and the activity requirement. Mathematics divides into Analysis and Approaches, built on proof and calculus, and Applications and Interpretation, built on modelling and statistics. The extended Middle Years route is the natural feeder into Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level.
programmes.countryNote: Fewer Al Ain campuses run the Diploma than run the years beneath it, so a proportion of students finish MYP 5 here and either move to an Abu Dhabi island campus, commute, or switch to an A-Level route locally. That makes the standard-or-extended decision in MYP 4 consequential in a way it is not for a student who will certainly stay on one campus.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry built around transdisciplinary themes, with mathematics appearing inside units rather than as a separated subject, and an exhibition in the final year where students present and defend their own work. Number sense and pattern recognition are taught through investigation rather than through drill.
programmes.countryNote: Primary provision in Al Ain is dominated by British and Indian curricula, so most students joining a Middle Years campus at MYP 1 arrive from a system that taught mathematics as content and reported it as a percentage. Families who understand that difference early stop misreading the first Middle Years report, which is the most common source of unnecessary worry in MYP 1.

al-ain/ib-myp-mathematics-tutor.subjectsIntro: A Middle Years mathematics course has four content branches and two routes, and in an Al Ain school it runs alongside a mandatory-subject load. The list below covers both halves of that week.

subjects.name: Number
subjects.description: Integers, fractions, decimals, ratio, percentage, indices and standard form. Mostly criterion A territory, and the branch where losses are arithmetic habits rather than conceptual gaps, which makes them quick to repair with short regular drilling.

subjects.name: Algebra
subjects.description: Expressions, equations, inequalities, sequences and functions, with the extended route adding harder manipulation. Students who can solve an equation but cannot set out the steps acceptably lose on criterion C while being mathematically right.

subjects.name: Geometry and trigonometry
subjects.description: Angle reasoning, transformations, Pythagoras, right-angled trigonometry, area and volume, with non-right-angled work on the extended route. Unlabelled diagrams are a steady and invisible drain on marks here.

subjects.name: Statistics and probability
subjects.description: Collection, representation, averages, spread and probability including combined events. The easiest branch in which to build a genuine criterion D task, because an authentic local context with real numbers is straightforward to assemble.

subjects.name: Mathematics, extended route
subjects.description: Additional content layered on the standard route for students heading towards Higher Level Analysis and Approaches or a demanding A-Level start. Moving a student onto it late is substantially harder than deciding early, which is why the decision belongs in MYP 4.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first language
subjects.description: A mandatory UAE subject running alongside the licensed curriculum, with its own curriculum expectations and language of instruction. It is one of the reasons an Al Ain Middle Years week has fewer free evening hours than a timetable implies.

subjects.name: Arabic as an additional language
subjects.description: Also mandatory, taught separately from Arabic as a first language because the curriculum expectations differ. Families relocating into the UAE are often surprised by it, and it should be in any honest plan for a student's weekly workload.

subjects.name: Islamic Education
subjects.description: A mandatory subject with separate provision for Arab and non-Arab students and different languages of instruction. Dubai's regulator requires teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic to hold its own approval to teach those subjects; confirm the Al Ain arrangement with the school.

subjects.name: Social and moral studies
subjects.description: Social Studies and moral or cultural studies are part of the federal baseline every private school follows, with the language of instruction set by the student's group. Content substitution is not permitted without prior ministry permission.

subjects.name: Sciences and Design
subjects.description: Both generate maths evidence parents overlook: graph plotting, units, significant figures, tolerance and specification. A science practical with unlabelled axes is showing exactly the criterion C habit that is costing marks in mathematics.

al-ain/ib-myp-mathematics-tutor.regionsIntro: Al Ain is low-rise and spread across oases and districts, and the practical variable is the school run rather than the distance to a tutor. The notes below cover timing and the school clusters each district feeds.

regions.name: Al Jimi
regions.note: Central, near the oasis and a cluster of long-established private campuses. Short school runs mean a 4:30pm session is realistic here, which makes Al Jimi the easiest district in the city to hold a fixed weekly slot in.

regions.name: Al Khabisi
regions.note: Residential and close to several of the city's larger campuses. Connectivity is good and a 5pm start is normal. Households here often have children at two different schools, so the maths slot has to sit around a sibling's timetable.

regions.name: Asharej
regions.note: Near the university district, with a high proportion of academic and professional households. Expectations around mathematics tend to be explicit here, and parents arrive already knowing the criterion levels, which shortens the diagnosis considerably.

regions.name: Al Towayya
regions.note: Established housing with a long run to the campuses on the far side of the city. A 4pm session is unrealistic on a school day; from 6pm the slot holds reliably, which also suits the longer blocks an investigation task needs.

regions.name: Zakher
regions.note: On the southern edge of the city towards the dunes, with newer family housing and a longer commute in both directions. The distance is exactly why a travelling tutor prices Zakher higher, and why video removes the premium rather than the lesson.

regions.name: Al Muwaiji and Falaj Hazza
regions.note: Western districts with a mix of villa compounds and older housing. Weekend mornings fill more easily here than weekday evenings, which is useful because criterion D work needs an uninterrupted block rather than a rushed half-hour.

regions.name: Hili and Al Qattara
regions.note: Northern Al Ain, closer to the Dubai road and the archaeological sites. Families here are furthest from the southern campuses, and the drive is long enough that no sensible in-home quote exists for a weekly session.

regions.name: Al Maqam and Al Yahar
regions.note: Outer districts towards the Abu Dhabi road, where some households also consider island schools. The commute decision shapes the maths plan, because a student travelling further has fewer usable evening hours than one in Al Jimi.

sections.heading: ADEK, and what an Abu Dhabi regulator decides about an Al Ain classroom
paragraphs: Al Ain is part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so its private schools sit under the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. There is no separate Al Ain authority. That is worth stating because families relocating here sometimes assume an inland city has its own regulator, and because ADEK is named by none of the competitor pages researched in this market, which means parents searching in English are unlikely to have met it in any tutoring context.

The complete regulator map for UAE private schools has five bodies. Dubai has the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. Abu Dhabi, and therefore Al Ain, has ADEK. Sharjah has the Sharjah Private Education Authority, which regulates private education in that emirate. Ras Al Khaimah has its Department of Knowledge. The Ministry of Education plays a pivotal role in supervising private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah.

What the regulator reaches is the school: licensing, accreditation, policy compliance, fees and staff conduct. What it does not reach is the Middle Years mark scheme. Criterion levels, band descriptors and the on-screen assessment route are set by the IB and are identical in Al Jimi and in Geneva. So the division of questions is clean, and knowing it saves weeks of circular email: school licensing and fee questions to ADEK, criterion levels and task dates to the school, assessment rules to the IB through the programme coordinator.

There is a fourth layer underneath all of it. Federally, private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. That is the rule behind every emirate's mandatory-subject requirement, and it is the reason an Al Ain Middle Years student carries hours a Middle Years student in Europe does not. Those hours get a section of their own below, because they are the real constraint on a maths plan.

sections.heading: Why the inland school set is smaller, and what that does to maths staffing
paragraphs: Abu Dhabi island and the Khalifa City corridor hold the bulk of the emirate's international school capacity. Al Ain's private-school set is substantially smaller, and within it the schools running the Middle Years Programme are a minority: most of the city's private provision is British, Indian or American curriculum. That is not a judgement about quality. It is a statement about the size of the pool from which a Middle Years mathematics specialist could be drawn locally.

The practical consequence shows up in staffing patterns rather than in anything a prospectus would mention. In a school with one Middle Years year group per cohort, mathematics is often taught by one or two teachers across all five years, sometimes alongside a Diploma class. Those teachers are frequently excellent. What they do not have is a departmental colleague to give a second explanation when the first one has not landed, or spare capacity for sustained one-to-one work during a term.

There is a second-order effect families notice in MYP 4. The standard-and-extended split requires the school to run two routes, which in a small cohort can mean setting arrangements that are tighter than a larger campus would need. A student who sits near the boundary between the two routes gets a decision made in a small-group context rather than from a wide spread of evidence, which is an argument for a parent being clear about the four criterion levels early rather than discovering the route after it is set.

The upside is real and worth naming. Small cohorts mean a Middle Years maths teacher in Al Ain knows the student properly, and a parent can usually get a specific, honest answer from them in a ten-minute conversation. That conversation is the first and cheapest step in any tutoring decision, and it should produce three facts: the four criterion levels, the next assessed task and its criterion, and the teacher's view of which criterion is actually weak.

sections.heading: The rule that rules out your child's own maths teacher
paragraphs: The most natural thought a parent in a small city has is also the one to set aside. Press reporting on Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff describes a prohibition on teachers providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and states that teachers tutoring outside school hours must hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, whose code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with their own school. Treat that as press-reported rather than as ADEK's exact wording, and verify against the current policy document before relying on it.

Whichever way the detail reads, the direction is clear enough to plan around, and the reason behind it is sound. A teacher who both sets a student's assessed tasks and is paid privately by that student's family is in an obvious conflict, and the integrity of the criterion levels that go on the report depends on that conflict not existing. In a small Al Ain cohort the conflict would be sharper than on a large campus, because the same teacher may be the only person marking that year group.

What a family can legitimately ask of the school teacher is substantial and free. The four criterion levels separately. A marked task with annotations. The date and criterion of the next assessed piece. Their honest view of the weakest criterion. The school's scheme of work for the term, so external support follows it rather than running a parallel course. None of that is tutoring, all of it is normal professional communication, and together it is the brief any external tutor needs.

For anyone who is paid, the permit question applies. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued by the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone tutoring without one is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so treat quoted figures as invention. Ask for the permit reference.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies: the other hours in an Al Ain week
paragraphs: Any maths plan that ignores the mandatory UAE subjects is a plan that will be abandoned. Federally, private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations. Every emirate implements that baseline, and the published detail is most complete for Dubai, where the requirements must be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year starts in April.

Dubai's documented rules are worth knowing even in Al Ain, because they show the shape of the requirement a family is dealing with. Schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, with the school's licensed-curriculum language used for non-Arabs.

Two further details matter for timetabling. Mandatory-subject instructional time in Dubai is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and it is advised that any mandatory subject lesson lasts at least 25 minutes. And the use of any different or additional content, without prior permission from the Ministry of Education, is strictly prohibited — which is a real constraint on how any Arabic, Islamic Education or social studies tutoring can honestly be described, by us or by anybody else.

Confirm your own campus's arrangement with the school, because Al Ain sits under ADEK and the emirate-level detail is not identical to Dubai's. What generalises is the arithmetic: a Middle Years student with eight subject groups, Arabic, Islamic Education, a social and moral studies requirement and a Personal Project in MYP 5 has fewer free evening hours than the timetable suggests. A maths plan assuming three sessions a week is a plan that collapses in week three; one weekly slot, held reliably, outperforms it.

sections.heading: The Al Ain academic year, and the weeks a maths plan actually has
paragraphs: An Al Ain school year runs from late August or early September to late June or early July, with a winter break around late December, a spring break in March and a long summer. Ramadan moves roughly eleven days earlier each year, so its position relative to the term changes annually and has to be checked rather than assumed. Written as months, a school year looks like ten. Written as usable weeks for a Middle Years maths intervention, it is considerably fewer, and the losses are predictable.

The first term is the most productive and the least used. September and October are the weeks in which a criterion weakness can be diagnosed and fixed before it has cost anything on a report, and they are the weeks most families spend waiting for a report to tell them something they could have asked for directly. By the time the first reporting cycle lands in November or December, a term of the best available time has gone.

The second term is where the assessed tasks cluster. Criterion B investigations and criterion D context tasks tend to fall in this stretch, along with any mock arrangements the school runs for MYP 5. This is when a parent most wants tutoring and when it is hardest to do well, because a task the school is about to mark is precisely what a tutor must not touch. Work in this term has to be on task types, which is less satisfying and entirely necessary.

The third term is short, hot and dominated by end-of-year assessment, and the long summer that follows it is the single most underused asset an Al Ain family has. A student who closes a criterion C habit over July and August starts the next year without it, which is worth more than a term of in-year firefighting. Term dates vary between campuses, so build any plan from your own school's published calendar rather than from a generic one, and confirm IB assessment dates through the programme coordinator.

sections.heading: What the four criteria mean on an Al Ain school report
paragraphs: A Middle Years report shows a grade from 1 to 7 for mathematics, and behind it sit four criterion levels each marked out of 8. Criterion A is knowing and understanding, including application in unfamiliar situations. Criterion B is investigating patterns: finding a general rule, describing it and justifying or proving it. Criterion C is communicating, which means mathematical language, movement between representations and complete lines of reasoning. Criterion D is applying mathematics in real-life contexts, including explaining accuracy and whether the answer makes sense.

ADEK's reporting expectations shape how schools present this, and practice varies between campuses in ways that confuse parents comparing notes. Some schools report all four criterion levels every cycle; some report a subset and a converted grade; some give a best-fit judgement across a reporting period rather than a task-by-task mark. None of those are wrong, but they measure differently, and a parent judging whether tutoring is working needs to know which one their school uses before interpreting a number that has not moved.

The most useful request, then, is not for more detail but for more precision. Ask: are these four levels from single tasks or a best-fit across the term; which criterion was the last assessed task marked against; and what is the next assessed task and its criterion. Those three answers turn a report from a verdict into a plan, and they are available to any parent who asks the subject teacher directly rather than through a general query.

The conversion itself is worth understanding once. The four levels sum to a figure out of 32, which converts to the reported 1 to 7 grade through published boundaries. It is not a percentage and does not behave like one: a student can move up a grade on one criterion level if they were sitting at a boundary, or gain three levels and not move at all. That is why 'she went up a grade' is a weaker piece of information than 'criterion C moved from 4 to 6'.

sections.heading: The standard or extended decision, in a school that may not run the Diploma above it
paragraphs: From MYP 4, mathematics splits into a standard and an extended route, and the choice determines the content a student is taught across two years rather than the difficulty of a paper. In Al Ain the decision carries an extra weight, because fewer campuses here run the Diploma than run the years beneath it. A meaningful number of students will finish MYP 5 and move to an Abu Dhabi island campus, commute, or switch locally to an A-Level route, and the right route depends partly on where they are going.

The evidence that should drive it is specific. Criterion A in unfamiliar situations, and criterion B, across the previous year. A student who handles unseen problem types and produces real justifications rather than worked examples is an extended candidate. A student strong on familiar problems and weak on both will find the extended content a source of anxiety rather than stretch, and may well be better served by being genuinely excellent on the standard route than mediocre on the extended one.

Where destination matters is in what comes after. Higher Level Analysis and Approaches expects the algebraic fluency the extended route builds. Applications and Interpretation is more forgiving on that front and more demanding on modelling and technology. An A-Level maths start assumes a particular algebraic baseline. None of these is a reason to push a student onto a route they cannot sustain, but all of them are reasons to have the conversation in MYP 4 rather than discovering the mismatch in the first Diploma term.

Three questions to the school in MYP 4 settle it: which route is my child currently on, when is the entry confirmed, and what evidence will decide it. Then one for the family: where is this student likely to be at 16, given that not every Al Ain campus runs the Diploma. A tutoring plan built from those four answers is a plan; one built from a general wish for better maths is a standing order.

sections.heading: What a Middle Years maths tutor costs in Al Ain, against the rest of an Al Ain school bill
paragraphs: Tutoring is easier to judge next to the other education costs a family already carries than in isolation. School fees are the anchor, and the regional context is documented: Dubai's regulator confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in that emirate for the 2026-27 academic year, under the city's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total. Abu Dhabi fee approvals, including for Al Ain, sit with ADEK, and the school is the right source for its own fee schedule.

Against that annual commitment, a weekly tutoring hour is a marginal cost and should be assessed as one. Bestimate's monthly estimates for weekly one-hour sessions run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. Middle Years work normally sits in the middle band. Published packages in this market run around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions against AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions.

The hourly bands behind those monthly figures are these. Budget online tutoring is AED 45 to 150, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52 — relevant in a university city where mathematics undergraduates are available and cheap. A qualified subject teacher online is AED 150 to 300, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. Specialists sit at AED 200 to 450 or more, with TutorChase quoting AED 270 and BartyED publishing AED 650.

The Al Ain-specific line is the in-home band of AED 180 to 350 from Bestimate and AED 200 to 500 from independent home tutors. For a city 130 kilometres from the island, that premium buys a two-hour round trip, not better teaching, and a specialist asked to make it weekly will either price it accordingly or decline. Every figure here is a published market rate attributed to its source rather than an IB Gram price list; our own number comes from the consultation after a free trial lesson.

sections.heading: Academic honesty, and what to tell an Al Ain school
paragraphs: Middle Years mathematics looks like low-risk territory for academic honesty right up to the point a criterion B or D task is set, at which point it is an assessed project like any other. The task is set, marked and reported by the school, and it must be the student's own work. A tutor who works through a live investigation with a student, suggesting the rule and the justification, has produced a level that measures the tutor rather than the child, and that level then feeds a route decision in MYP 4.

The boundary we hold is worth asking of anybody. Teaching happens on task types, not on the live assessed task. A tutor may explain what a general rule is, demonstrate the difference between an example and a justification, work an unrelated pattern problem through from scratch, and give written feedback on the student's own practice attempts. A tutor may not touch the task the school is about to mark, suggest the student's rule, or write any part of what is submitted.

Telling the school is the simple part and the part families skip. A maths teacher who knows a student has weekly external support reads their work differently and more usefully, and in a small Al Ain cohort that teacher is also the person whose judgement will set the route in MYP 4. Ask what the school wants to be told and then tell them. A tutor who suggests keeping the arrangement quiet has told you what they intend to do in the sessions.

One last point about this city specifically. Al Ain is a university city, so permitted university students offering cheap mathematics tuition are genuinely available, and the permit guidance names university students as eligible. A permit answers a legal question, not a competence one, and Middle Years criteria work is not the same as being good at mathematics. Ask any prospective tutor which criterion they would target first and why. The answer separates the people who know this programme from the people who know maths.

process.title: Get four numbers and three dates from the school
process.description: Before booking anything, ask for the criterion A, B, C and D levels separately, the criterion the last assessed task was marked against, the date and criterion of the next one, and the school's term calendar. All of that is free and it is the brief any external tutor needs.

process.title: Free first lesson with the named tutor
process.description: The first session costs nothing, takes no card details and is taught by the tutor who would continue. It works from the student's own marked task rather than a placement test, and it ends with a written statement of which criterion to target and why.

process.title: A plan built on your school's calendar
process.description: The tutor builds the block around the Al Ain term dates, the mandatory-subject timetable and Ramadan's position in that year. Term dates differ between campuses here, which is why we ask for yours rather than working from a generic academic year.

process.title: One weekly slot, held reliably
process.description: A Middle Years week in Al Ain has fewer free evening hours than the timetable suggests, so one slot that always happens beats three that half happen. Sessions move to post-Iftar timing in Ramadan rather than pausing, and a short written note follows each one.

process.title: A route conversation in MYP 4, not MYP 5
process.description: Before the standard-or-extended entry is confirmed, we set out what the evidence says and what the student's likely destination at 16 implies, given that not every Al Ain campus runs the Diploma. The decision stays with the school and the family.

whyPoints.title: Anchored to ADEK, not to generic UAE copy
whyPoints.description: Al Ain is in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi and has no separate regulator. ADEK is named by none of the competitor pages researched in this market, so a parent searching in English has probably never seen it in a tutoring context. This page sets out what it decides and what it leaves to the school.

whyPoints.title: Specialist match instead of local availability
whyPoints.description: Al Ain's Middle Years provision sits across a small number of campuses, so the local pool of teachers trained in Middle Years assessment is short. Online matching draws on specialists who can work a Gulf Standard Time evening rather than on whoever lives within a 20-minute drive of Al Jimi.

whyPoints.title: The mandatory-subject load taken into account
whyPoints.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and social or moral studies run alongside the eight Middle Years subject groups. A plan that assumes three maths sessions a week ignores that and collapses by week three. One reliable weekly slot is the honest design for an Al Ain week.

whyPoints.title: Costs set against the rest of the school bill
whyPoints.description: Monthly figures matter more than hourly ones, and both are quoted here in dirhams with the publisher named. The in-home premium of AED 180 to 500 an hour buys a round trip from the island rather than better teaching, which is worth knowing before anyone quotes it to you.

whyPoints.title: A stated honesty line, and told to the school
whyPoints.description: Teaching happens on task types, never on the live assessed task the school will mark. We will not work on a criterion B or D investigation in progress, and we encourage families to tell the school about external support rather than keep it quiet.

faqs.question: How does ADEK regulate private schools in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Al Ain is part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so there is no separate inland authority. The Department of Education and Knowledge supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate, which covers licensing, policy compliance, fees and staff conduct on an Al Ain campus exactly as on an island one. What it does not set is the Middle Years mark scheme: criterion levels, band descriptors and the on-screen assessment route are the IB's and are identical everywhere. School licensing and fees to ADEK, criterion levels and task dates to the school.

faqs.question: Which Al Ain schools offer the IB Middle Years Programme?
faqs.answer: A small number, with most of the city's private provision running British, Indian or American curricula instead. Programme offerings change, so the reliable answer is to check each school directly or through ADEK rather than trusting a list. If your child already attends a Middle Years campus, the more useful questions are which route they will take in MYP 4, when that is confirmed, and whether the same campus runs the Diploma above it, because a meaningful number of Al Ain students move at 16.

faqs.question: Can my child's own Al Ain school teacher tutor them privately for maths?
faqs.answer: Treat the answer as no and verify with the school. Press reporting on Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules describes a prohibition on private and charter school staff providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE private tuition work permit carries a code of conduct barring service to students affiliated with the permit-holder's school. Confirm against the current ADEK policy document rather than relying on press reporting. What you can ask the teacher for, free, is the four criterion levels, a marked task and the next task's criterion.

faqs.question: How does the Al Ain school calendar affect an MYP maths plan?
faqs.answer: More than families expect. September and October are the most productive weeks and the least used, because most parents wait for a first report that lands in November or December. The second term is where criterion B and D tasks cluster, which is when tutoring is most wanted and hardest to do properly, since the live assessed task is exactly what a tutor must not touch. Ramadan moves earlier each year and needs checking rather than assuming. The long summer is the single most underused block in the year.

faqs.question: Are Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies compulsory alongside the MYP in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Yes. Federally, private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations, and every emirate implements that baseline. Dubai's published rules are the most detailed worked example: separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, with combined classes strictly prohibited. Confirm your own campus's arrangement with the school, since Al Ain sits under ADEK rather than Dubai's authority.

faqs.question: How much does an MYP mathematics tutor cost in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Market rates rather than ours, and monthly is the better unit. Bestimate's estimates for weekly one-hour sessions put the budget band at AED 240 to 600 a month, the middle band at AED 600 to 1,200 and specialist exam-year support at AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more. Hourly, budget online tutoring runs AED 45 to 150, a qualified teacher online AED 150 to 300 with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200, and specialists AED 200 to 450 or more with TutorChase at AED 270. Our figure follows a free trial lesson.

faqs.question: Is it worth driving to Abu Dhabi for an MYP maths tutor?
faqs.answer: Almost never, and the numbers explain why. Al Ain is roughly 130 kilometres from Abu Dhabi city, so a weekly in-home session from an island-based tutor is a two-hour round trip on top of the hour taught. Published in-home rates of AED 180 to 350 from Bestimate and AED 200 to 500 from independent home tutors overlap the online specialist band of AED 200 to 450 almost exactly, so the premium is travel rather than teaching. A specialist asked to make that drive weekly will price it accordingly or decline it.

faqs.question: What does MYP mathematics cover in Al Ain schools that IGCSE does not?
faqs.answer: The assessment, mainly. Both cover number, algebra, geometry and statistics, but the Middle Years Programme assesses four criteria out of 8 each — knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts — and converts the total into a grade from 1 to 7. IGCSE assesses written papers against a mark scheme. The practical difference is criteria B and D: finding and justifying a general rule, and judging whether an answer makes sense in a real context. Students moving from an IGCSE track find those two unfamiliar.

faqs.question: Does Al Ain have fewer specialist maths teachers than Abu Dhabi?
faqs.answer: Fewer, because the inland private-school set is substantially smaller than the island and Khalifa City corridor, and only a minority of Al Ain's schools run the Middle Years Programme. In a school with one cohort per year group, mathematics is often taught by one or two teachers across all five Middle Years years. That usually means the teacher knows your child properly, which is an advantage, and that there is no departmental colleague with spare capacity for sustained one-to-one work during a term, which is the gap external support fills.

faqs.question: When should an Al Ain MYP 3 student start thinking about the Diploma?
faqs.answer: In MYP 3, at least in outline, because the standard-or-extended decision arrives in MYP 4 and not every Al Ain campus runs the Diploma above the Middle Years years. Two questions matter: what does the criterion evidence say about unfamiliar problems and about justification, and where is this student likely to be at 16 — the same campus, an Abu Dhabi island school, or a local A-Level route. Higher Level Analysis and Approaches expects the algebraic fluency the extended route builds, so the destination informs the route.

faqs.question: What happens to MYP maths tutoring during Ramadan in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Sessions move to post-Iftar timing rather than stopping. Ramadan shifts about eleven days earlier each year, so its position in the school term changes annually and has to be checked rather than assumed. Shorter, later sessions in that month preserve two or three weeks of continuity that families often write off in advance, and they work better than trying to hold a 5pm slot during fasting hours. Al Ain term dates vary between campuses, so any plan is built from your school's own published calendar.

faqs.question: Who do I complain to about an Al Ain private school?
faqs.answer: The Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, including Al Ain. Take school licensing, fee and conduct matters there. Questions about a criterion level, an internal task date or a route decision go to the school first, because those are the school's judgements. Questions about the Middle Years assessment rules themselves go to the IB through the school's programme coordinator. Families regularly take all three to the same office and get an unhelpful answer.

faqs.question: How do I check an Al Ain tutor is legally allowed to teach?
faqs.answer: Ask for the private tuition work permit reference. The permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued by the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation through its smart app, website and e-services system, and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Tutoring without one brings fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule is published, so treat any quoted amount as invention.

faqs.question: Does MYP mathematics in Al Ain lead to IGCSE or to the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Either, and in this city that is a real decision rather than a formality. Fewer Al Ain campuses run the Diploma than run the years beneath it, so some students finish MYP 5 and continue to the Diploma on the same campus, some move to an Abu Dhabi island school, and some switch to a local IGCSE and A-Level route. The extended Middle Years route suits a student heading for Higher Level Analysis and Approaches or a demanding A-Level start. Ask the school which route your child is on and when entry is confirmed.

al-ain/ib-myp-mathematics-tutor.closingHeading: Start with the school's four numbers and its calendar
al-ain/ib-myp-mathematics-tutor.closingBody: If you are looking for an IB MYP mathematics tutor in Al Ain, two free requests make everything afterwards easier. Ask the school for the criterion A, B, C and D levels separately, and for its term calendar with the next assessed task date and criterion on it. Send those, and the free first lesson will be spent on your child's own marked work rather than on a placement test, ending with a written statement of which criterion to target. Sessions run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, built around the Al Ain school run, the mandatory-subject timetable and Ramadan's position in that year.

intro.heading: Why an MYP report is harder to read than any other school report
paragraphs: A parent in Al Ain who receives a Middle Years Programme report sees eight subject groups, a grade from one to seven in each, and four letters with numbers beside them. Nothing on the page explains what the letters mean, why a child scored six on one criterion and three on another in the same subject, or what to do about it. The report is accurate and detailed, and it is almost unusable without a translation. That translation is the first thing an IB MYP tutor in Al Ain should be providing, before any teaching happens at all.

The system is criterion-referenced rather than norm-referenced. Each subject group has four criteria, A to D, with their own published strand descriptors, and each is marked out of eight. The four marks add to a raw total out of thirty-two, which the school converts to a grade from one to seven using the published boundary table. Nothing is averaged against the rest of the class. A student is measured against a written description of what the work has to show, which is the fairest system in secondary education and the least intuitive to read from outside.

Two consequences follow, and both surprise parents. The first is that a child can produce visibly better work than last term and still see the grade fall, because the units assessed that term weighted different criteria. A Sciences unit assessed on Criterion A, knowing and understanding, measures something quite different from one assessed on Criterion B, inquiring and designing. Marks move when the thing being measured moves. The second is that revision, in the sense a parent remembers it, is close to useless here. There is nothing to revise for a Criterion C task; there is a skill to build.

Al Ain adds its own texture. The city is part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so every private school here is inspected by the Department of Education and Knowledge rather than KHDA, and the number of IB World Schools running the MYP locally is small. Several Al Ain schools run the MYP to Year 9 and then move students onto Cambridge or Pearson international GCSE papers for Years 10 and 11, rather than continuing to MYP Year 5. That fork changes what MYP support should be aiming at, and it is the single most important thing to establish before booking anything.

This page sets out the criteria group by group, the boundary arithmetic, why a band drops without the work worsening, what the Personal Project is and where a tutor must stop, the honest size of the gap from MYP into the Diploma, and what support costs in this market with every AED figure attributed. Lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; visiting tutors are a service offered only in India.
bullets: Four criteria per subject group, each marked out of eight, totalling thirty-two
The total converts to a one-to-seven grade using the published boundary table
Not every unit assesses every criterion, which is why bands move
Several Al Ain schools leave the MYP after Year 9 for IGCSE papers
Lessons are one-to-one over live video at Gulf Standard Time

al-ain/ib-myp-tutor.programmesIntro: Three programmes bracket an Al Ain MYP student: the Primary Years Programme behind them, the MYP itself, and whichever of the Diploma or international GCSE the school moves them onto. The notes below are about the joins between them.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups studied each year, each assessed against four criteria marked out of eight, with at least one interdisciplinary unit and a culminating project. Approaches to learning skills are taught across subjects in five categories: thinking, communication, social, self-management and research. Service as action runs alongside. Nothing in the programme is assessed by a single terminal examination unless the school opts into the IB's on-screen assessments.
programmes.countryNote: In Al Ain the MYP is offered by a small number of IB World Schools, which has a practical effect families notice quickly: there is rarely a classmate at another local school working on the same unit, so comparing notes across schools is not available in the way it is for IGCSE cohorts. It also means local MYP-specialist tutors are genuinely scarce, more so than for IGCSE subjects.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led and transdisciplinary, with no criterion marks of the MYP kind and no numerical grades in most schools. The move into MYP Year 1 is therefore the first time a student meets a four-criterion mark scheme, and the first time a parent sees a grade from one to seven. The content step is mild; the assessment step is not.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain families moving a child from a PYP school into MYP Year 1 most often ask for help in the first term of the new year, when the grades arrive and look lower than the primary reports suggested. In almost every case the work has not deteriorated; the measurement has changed. One or two sessions explaining the criteria to the student directly often does more than a term of subject tuition.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at Higher and Standard Level with Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Assessment returns to examination papers with internal assessment attached, graded one to seven per subject, out of a maximum total of forty-five. The criteria habits built in the MYP transfer directly to Diploma internal assessment, which is the strongest argument for taking MYP criteria seriously in Year 9.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain's Diploma cohorts are small and option blocks are tight, so a student who wants a particular Higher Level combination may find the local timetable will not permit it. An MYP student aiming at Higher Level sciences is worth steering early, because subject choices made in MYP Year 4 narrow the Diploma options available two years later.

programmes.name: International GCSE
programmes.description: The route several Al Ain schools take after MYP Year 3, under Cambridge or Pearson. Assessment flips from criterion-referenced coursework to terminal papers with mark schemes and tiered entry, Core or Extended. A student who has spent three years being assessed against descriptors meets, for the first time, a scheme that awards marks for specific stated points in a specific order.
programmes.countryNote: This is the fork that defines MYP tutoring in Al Ain. Ask your school directly whether your child continues to MYP Year 5 and the Personal Project, or transfers to IGCSE papers in Year 10. The answer changes what the next two years of support should be building, and the two destinations reward almost opposite habits.

al-ain/ib-myp-tutor.subjectsIntro: Each MYP subject group has its own four criteria with its own wording. The notes below name them and say where Al Ain students most often lose marks, which is rarely where the parent expects.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Criteria are A knowing and understanding, B investigating patterns, C communicating, D applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Most marks are lost on B and D, not A. A student who can solve the equations can still score three on B because the general rule was never stated and justified, which is what the descriptor asks for.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: A knowing and understanding, B inquiring and designing, C processing and evaluating, D reflecting on the impacts of science. B and C are where the drop happens: a hypothesis without a scientific reason behind it, and a conclusion that restates the data instead of evaluating method and reliability.

subjects.name: Language and Literature
subjects.description: A analysing, B organizing, C producing text, D using language. Strong writers often score lowest on A, because analysis means explaining the effect of a writer's choices rather than describing what happens. Al Ain students arriving from systems that reward summary feel this most sharply.

subjects.name: Language Acquisition
subjects.description: A listening, B reading, C speaking, D writing, assessed by phase rather than by year group. A student can be in Phase 4 for reading and Phase 2 for speaking, and the single reported grade hides that. Asking the school which phase applies per criterion is the useful question.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: A knowing and understanding, B investigating, C communicating, D thinking critically. D is the criterion that separates grades here. Source evaluation that names the origin and purpose of a source, rather than calling it biased, is the specific skill the descriptor rewards.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: A inquiring and analysing, B developing ideas, C creating the solution, D evaluating. The design cycle is the mark scheme, and students who build an excellent product while skipping the research and specification stages score poorly. The documentation is not paperwork; it is where most of the marks live.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: A investigating, B developing, C creating or performing, D evaluating. The process journal carries marks in its own right. A finished piece with no recorded development behind it cannot reach the upper strands of B, however accomplished the outcome is.

subjects.name: Physical and Health Education
subjects.description: A knowing and understanding, B planning for performance, C applying and performing, D reflecting and improving performance. Written work counts here, which surprises parents whose children are physically capable and score mid-band because the planning and reflection components were treated as optional.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.description: Mandatory alongside the international curriculum for the groups the regulator specifies, and in Al Ain a heavily requested stream. A student may sit Arabic as a first language under Language and Literature criteria or in Language Acquisition phases, and the two are marked against entirely different descriptors.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary units
subjects.description: Marked against their own four criteria rather than the contributing subjects' criteria, which is why a separate grade appears on the report. Students lose marks by writing two subject essays side by side instead of producing one piece that genuinely integrates both disciplines.

al-ain/ib-myp-tutor.regionsIntro: Where a family lives in Al Ain decides which campuses are realistic and what time a weekday session can start. For MYP students, who typically finish school earlier than Diploma students, the practical slot is earlier in the evening.

regions.name: Al Jimi
regions.note: Central, close to several long-established campuses, with short school runs. A four o'clock start is realistic here, which suits an MYP student better than a seven o'clock slot does.

regions.name: Falaj Hazza
regions.note: South-west, with overlapping catchments and families weighing an MYP school against a British-curriculum one. The Year 9 fork between continuing MYP and moving to IGCSE is a live question in these households.

regions.name: Asharej
regions.note: East of the centre, near United Arab Emirates University. Academic households here tend to ask about the MYP-to-Diploma join early, often in MYP Year 3 rather than Year 5.

regions.name: Al Muwaiji
regions.note: Western and heavily Emirati, with high demand for Arabic as a first language alongside the MYP subject groups. Two Arabic streams in one family is common, marked against different descriptors.

regions.name: Zakher
regions.note: Southern villa belt with long runs to the central campuses. Siblings at different MYP years often share one evening, which works because MYP sessions are typically shorter than Diploma ones.

regions.name: Al Mutaredh
regions.note: Older central district near the Al Ain Oasis. Households here frequently have one child still in the MYP and an older one already on IGCSE papers at a different campus.

regions.name: Al Towayya
regions.note: Near the hospital campus, where shift rotas shape the week. A fixed weekly video slot survives a changed rota better than an arrangement requiring anyone to travel.

regions.name: Hili
regions.note: Northern Al Ain near the Buraimi crossing. Some households cross the border daily, which makes an early fixed online slot more reliable than a late one.

The set is small compared with Abu Dhabi island, which is why MYP-specific tutoring demand in Al Ain is concentrated in a handful of year groups.
