al-ain/ib-tutor.programmesIntro: Three IB programmes appear in Al Ain schools, plus the Diploma core that sits across all six subjects. A student's position on the timeline means something different in each one. The notes below give the age range, what the programme actually assesses, and what the Al Ain picture looks like at that stage, including where the city's smaller school set makes a subject harder to staff locally.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The Primary Years Programme is organised around transdisciplinary units rather than separate subject syllabuses, and it reports against learner attributes and approaches to learning instead of numbered grades. Support at this stage is almost never about content coverage. It is about English reading fluency, number facts held in memory, and the habit of recording a method so it can be checked later. Those three things are what a Middle Years teacher inherits, and they are far cheaper to build at nine than to repair at fifteen.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain's primary intake is unusually mixed: a high Emirati household share in districts such as Falaj Hazzaa and Al Muwaiji, long-settled Indian and Pakistani families in Al Towayya, and university households around Asharej. Children arrive in the same Year 4 classroom from three different early-years systems, so the gap a parent notices in Year 5 is often a mismatch in prior curriculum rather than ability. Naming which system a child came from is the first diagnostic question we ask here.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The Middle Years Programme marks each subject against four criteria, A to D, on a one-to-eight scale, and those criterion marks are the only numeric evidence a family has before the Diploma begins. A six in criterion A with a three in criterion D is a specific, fixable problem, usually in communication or in reflection rather than in knowing the material. Year five of the programme, with its personal project, is where workload management is first tested properly and where most Al Ain referrals to us begin.
programmes.countryNote: Several Al Ain schools run Middle Years alongside a British Year 10 and 11 stream in the same building, so siblings in one Al Ain household may sit criterion-marked assessments and IGCSE papers in the same term. That makes the family calendar harder than the academic work. We schedule those households back to back on one evening so a single quiet room covers both lessons, which matters in the villa districts where study space is genuinely contested.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: The Diploma asks for six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard, graded one to seven, with externally marked papers in the final May session and internally assessed work completed during the two years. Higher Level is not Standard Level with extra homework. It carries extra syllabus content, an extra paper in most sciences, and a different expectation of independence in the internal assessment. The decision about which three sit at Higher Level is the single largest determinant of how many tutoring hours a family ends up buying.
programmes.countryNote: Al Ain has far fewer IB World Schools than Abu Dhabi island, and the shortage shows in a predictable pattern: Higher Level Physics, Higher Level Chemistry, Economics and the less common languages are the subjects families here struggle to staff within driving distance. That is the specific gap a live online match closes. A student in Al Maqam can work with a Higher Level Physics specialist without anyone estimating how long the drive from the city centre takes at six in the evening.

programmes.name: The Diploma core
programmes.description: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and creativity, activity and service run across both Diploma years and sit outside the six subjects. Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay together carry up to three bonus points on the total, and a failing condition in either can cost the whole Diploma regardless of subject grades. Families consistently underestimate the core because it has no weekly lesson and no obvious homework, which is exactly why its deadlines are the ones that collide with everything else.
programmes.countryNote: Core deadlines in Al Ain schools cluster in the same months as everywhere else in the emirate, but the supervisor pool is smaller, so an Extended Essay in a specialised topic may be supervised by a teacher outside that field. Independent subject review is most useful at the research-question stage, before a student has spent eight weeks on a question that cannot be answered in four thousand words. A tutor comments and questions; the drafting stays with the student.

al-ain/ib-tutor.subjectsIntro: The subject list below reflects what Al Ain households actually request, in rough order of volume, with the level split and the place on the timeline where each one usually starts to hurt. Each note names what the subject assesses and where marks go missing, because that is the detail that tells you whether one term of support is enough or whether you are looking at a two-year plan.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Proof, calculus and algebraic fluency carry this course, and the Higher Level paper set rewards students who can move between an algebraic and a graphical argument quickly. Marks disappear in unjustified steps rather than wrong answers. The exploration is where a weak start in stage three shows up most visibly, because a poorly chosen topic limits the mathematics available to demonstrate.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics and technology use define this route, and the graphic display calculator is assumed rather than optional. Students who moved across from a Middle Years course often arrive fluent in procedure but unused to interpreting output in context, which is where the command terms bite. Higher Level adds substantial statistical inference that cannot be learned in the final term.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The hardest topic for Al Ain students is rarely mechanics; it is the combination of fields, circuits and the quantitative treatment of waves. Higher Level carries additional content and an additional paper, and the data-analysis questions reward practice with uncertainty and gradient work. This is the subject most often unavailable locally, and the one most commonly matched online.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and energetics generate the most requests, but the marks most reliably recovered sit in stoichiometry and in reading multi-step calculation questions carefully. The internal assessment needs a measurable, controllable variable chosen early; students who leave the choice late end up with data that cannot support an analysis section.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: A content-heavy course where the limiting factor is almost always recall structure rather than understanding. Students who build their own topic summaries from the syllabus statements outperform those revising from class notes. Extended-response questions need command-term discipline: explain, outline and evaluate each earn marks for different things and students answer all three the same way.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy and the internal assessment commentaries decide most grades here. Students lose marks by drawing a diagram that does not match the article in front of them, or by writing evaluation that lists both sides without reaching a judgement. Higher Level adds quantitative content that families rarely budget hours for until the first mock comes back.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Tool-based answers, where a student is expected to apply a named framework to a given organisation rather than describe it, separate grades in the upper bands. The Higher Level internal assessment is a research project on a real organisation and needs its scope agreed early. Al Ain students often choose a family business, which works well when the data is genuinely available.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Two assessed orals and a paper on unseen non-literary texts make this a skills course disguised as a reading list. The individual oral is where preparation pays most, because the extract and the global issue are chosen by the student. Higher Level adds the essay on a studied work, which demands an argument rather than a summary of the text.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: Al Ain requests Arabic more often than most UAE cities, and the split matters: Arabic A is a language and literature course for first-language speakers, while Arabic B is an acquisition course with a different assessment structure. Matching the wrong route wastes a term. The written assignment and the oral components reward sustained, structured practice rather than vocabulary drilling.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: The programming solution dominates the internal assessment, and students frequently build something impressive that documents poorly. Paper questions on data structures, resource management and system fundamentals need taught content rather than coding practice. Higher Level adds abstract data structures and a case study set annually, which rewards starting early.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Three bonus points sit here and a failing condition can cost the Diploma, yet neither component has weekly homework to keep it visible. The highest-value intervention is at the question stage: a research question that is too broad is the most common reason an Extended Essay underperforms. Support is comment and challenge on the student's own drafting.

al-ain/ib-tutor.regionsIntro: Al Ain is spread out, and the district a family lives in changes when tutoring can realistically happen and often when in the year they start. The notes below describe that pattern rather than the character of each neighbourhood, because the scheduling question is the one that decides whether a weekly slot survives past February.

regions.name: Al Jimi
regions.note: Central and close to several long-established private campuses, so pick-up is short and a five o'clock weekday start holds even in exam term. Families here tend to begin in stage two, when the first Diploma reports land, and keep the same slot through to May.

regions.name: Al Mutaredh
regions.note: Villa district near the oasis and the main hospital, with a high share of medical and university households. Shift patterns make a fixed early-evening slot more valuable than a flexible one, and Higher Level sciences dominate the requests that come from here.

regions.name: Asharej
regions.note: Next to the United Arab Emirates University campus, so a parent or older sibling is frequently on the UAEU timetable. Quiet study space at home is contested in the late afternoon, which pushes sessions past seven and makes the maths route choice an unusually live question here.

regions.name: Al Towayya
regions.note: Established residential area where British and Indian curriculum timetables often run in the same household. Siblings are best booked back to back on one evening. Enquiries from Al Towayya arrive earliest in the timeline, usually during Middle Years rather than the Diploma.

regions.name: Falaj Hazzaa
regions.note: Large villa neighbourhood with a strong Emirati household share, so Arabic as a first language and Islamic Education sit alongside Diploma subjects in the same week. We coordinate timing so tuition does not collide with the school's own Arabic support sessions.

regions.name: Al Muwaiji
regions.note: West of the centre and a longer run back from the newer campuses on the city edge. A five-thirty start is safer than a four-thirty one. We set the first session late and bring it forward once the family has seen the real arrival time for a fortnight.

regions.name: Zakher
regions.note: On the southern edge towards Jebel Hafeet, with the longest school commute in the city for children at central campuses. Weekday work realistically begins at six, and many Zakher households move the heavier revision blocks to Friday or Saturday mornings.

regions.name: Hili and Al Foah
regions.note: Northern districts towards the Omani border crossing. Families here drive further for school than anyone else in Al Ain, and removing the second journey is the main practical gain from working over video. Winter sunset timings change what counts as a late slot.

regions.name: Al Khabisi and Al Maqam
regions.note: Inner districts with a mix of apartment and villa housing and short runs to the central schools. These households are the most likely to want two subjects in one evening, which works if the two tutors hand over through a shared note rather than duplicating diagnosis.

al-ain/ib-tutor.modesIntro: Three formats cover almost every Al Ain request, and the right one depends far more on where your child sits on the timeline than on budget. A student eighteen months out and a student eleven weeks out should not be buying the same thing, and the commonest mistake is paying stage-four prices for stage-two work.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one, held all year
modes.description: A fixed slot in the same subject each week, running from the point a gap is identified through to the final session. This is the format that suits stages one to three, because its value comes from nothing compounding rather than from intensity. The tutor holds a running record of what has been covered and what the school has set, so each session starts from the current week rather than from a fresh diagnosis.

modes.title: Coursework review blocks

The work reviewed is the student's own at every stage: a tutor questions the research question, points at the criterion a paragraph is failing to address, and explains what the criterion wants. No finished text is supplied.

This is stage four and it is the most expensive hour a family buys, which is why the page above spends so long on the earlier stages. It works when the content is broadly in place and technique is the limiting factor, and it works poorly when half the syllabus is missing.

sections.heading: Reading the report you already have
paragraphs: Before any decision about tutoring, read the document in front of you properly. A Middle Years report gives criterion marks out of eight in four strands per subject; a Diploma report gives a predicted grade out of seven plus component feedback. These are different measurements and they answer different questions. A criterion mark tells you which skill is weak. A predicted grade tells you what a teacher currently expects in May, which is a forecast rather than a measurement.

The most common misreading in Al Ain households is treating a Diploma four as a slightly worse five. It is not. A four in a Higher Level science usually means one or two whole topics are absent rather than that everything is slightly shaky, and the fix is a content audit against the syllabus before any past-paper work begins. Equally common is reading a strong criterion A mark as evidence that a subject is safe, when criterion D is the one that most often limits the final grade.

The table below sets out what a reported mark at each stage is measured against, and what it does not yet tell you. Use it to generate one question for the subject teacher rather than a general enquiry. A teacher asked which two syllabus topics are weakest will usually answer specifically; a teacher asked whether a child needs a tutor will usually say it could not hurt. The first answer is worth a term of correctly aimed work.

sections.heading: Stage one: the months before the Diploma starts
paragraphs: The cheapest hours a family will ever buy sit in Middle Years four and five, or in Year 11 for a British-stream student heading into the Diploma. There is no exam pressure, nothing compounds, and the three things that most reliably limit a Diploma grade two years later are all fixable here: algebraic fluency, the ability to write a structured analytical paragraph, and the discipline of recording a method so it can be checked.

Algebra is the clearest case. A student entering Diploma mathematics who still rearranges equations slowly will lose time on every paper for two years, regardless of which route they take. Fixing that takes perhaps a term of weekly work at fifteen. Working around it at eighteen costs several times as much and never fully succeeds, because the Higher Level papers assume the fluency rather than testing it.

Subject choice is the other stage-one decision, and it is where the Al Ain school picture matters most. A smaller private-school set means fewer Higher Level options actually run, and a student may be steered towards the combination the timetable permits rather than the one their university plans need. This is worth a conversation before options are submitted, because unwinding a Higher Level choice six months into the Diploma is the single most disruptive thing that can happen to a two-year timeline. The maths route decision deserves particular attention: Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation are accepted differently by different degree courses, and that is a question for the universities on the student's list rather than for a general rule.

sections.heading: Stage two: keeping the first Diploma year level
paragraphs: The first Diploma year is where content load doubles and where almost nobody asks for help early enough. A student who was comfortable in Middle Years meets six subjects at once, three of them at Higher Level, and the gap between following a lesson and being able to reproduce the argument unaided opens quietly. By the first set of internal tests it has usually opened in two subjects, not six, which is useful information if anyone is looking for it.

The work at this stage is maintenance rather than rescue, and it looks unexciting: one subject, one hour a week, covering what the school covered, with the student reproducing the method rather than watching it. The test of whether it is working is not confidence. It is whether the student can do last week's question cold at the start of this week's session. That check takes four minutes and is the only honest early indicator available.

Stage two is also when the first internal deadlines appear and are underestimated. A science internal assessment proposal, a maths exploration topic or an Extended Essay research question submitted in the first year sets the ceiling for a piece of work marked in the second. A weak research question cannot be fixed later by good writing. Getting independent challenge on that question while it is still a sentence, rather than after eight weeks of data collection, is the highest-value hour in the whole stage.

sections.heading: Stage three: the coursework middle, counted backwards
paragraphs: The middle of the second Diploma year is where timelines actually break. New teaching continues while coursework from every subject arrives, and because each department sets its own internal deadline, three or four pieces routinely converge on the same fortnight. No individual deadline is unreasonable. The collision is what does the damage, and it is entirely predictable from a calendar nobody builds.

Build it. Ask each subject teacher for their internal deadline, write all of them on one page with the school's own mock window marked, and work backwards. A science internal assessment needs its variable chosen and data collected weeks before writing starts. A maths exploration needs the mathematics to exist before the topic is fixed. An Extended Essay needs a complete first draft long before the final submission, because the supervisor's comments on that draft are the main mechanism by which it improves.

A tutor's role across this stage is narrow and should be stated plainly. The research question can be challenged. The criterion a paragraph is failing to address can be named, with the published criterion wording explained. A method can be questioned for validity. What cannot happen is any part of the text arriving from the tutor: assessed work must be the student's own, and IB academic-honesty rules make a breach here a malpractice matter for the student rather than a style question for us. Writing the boundary down before the first session protects the student more than any amount of reassurance.

sections.heading: Stage four: the last twelve weeks, week by week
paragraphs: The final stretch before the May papers is the stage families imagine when they search for a tutor, and it is the one with the least room in it. Twelve weeks at two sessions a week is twenty-four hours. Spread across three subjects that is eight hours per subject, which buys technique and targeted repair. It does not buy a missing syllabus, and any provider who implies otherwise is selling the wrong thing.

What works here is narrow and repetitive. One session teaches the specific topics the last timed paper exposed; the second session is a paper written under timed conditions and marked against the published mark scheme, with the marks lost listed individually. The list is the product. A student who can say that six marks went on command terms and four on unit errors has something to act on; a student who felt the paper went badly has nothing.

The block below is the shape we use when a family arrives with roughly twelve weeks left. It front-loads content repair, moves to full papers in the middle, and in the last fortnight does almost nothing new, because new material introduced in the final two weeks displaces secure material and reliably costs more than it adds. Confirm the actual session dates with your child's IB coordinator: the May window and the results release are set by the IB, and no date in this project has been verified against the IB's own publications.

sections.heading: What the whole timeline costs at Al Ain market rates
paragraphs: Private tuition in the UAE is priced by the hour and the published spread is wide. The figures below are what other providers publish, with the provider type attached, and they are given as market context rather than as our price list. Read them against the timeline: the same hourly figure buys very different value at stage one and stage four, and the total a family spends is decided far more by when they start than by which tier they pick.

Working the arithmetic through is instructive. One hour a week for a single subject across both Diploma years is roughly seventy teaching weeks, so even at the lower qualified-tutor band the total is substantial. Twelve weeks of twice-weekly work across three subjects in stage four is seventy-two hours bought at the highest band, compressed into one term, usually on top of whatever was already being paid. The expensive route is not the specialist tier. It is the late start.

A home visit sits at the top of the range because travel time is inside the price, and in a city as spread out as Al Ain that is a real component rather than a rounding error. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; lessons are delivered live online, and home tutoring is a service we provide only in India. That means the figure a family compares is the online band, with the specialist pool no longer limited to people living within a reasonable drive of the house.

sections.heading: Distance, the school run and where the weekly slot really goes
paragraphs: A weekly slot survives the year or it does not, and in Al Ain the thing that kills it is almost always the drive. Families book a four-thirty session in September because school finishes at two-forty, then discover in October that between the bus, the sibling pick-up and the actual arrival home, four-thirty means a student walking through the door at four twenty-eight. Two missed sessions later the slot moves to a weekend, where it competes with everything else, and by December it has quietly stopped.

The fix is unglamorous: set the first slot later than feels necessary, hold it for a fortnight, and bring it forward only once the family has seen the real arrival time. Across the outer districts that usually means a six o'clock start rather than four-thirty, which is perfectly workable over video and impossible for a visiting tutor who has somewhere else to be at seven. The format is what makes the honest time available.

Ramadan moves the whole pattern. School hours shorten, energy in the late afternoon drops, and most households prefer to work after Iftar. We move slots rather than pausing them, because a four-week gap in stage three is expensive and a shifted time costs nothing. The same applies to travel: families who spend part of the summer abroad keep the slot and change only the clock it is set against. Winter changes it again in the other direction, because sunset arrives early and what counted as a late slot in May feels ordinary in January. None of this needs renegotiating each time if the weekly time is agreed as a working arrangement rather than a fixed appointment, and the tutor holds the same record either way.

sections.heading: When the timeline is genuinely too short
paragraphs: Sometimes a family arrives with five weeks, two Higher Level subjects in trouble and a predicted grade that will not carry the offer they are holding. The useful response is not optimism. It is triage: decide which single subject moves the total most, put the hours there, and leave the others on maintenance. Spreading five weeks across three subjects produces three small improvements and no change to the outcome that matters.

The second honest conversation is about what else exists. A predicted grade can be discussed with the school if there is evidence it is out of date, and universities differ widely in how they treat a missed condition. Retake routes exist for both the Diploma and individual subjects, and a planned retake with a proper timeline is a better outcome than a panicked term. None of this is advice IB Gram can give on a university's behalf, and we point families to the school's university counsellor for it.

There is also the paperwork that an Al Ain leaver will need regardless of grade. Students taking a British-track route to a UAE university need equivalency from the Ministry of Education, and the published British-track requirement is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or grade three, with Arabic and Islamic Education excluded from that count, plus one subject at Advanced Level at grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. No IB points threshold for equivalency has been read on the Ministry's own pages, so we do not publish one. Equivalency is a process families complete through the Ministry's own channel; it is not something a tutoring service performs on anyone's behalf, and no part of it requires tutoring.

process.title: Say where on the line your child sits
process.description: The first message we need is the stage, the subjects and the next fixed date. Middle Years four with weak algebra and no deadline is a different request from Diploma two with a mock in three weeks. Naming the stage lets us match a tutor whose experience fits it rather than one who merely teaches the subject.

process.title: Send the evidence you already have
process.description: A recent report, a marked paper or the criterion marks from a Middle Years subject tell a tutor more in two minutes than a conversation does in twenty. A marked paper is the most useful single document, because the pattern of lost marks is visible on it rather than inferred.

process.title: Trial the match before paying
process.description: One lesson at no charge, with no card details taken beforehand, one per family. It runs as a working session rather than a sales call: the tutor diagnoses, teaches something, and sets out what the next six weeks would contain. If the match is wrong, say so and we change the tutor rather than the student.

process.title: Fix the slot against the real arrival time
process.description: We set the weekly time against when your child is genuinely home and able to work, which in the outer Al Ain districts is later than the school day suggests. Hold it for two weeks before adjusting. A slot that survives February is worth more than one that looked ideal in September.

process.title: Review against the timeline, not the feeling
process.description: Every few weeks the question is the same: can the student do the work from three weeks ago, cold, today? That check is quick and honest, and it is the only early signal worth anything. If the answer stays no, the plan changes rather than continuing at a higher intensity.

whyPoints.title: The stage decides the plan
whyPoints.description: A Middle Years student and a Diploma candidate eleven weeks from a paper need different tutors, different session shapes and different hours. We match against the stage on the timeline rather than selling one format to everyone, and we say plainly when an earlier start would have cost a family less.

whyPoints.title: Al Ain's subject gaps closed by format
whyPoints.description: The city's smaller private-school set means Higher Level Physics, Higher Level Chemistry, Economics and the less common languages are hard to staff within driving distance. Live online one-to-one removes the radius entirely, so the match is made on subject and level rather than on who happens to live nearby.

whyPoints.title: Coursework boundaries written down
whyPoints.description: What a tutor may and may not do with an internal assessment, Extended Essay or Theory of Knowledge essay is agreed in writing before the first session. Review, challenge and criterion explanation are in scope. Supplying text that will be assessed is not, under any circumstances or deadline pressure.

whyPoints.title: Figures with their sources attached
whyPoints.description: Every AED figure on this page is market context from a named provider, not our price. Nothing about outcomes is promised, no statistic appears without a source, and no regulator approval is claimed. IB Gram holds no accreditation from ADEK, the Ministry of Education, the IB or any examination board.

whyPoints.title: Scheduling built for this city
whyPoints.description: Slots are set against the real arrival time from the school run, moved rather than paused through Ramadan, and kept across a family's travel. In a city where the drive home differs by half an hour between Al Jimi and Hili, that is the difference between a weekly habit and a cancelled plan.

whyPoints.title: Permits treated as a question to answer
whyPoints.description: Private tutoring in the UAE runs on the MoHRE private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years. We ask tutors for theirs and we tell parents to ask any provider the same question, including providers other than us.

faqs.question: My child is in DP1 with a 4 in Chemistry. How many weeks of work is a 6 realistically?
faqs.answer: Nobody can put a number of weeks on a grade, and anyone who does is guessing. What can be measured is the gap. A four in a Higher Level science usually means one or two whole syllabus topics are absent rather than that everything is slightly weak, so the first two sessions should be an audit against the syllabus statements rather than past papers. Once you know which topics are missing, the repair time is estimable: roughly two to three hours of taught work per absent topic, plus paper practice afterwards. In the first Diploma year there is normally time for that. The honest answer arrives after the audit, not before it.

faqs.question: How do I read my child's MYP grades to predict a Diploma score?
faqs.answer: Middle Years criterion marks do not convert to Diploma grades, and schools that publish a conversion table are offering a rough guide rather than a measurement. What the criterion marks do give you is a diagnosis. Look at the spread rather than the total: a strong criterion A with a weak criterion C or D points at communication, structure or reflection rather than at knowledge, and those are the skills the Diploma punishes hardest. A student with even marks across all four criteria at six or above is well placed for Higher Level. A student carrying a three in one criterion across several subjects has one fixable habit, not several subject problems.

faqs.question: When in the two-year Diploma does tutoring make the most difference?
faqs.answer: Measured per hour spent, the first Diploma year and the months before it. Work done then stops problems compounding, costs the lower market band rather than the specialist band, and leaves the second year free for coursework and technique. Measured by how families actually behave, most support is bought in the last twelve weeks, which is the most expensive hour available and the one with the least room to fix content. The pattern is well known and the arithmetic is unflattering: a late start usually costs more in total than an early one, because it buys specialist hours under deadline pressure instead of ordinary hours with time to spare.

faqs.question: We are eleven weeks into DP1 and already behind. Where do we start?
faqs.answer: Start with which subjects, not how much. Ask each teacher one question: which two syllabus topics is this student not yet secure in? Teachers answer that specifically, where they answer a general question about tutoring vaguely. Then pick the subject where the gap is widest and the level is highest, usually a Higher Level science or mathematics, and put one weekly hour there. Leave the rest alone for six weeks. Eleven weeks into the first year is early, nothing has compounded, and one subject done properly changes more than three subjects touched lightly. Add a second subject only once the first is holding week to week.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week does a Diploma student in Al Ain normally take?
faqs.answer: Through the first year and the coursework middle, one hour a week in one or two subjects is the common pattern, which is enough to stop content slipping without displacing school work. In the final twelve weeks families typically move to two sessions a week in the weakest subject: one teaching, one timed paper marked against the published mark scheme. More than three hours a week across all subjects is usually a sign the plan is wrong rather than insufficient, and it crowds out the independent practice that actually moves marks. The constraint in Al Ain is rarely appetite. It is the hour at which a student is home and able to concentrate.

faqs.question: What should be finished by the end of DP1 for a student to be on track?
faqs.answer: Roughly: first-year syllabus content secure enough to answer a question on it cold, an internal assessment topic or variable chosen and trialled in each science, a mathematics exploration topic identified with the mathematics it will use, and an Extended Essay research question agreed with a supervisor. Theory of Knowledge should have moved past general discussion to specific knowledge questions. None of that is a formal requirement, and schools set their own internal deadlines, but a student who finishes the first year with all five in place has a manageable second year. A student missing three of them is facing the convergence described above.

faqs.question: My child's predicted grades came back lower than expected. What can change them?
faqs.answer: A predicted grade is a teacher's forecast based on the evidence they hold, so what changes it is new evidence. That means performing better on the next internal assessment or mock paper, not a conversation. Ask what specifically produced the prediction: if it rests on one weak mock, the next one matters a great deal; if it reflects a pattern across the year, more is needed. Where a prediction is clearly out of date, the school can be asked to review it, and the person to raise that with is the subject teacher or university counsellor rather than a tutor. Universities also vary widely in how they treat a missed condition, which is worth checking early.

faqs.question: Is there any point starting tutoring in the final term of DP2?
faqs.answer: Yes, with a narrow aim. Final-term work buys technique: command-term discipline, timing, the specific question types that keep costing marks, and the structure of extended answers. It does not buy a missing syllabus, and a provider implying otherwise is selling the wrong product. The decision is about triage. Pick the single subject where a one-band move changes the total most, put the hours there, and keep everything else on maintenance. Spreading a short final term across three subjects reliably produces three small improvements and no change to the result that matters to the family.

faqs.question: How long does it take to find a Higher Level specialist for an Al Ain student?
faqs.answer: For the common Higher Level subjects, matching usually takes a few days, and the trial lesson is normally the slower step because it has to fit the family's real evening. For the subjects Al Ain is thinnest in, which tend to be Higher Level Physics, Higher Level Chemistry and the less common languages, it can take longer, and we say so rather than offering a generalist to fill the slot. Because lessons run over live video, the search is not limited to people living within driving distance of your district, which is the main reason the wait is shorter than it would be for a visiting tutor in this city.

faqs.question: What does two years of weekly one-to-one tuition cost at Al Ain market rates?
faqs.answer: Work it from published market bands rather than from a promise. One hour a week in a single subject across both Diploma years is roughly seventy teaching weeks. At the qualified online band that other providers publish, around AED 150 to 300 an hour, that is a substantial but predictable total, spread over twenty-four months. The same subject bought as seventy-two hours of specialist work compressed into a final term costs more and arrives when it can do less. These are market figures from named providers, not our price list; what IB Gram's own sessions cost is set at consultation, after the trial.

faqs.question: Can one tutor carry a student through both years of the Diploma?
faqs.answer: In a single subject, usually yes, and continuity is worth a lot. A tutor who has held the running record since the first year knows which topics were repaired, which internal deadline is next and how this student answers under time pressure, none of which transfers cleanly to a replacement. Across subjects it is different: Higher Level Physics and Higher Level English are not taught well by the same person, and a tutor offering every subject is usually offering none of them at specialist depth. Where two tutors are involved, they should hand over through one shared note rather than each running a separate diagnosis.

faqs.question: How do we fit tuition around the school run from Zakher or Hili?
faqs.answer: Set the slot later than the school day suggests and hold it. From Zakher and from Hili or Al Foah, the realistic weekday start is six or six-thirty rather than four-thirty, once the bus, the sibling pick-up and the actual arrival home are counted. A session that assumes a two-forty finish will be missed twice and then quietly abandoned. Because the lesson runs over video there is no second journey and no tutor who needs to be elsewhere at seven, so the late slot is genuinely available. Many families in these districts also move the heavier revision blocks to Friday or Saturday mornings.

faqs.question: What does a realistic weekly plan look like twelve weeks before the first paper?
faqs.answer: Twelve to nine weeks out: audit against syllabus statements and repair the topics found absent. Eight to six weeks out: section-by-section past-paper work on exactly those topics. Five to three weeks out: full papers under timed conditions, marked against the published mark scheme, with the marks lost itemised by cause. Two weeks out: command terms and the weakest paper only. The final week: nothing new, recall practice on secure material, and sleep protected. Two sessions a week per subject is the normal intensity. Confirm your own session dates with the school's IB coordinator rather than relying on any date published online, including ours.

faqs.question: Should we pause tutoring during the mock exam fortnight?
faqs.answer: Pause the teaching, keep the slot. A mock fortnight is when a student has the least capacity for new content and the most need for someone to read the papers afterwards. The useful pattern is to drop to a short session during the mocks themselves, then use the following week to go through each paper line by line while the questions are fresh. The output should be a written list of where marks went and why, by cause rather than by topic. Cancelling the slot entirely tends to mean it does not come back, which is the most common way a plan dies in February.

faqs.question: How do we know the tuition is working rather than just filling an evening?
faqs.answer: One test, applied every few weeks: can the student do a question from three weeks ago, cold, at the start of the session? Not recognise it, not follow it being worked through, but produce it. If yes, the work is landing. If no, something is wrong with the method rather than the quantity, and the plan should change rather than intensify. Confidence is not evidence, and neither is a student enjoying the sessions. Marks on timed questions against published mark schemes, and that cold-recall check, are the only early indicators worth tracking in the first half of a plan.

faqs.question: My child wants to add a subject back to Higher Level. Is that recoverable?
faqs.answer: It depends almost entirely on when. In the first term of the first Diploma year it is usually recoverable with a term of concentrated work, because the Higher Level content that Standard Level students skip has barely begun. Later in the first year it is harder and needs the school's agreement as well as the extra teaching. Part-way through the second year it is rarely sensible, because the additional content and the different internal assessment expectations arrive on top of an existing timeline. The school decides whether a change is permitted at all; what a tutor can tell you is how many hours the gap would take to close.

al-ain/ib-tutor.closingHeading: Start by counting the weeks, not the subjects
al-ain/ib-tutor.closingBody: If you take one thing from this page, let it be the first move: find out where your child sits on the two-year line and when the next fixed date falls, before you buy a single hour. Ask each teacher which two syllabus topics are not yet secure. Write every internal deadline on one page. Then decide what the weeks in between have to contain. We will give you an honest read on that in the trial lesson, which runs at no charge, one per family, with no card details taken first. If the timeline is too short for what you are hoping for, we would rather say so in that session than sell you a term that cannot deliver it.

al-ain/ib-tutor-near-me.heroSubtitle: Typing "IB tutor near me" into a phone in Al Ain produces a map, and the map is the least useful thing on the screen. Distance is a poor proxy for whether somebody can teach Higher Level Chemistry to a Diploma candidate, and in a city this spread out with this few IB World Schools, the nearest option and the right option are rarely the same person. This page sets out exactly what the radius costs you and when it is worth paying.

al-ain/ib-tutor-near-me.tutorsIntro: The tutors listed below are matched on subject and level rather than on postcode, because a Diploma Higher Level match made inside a twenty-minute radius of an Al Ain villa is a very short list. Each profile names what that person teaches, so you can compare a specific match against whatever your local search returned.

intro.heading: The map is answering a different question
paragraphs: A proximity search is a sensible instinct applied to the wrong problem. For a plumber, a dentist or a car service, distance is a genuine measure of convenience and the skill is broadly comparable across providers. For Diploma teaching it is neither. The variable that decides whether an hour is worth buying is whether the person has taught that subject at that level to that assessment model, repeatedly, and that variable has no relationship at all to how far away they live.

In Al Ain the mismatch is unusually sharp, for two reasons that compound. The first is geography: this is a low-density city where Zakher in the south, Hili in the north and the central school cluster are a substantial drive apart, and at school-run time that drive is twenty to thirty minutes between districts. A twenty-minute radius around a villa in Al Maqam is a real constraint rather than a formality. The second is supply: Al Ain has far fewer IB World Schools than Abu Dhabi island, so the number of adults living here who teach Higher Level sciences, Higher Level mathematics, economics, computer science or psychology at Diploma depth is genuinely small.

Multiply those two and the arithmetic is unforgiving. The pool is small; the pool free at the hour your child is actually home is smaller; the pool free at that hour and within reach of your particular district is smaller still. What happens next is the part nobody describes out loud: the family does not wait, they substitute. A capable generalist takes the slot, the sessions feel productive, and the specific thing that was wrong in Higher Level Physics is still wrong in March.

The alternative is to drop the radius. Live one-to-one over video keeps the one-to-one attention and the at-home convenience, and matches on subject and level instead of geography. That is the service IB Gram provides to Al Ain families; we do not sell home visits in the UAE, where in-home tutoring is not part of our model, and we are explicit about the cases where a local visiting arrangement is the better answer. A distractible eight-year-old who will not sit at a table without an adult beside them is one of those cases.

The rest of this page is the detail a map cannot give you: what a local listing actually tells you and what it hides, which subjects the Al Ain pool covers adequately and which it does not, how long a match honestly takes for each, what the drive times do to the earliest workable slot in each district, and the five questions worth asking any candidate, local or not. Where proximity genuinely wins, it is said plainly. Where it genuinely wins, that is said plainly rather than argued around, because a page that recommends itself in every case is not advice.

al-ain/ib-tutor-near-me.programmesIntro: How much proximity matters depends almost entirely on the programme. At primary level the local pool is adequate and the convenience argument wins. By Diploma Higher Level the local pool is the constraint. The notes below set out each programme and then how the radius question plays out inside it.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Transdisciplinary units rather than separate syllabuses, with reporting against learner attributes instead of numbered grades. The useful targets are narrow and general: reading fluency, number facts held in memory, and the habit of recording a method. None of those requires subject specialism, and all of them benefit from an adult who can keep a young child on task for forty minutes.
programmes.countryNote: This is the one level where an Al Ain proximity search works well. The requirement is general, and the city has a large student population around the United Arab Emirates University, so households in Asharej and the central districts find local primary tutors without difficulty. We say so rather than arguing for video where it adds little, and the honest recommendation for a six-year-old is usually somebody nearby.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, marked one to eight, and the diagnosis is in the spread rather than the total. Knowing what criterion C rewards in a science investigation is specific knowledge rather than general teaching competence, so the pool who know a subject's criteria properly is smaller than the pool who know the subject. The radius starts to bite here.
programmes.countryNote: Several Al Ain schools run Middle Years and a British Year 10 and 11 stream in the same building, so a local tutor advertised for one is often assumed to cover the other. They are different assessment systems. Ask any candidate which of the two they have actually taught and for how many cohorts, and the local shortlist usually shortens by half.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, graded one to seven, with externally marked papers in May and internally assessed work across two years. Higher Level carries additional content, usually an extra paper in the sciences, and a different expectation of independence in the internal assessment. Specialism at the right level is the whole value of the hour, and a generalist cannot substitute for it.
programmes.countryNote: This is where the radius does real damage in Al Ain. The city's smaller IB school count means few resident adults teach Higher Level Physics, Chemistry, Economics, Computer Science or Psychology at Diploma depth, and those few are wanted by every family at the same hour of the same weekday. Removing the radius changes the pool from one city to one timezone.

programmes.name: The Diploma core
programmes.description: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and creativity, activity and service sit outside the six subjects, carry up to three bonus points, and have failing conditions capable of costing the whole Diploma. The support shape is episodic rather than weekly, which means a block of sessions at the research-question stage and another at the draft stage, not a standing appointment.
programmes.countryNote: Because core support is episodic, proximity matters even less here than elsewhere: nobody needs a person in the house for two hours in October and two more in February. What matters is finding somebody who knows the subject the essay sits in, which in Al Ain's smaller supervisor pool is exactly what the school may not be able to supply.

al-ain/ib-tutor-near-me.subjectsIntro: The list below is ordered by how well the pool of adults resident in Al Ain covers each subject at Diploma level, because that is the real content of a proximity search. Where the local pool is adequate, a nearby tutor is a reasonable choice. Where it is thin, the radius is what is limiting your options rather than your budget.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The thinnest Diploma subject in the Al Ain resident pool, and the one where substitution happens most. Higher Level adds content and an extra paper, and the data-analysis questions need practice with uncertainty and gradient work. A science teacher comfortable at Middle Years level is not interchangeable with one who teaches Higher Level fields and circuits.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Rarely available locally at Diploma depth. The programming solution dominates the internal assessment and documents badly without a supervisor who has seen one before, while paper questions on data structures and system fundamentals need taught content rather than coding practice. A local enthusiast and an experienced Diploma teacher are not close substitutes here.

subjects.name: Psychology
subjects.description: Requested steadily in Al Ain and almost never covered locally at Diploma level. Studies must be recalled precisely and used as evidence rather than retold, and the internal assessment is a replication with strict reporting conventions. Nearly every match in this subject is made beyond the city, which is simply a fact rather than a sales point.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy and the internal assessment commentaries decide most grades, and marks go on diagrams that do not match the article or on evaluation that never reaches a judgement. Higher Level adds quantitative content. Economics specialists are notably scarce among Al Ain residents, more so than business teachers.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Thin at Higher Level locally, better at Standard. Organic mechanisms and energetics generate requests; stoichiometry and careful reading of multi-step calculations are where marks come back. A teacher comfortable at IGCSE depth is a different proposition from one comfortable with Higher Level energetics.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Local maths availability is reasonable, but availability in this specific route at Higher Level is not. Proof, calculus and algebraic fluency carry the course, and marks go on unjustified steps rather than wrong answers. Ask which of the two Diploma maths routes a candidate has taught, because many have taught only one.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics and assumed calculator fluency define this route, with Higher Level adding statistical inference that cannot be absorbed late. Students crossing from Middle Years are often procedurally sound but unused to interpreting output in context. Coverage is moderate locally and better at Standard Level than at Higher.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The best-covered Diploma science in the local pool, so for biology a nearby tutor is often a genuine option. Recall structure rather than understanding is the usual limiting factor, and extended responses need command-term discipline because explain, outline and evaluate reward different things.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Reasonably covered locally, with the caveat that experience of the current assessment model rather than an older one is the question to ask. Two assessed orals and a paper on unseen non-literary texts make this a skills course, and the individual oral rewards preparation because the student chooses the extract and the global issue.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: First-language teaching capacity in Al Ain is strong; capacity for the Diploma assessment model specifically is narrower. The route matters, because Arabic A is language and literature for first-language speakers while Arabic B is an acquisition course with a different structure, and matching the wrong one wastes a term.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: More widely taught than economics, so the local pool is deeper. Upper-band answers apply a named framework to a given organisation rather than describing it, and the Higher Level research project needs its scope agreed early with genuine data available. At Higher Level, prior supervision of a research project still matters more than proximity.

al-ain/ib-tutor-near-me.regionsIntro: A proximity search is really a question about drive time, so the notes below describe each Al Ain district in exactly those terms: what a local arrangement would require there, and the earliest hour a weekday session can honestly begin. These are the numbers a map pin does not carry.

regions.name: Al Jimi
regions.note: Central and close to several established campuses, with the shortest gap between the bell and a student being ready to work. A proximity search returns the most options here, and a five o'clock session is realistic. This is the district where a nearby choice is least compromised.

regions.name: Al Khabisi
regions.note: Inner district with short runs to the central schools and a mix of apartments and villas. Two consecutive subjects on one evening is a common request. Local options exist at primary and lower-secondary level; at Diploma Higher Level the list collapses to the same few names as everywhere else.

regions.name: Al Mutaredh
regions.note: Villa area near the oasis and the main hospital, with many medical and university households on shift patterns. A local arrangement has to survive a changing rota, which is the specific thing that breaks after a month of rescheduling. A fixed slot the student keeps alone is worth more here.

regions.name: Asharej
regions.note: Beside the United Arab Emirates University campus, which makes the local pool unusually deep at primary and lower-secondary level and no deeper at Diploma Higher Level. Household study space is contested in the late afternoon, so seven o'clock is often the first genuinely quiet hour.

regions.name: Al Towayya
regions.note: Established district where British and Indian curriculum timetables often run in one household. Two siblings on different systems need two specialists, and expecting one nearby tutor to cover both is the commonest way a local arrangement disappoints a family here.

regions.name: Al Muwaiji
regions.note: West of the centre, with a longer return from city-edge campuses. A local tutor arriving at five-thirty must leave by six-thirty to reach a second household, which caps the session at a length that often does not suit Higher Level work.

regions.name: Falaj Hazzaa
regions.note: Large villa neighbourhood with a strong Emirati household share, where the school's Arabic and Islamic Education provision has to be scheduled around. That narrows the available window, which in turn narrows how many nearby tutors could actually take the slot.

regions.name: Zakher
regions.note: Southern edge towards Jebel Hafeet, with the longest commute in the city to central campuses. A local tutor here gives up an evening for one session and prices accordingly. Six o'clock is the realistic weekday start, and weekend mornings carry the heavier blocks.

regions.name: Hili and Al Foah
regions.note: Northern districts towards the border crossing, with the longest daily drive in Al Ain. A proximity search returns almost nothing relevant at Diploma level, and the second evening journey is precisely what families here are trying to avoid.

schoolClusters.city: Central Al Ain campuses
schoolClusters.note: Schools around Al Jimi, Al Mutaredh and Al Towayya, which pull children from every district at the same hour. Students we support from this cluster have most often tried a nearby arrangement first and ended it over scheduling rather than teaching.

sections.heading: What a local search result actually tells you
paragraphs: A proximity result gives you four things: a name, a distance, a star rating of unknown provenance and a claimed subject list. Only one of those is verifiable without doing work, and it is the distance. The subject list is self-reported, the rating may rest on a handful of entries or on nothing countable at all, and neither tells you which level the person has taught or which assessment model they know.

The claimed subject list is where most of the error sits. A listing that says mathematics does not distinguish Analysis and Approaches from Applications and Interpretation, or Higher from Standard Level, and a listing that says science does not distinguish Middle Years integrated science from Diploma Higher Level physics. Those are not fine distinctions. They are the difference between an hour that helps and an hour that keeps a student company while they struggle.

The table below sets out, field by field, what a local listing shows and what you would need to ask to make it meaningful. None of the questions is unreasonable and all of them are free. A capable tutor answers each in a sentence, and a listing that cannot survive three of them was never a shortlist entry, however short the drive. One more thing a listing never carries is whether the person is currently taking students at all, which is why a promising shortlist can evaporate on the first round of messages. Ask that question first and you will save a week. Ask it last and you will have wasted one on candidates who were never available in the first place, which is the most common reason a family starts a term later than they meant to.

sections.heading: The radius problem, counted honestly
paragraphs: Work the numbers for a specific case. A Diploma student in Al Maqam needs Higher Level Physics. Draw a twenty-minute evening radius around the house: that covers most of the central districts and reaches partway out, but not Zakher, not Hili and not Al Foah. Inside that area, how many adults teach Higher Level Physics to Diploma candidates? In a city with Al Ain's school count, the honest answer is a handful.

Now apply the second filter. Of that handful, how many are free between six and eight on a weekday, which is when a student from a central campus living in Al Maqam is home, fed and able to concentrate? Teachers with full timetables are usually the best-qualified candidates and the least available. Of those remaining, how many are taking new students this term rather than full? The list is now frequently empty.

What happens at that point is the whole subject of this page. Almost nobody waits. The family takes the nearest adult who can plausibly teach science, the sessions feel busy, and in March the Paper 2 marks have not moved because the specific gap in fields and circuits was never the thing being taught. The substitution is not dishonest; it is what a radius forces. The way to avoid it is to stop using the radius as a filter at all for subjects where the local pool is this thin. The same arithmetic explains why families in the central districts report better experiences with local tutors than families in Zakher or Hili do: the pool is identical, but the reachable fraction of it is not.

sections.heading: Coverage, match time and fallback, stated per subject
paragraphs: Every provider in this market claims availability in everything, and the competitor audit for this project found none of them disclosing a coverage limit anywhere. That is a strange thing to conceal, because a parent discovers it in week one regardless. Stating it up front is both more useful and easier to defend.

So here it is, by subject, for Al Ain specifically: how well the resident pool covers it, how long a match honestly takes through us, and what we do when nothing suitable is free. The fallback is always disclosed rather than substituted silently. If no specialist is available for a Higher Level subject this term, we say so and tell you when that changes, rather than putting a generalist in the slot and letting the trial lesson hide it.

One point on rates belongs here. We do not charge a different figure according to where the tutor happens to be, because the tutor's location is not something the family buys. Market context for reference: other providers publish online rates for a qualified subject tutor at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, specialist rates at AED 200 to 450 and above, and in-home visiting rates at AED 180 to 500 with travel inside the figure. Those are their published bands, not ours, and IB Gram does not sell in-home visits in the UAE. What a family is entitled to before paying is the wait, the limitation and the fallback in writing, which costs us nothing to provide and saves a term of the wrong lessons.

sections.heading: Proximity against specialism: when each one wins
paragraphs: The honest position is not that distance never matters. There are cases where a person in the room is the requirement and no amount of argument about tutor pools changes it. A six-year-old who will not stay at a table, a student with a specific need for physical prompting, a household with no quiet room and no device: in each of those, a local arrangement is the right answer and we would rather point a family there than take a booking that will not work.

Equally, there are cases where proximity is simply irrelevant. Episodic coursework blocks need four hours in a year, spread across two months, and nobody needs those four hours delivered in person. Diploma mathematics rewards watching written working, which a document camera or a stylus tablet shows line by line. A Higher Level science needs the one person in the region who has taught that paper repeatedly, and that person's address is not a feature of the service.

Between those poles sits the common case, and the test is a single question: is the limiting factor attention or expertise? If a student understands the content and will not do the work, presence helps and the subject matters less. If a student works willingly and still cannot answer the question, expertise is the whole problem and distance is noise. Most Diploma referrals from Al Ain are the second kind, which is why this page argues as it does, and most primary referrals are the first.

sections.heading: Drive times and the earliest slot each district supports
paragraphs: The reason a nearby tutor fails in Al Ain is rarely the teaching. It is that the arrangement was scheduled against the school bell rather than against the moment a student walks through the door. School finishes in the early afternoon; a child living in Zakher who attends a central campus, waits for a bus, collects a sibling and then drives south is not working at four-thirty whatever the timetable says.

Set the slot late and bring it forward, rather than the reverse. Hold the first choice for a fortnight, watch the real arrival time, and only then move earlier if the evidence supports it. Two missed sessions in September reliably push a slot to a weekend, where it competes with everything else a family does, and a weekend slot that competes usually loses by December. That sequence is the single most common way a tutoring plan dies in this city, and it has nothing to do with the tutor.

A video session can sit at six-thirty or seven because nobody has to be anywhere afterwards. That is the practical advantage, and it is larger in a spread-out city than in a dense one. During Ramadan the same flexibility moves the whole arrangement after Iftar rather than pausing it for a month, and when a family travels, only the clock reference changes. None of that is available to a visiting tutor with a second household to reach at seven. Setting the slot honestly in September is the cheapest decision in the whole plan, and it is almost always the one made carelessly.

sections.heading: The permit question, which no listing answers
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE runs on a work permit, and a proximity listing never mentions it. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, and is granted free of charge for two years. Published eligible categories include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen.

The route is the Ministry's own service for issuing a new private tutor work permit, which states a two-working-day completion time and no fee, applied for through its smart app, website and e-services system. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule has been published, so no amount is quoted here, and a figure circulating online could not be verified.

In Abu Dhabi emirate there is a second rule worth knowing before you follow a recommendation from the school gate. Reporting on ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff states that teachers may not provide paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and that the permit's code of conduct carries the same restriction. Verify the current wording with the school, but do not pursue that arrangement. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or permit from ADEK, the Ministry of Education, the IB or any examination board, and claims none.

sections.heading: Five questions worth asking anyone, local or not
paragraphs: First: which level and which assessment model have you taught, and how recently? A tutor who taught Higher Level Chemistry four syllabus revisions ago is a different proposition from one teaching it now, and the answer takes a sentence. Second: which weekday evenings after six are genuinely open? This eliminates more candidates than anything else and does it before anyone has spent money.

Third: what would the first two sessions consist of? The answer you want describes a diagnosis against syllabus content, not a general statement about building confidence. Fourth: what may you do with my child's internal assessment or Extended Essay? The correct answer names teaching, questioning and criterion explanation and rules out supplying any assessable text. Anything looser than that is a malpractice risk carried by the student rather than by the tutor.

Fifth: do you hold the private tuition work permit? Ask it of a local listing, of a centre about its own permissions and of a platform, including this one. Taken together, those five questions sort a shortlist far better than distance does, they cost nothing, and they can be asked by message before a single hour is booked. If a candidate from your local search answers all five well, take them. The argument on this page is about the radius as a filter, not about the people inside it. Keep the answers. A family who has five written replies from two candidates can compare them side by side a fortnight later, which is more than most parents have when they choose.

Precision at this step is what separates a specialist match from a general one, and in Al Ain that distinction matters more than in Abu Dhabi or Dubai because the resident pool is smaller.

process.description: Not the school finish, the actual hour your child is home, fed and able to concentrate. From Zakher, Hili or Al Foah that is usually after six. We set the slot against that figure, because a slot set against the bell is the commonest reason an arrangement stops in November.

Those two short documents prevent the two failures we see most: a slot that erodes into the weekend and then vanishes, and an academic-honesty problem that lands on the student rather than on the adult who caused it.
