sections.heading: The Al Ain school year and where the usable weeks are
paragraphs: Local conditions shape a revision plan more than families expect, and Al Ain's are not identical to the coastal cities'. Summers are long and intense, which affects what a family can realistically plan for the break. The Ramadan period brings a shortened school day. And the winter months, which are the most comfortable of the year here, happen to coincide with the mock window, which is a genuine piece of good fortune if a plan is ready to use them.

The Ramadan weeks are the part most often planned badly. Shorter school days read on paper as extra study time and rarely behave that way: children arrive home earlier with less energy. What works is treating the period as deliberate maintenance — shorter sessions, fixed in advance for the early evening or after Iftar rather than renegotiated weekly, with light retrieval practice instead of new content — and planning the weeks either side to carry the heavier work.

The long summer is the other local variable. For a student moving into Year 11, a short block across the break is among the best-value purchases available, because it closes coverage gaps while nothing else competes for the time. For a student who has just finished Year 11 and is considering a November resit, the same weeks are the only teaching window available before the entry deadline, which makes them unusually valuable and unusually easy to lose.

The practical discipline is to write the whole year on one page before buying anything: entry date, mock window, Ramadan period, study leave, examination window, results, November deadline. A family that does this buys fewer sessions and gets more from them, which is the opposite of what most providers would prefer to tell you.
bullets: Shortened school days lower energy rather than adding usable hours

sections.heading: Private candidate entry, when a school does not offer a subject
paragraphs: This is the option most families never hear about, and in a city with a compact school market it matters. Where a school does not enter candidates for a subject a student needs — a language, an extension course, a science the timetable cannot fit — a private candidate entry at a centre that accepts them is sometimes possible.

The constraints are real and worth knowing before anybody gets excited. Not every centre accepts private candidates, and those that do set their own deadlines and fees, which fall earlier than the school's internal timetable would suggest. Practical and coursework components are the usual obstacle: a subject with a practical requirement can be difficult or impossible to sit privately depending on the specification, which is a question for the centre rather than for a tutor.

Where the route is open, the teaching can be arranged independently, and this is a case where online delivery is the whole solution rather than a convenience. A student self-studying a subject the school does not run needs somebody who teaches that specification, and in Al Ain that person is very unlikely to live nearby.

The honest framing is that this is a project rather than a purchase. It needs a centre, a deadline, a syllabus, a teaching plan and a parent willing to manage the administration. It is worth it when a university prerequisite depends on the subject, and rarely worth it otherwise.

One caution on timing. Because centre deadlines for private entries fall earlier than a school's own internal calendar would suggest, the decision has to be made a term ahead of where it feels urgent. Families who start asking in the spring are usually told the window has gone, and the subject then slips a full year. If a prerequisite is in question, ask the centre in the autumn.
bullets: Not every centre accepts private candidates; ask early

sections.heading: What cannot be fixed late, said plainly
paragraphs: A page about calendars should be honest about the things no amount of late spending repairs, because the alternative is a family paying for a result that was never available.

A tier cannot be changed after entries are submitted. A subject never taught cannot be taught in four weeks to examination standard. A coursework component with a passed internal deadline cannot be resubmitted because a tutor was hired afterwards. A review of marking cannot be requested outside its window. And a grade cannot be guaranteed by anybody, at any price, which is why no page on this site offers one.

What can be done late is narrower and still worthwhile. Technique, timing and question order can move marks in four weeks for a student who understands the content. Command-term discipline is trainable in a session or two. A mechanical topic that has been avoided for two years can often be banked in two sessions, which makes it the rational first purchase when time is short. And where none of that is enough, the November series exists as a real route rather than a failure.

That is the whole of the honest offer, and it is still a good one. A family in Al Towayya who buys a three-session diagnostic block in the autumn, acts on what it finds, and keeps the November option in view will usually do better than one who spends three times as much in April. The difference is the calendar, not the money.

process.title: Get four dates in writing
process.description: The entry submission date, the mock window, the study-leave date and the November entry deadline. All four come from the examinations officer, all four are free, and together they decide what any block of sessions can realistically achieve.

process.title: Send the code, the tier and a marked paper
process.description: The code tells us which past material is correct, the tier tells us the ceiling, and a marked script tells us whether the problem is content or technique. Without those three, a recommendation about timing is guesswork.

process.title: Free trial lesson on your child's own questions
process.description: A real lesson with the specialist who would teach the block, using material from the correct specification. You should finish it with three named error types written down and a clear statement of what the remaining weeks can achieve.

process.title: A block scoped to the nearest closing door
process.description: If the tier door is still open, the plan produces evidence for it. If entries are in, the plan maximises the existing ceiling. Either way you get a session count and a finish date that sits before study leave rather than inside it.

process.title: A review that raises the November question
process.description: At the midpoint a second timed paper is compared with the first by topic, and the review says continue, change or stop. Where the evidence suggests June is not winnable, it says so and puts the November route on the table while there is still time to use it.

whyPoints.title: Planned from deadlines, not from a textbook
whyPoints.description: The first conversation is about the entry date, the mock window and study leave. What a block can achieve is set by those dates, and quoting the same plan in October and April would be selling the same words for two different things.

whyPoints.title: The right series named for this country
whyPoints.description: Cambridge candidates in the UAE sit June and November; the February and March sitting is offered to India only. Pages aimed at Gulf families routinely quote the Indian dates, and an entry deadline acted on in the wrong country is a serious error.

whyPoints.title: The November route raised early
whyPoints.description: A resit planned in the autumn is a strategy. A resit discovered in August is damage control. We put the question on the table at the midpoint review rather than after results, because that is when it is still a choice.

whyPoints.title: Zone timetables flagged
whyPoints.description: Cambridge allocates each centre to one of six administrative zones with its own timetable version and says it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who use the wrong one. We tell families to confirm the zone with the school rather than trust a date found online.

whyPoints.title: Short Al Ain journeys used properly
whyPoints.description: Early arrivals here make genuinely early session slots possible, which matters for timed-paper work that needs a student who can still concentrate. We set the slot after knowing the real arrival time rather than before.

whyPoints.title: Honest about what cannot be fixed
whyPoints.description: A closed tier, a missed coursework deadline and an expired review window do not reopen. Saying so costs us sessions and saves families money, which is the trade this page is willing to make.

faqs.question: Which decisions about my child's IGCSEs have already closed by Year 11?
faqs.answer: Usually the subject list and the tier. Dropping or changing a subject depends on timetable capacity and becomes impractical once teaching is underway; the tier is decided by the school on evidence and submitted to a board deadline months before the papers. What remains open in Year 11 is how fully the existing ceiling is used, whether to request a review of marking after results, and whether to enter the November series. Ask the examinations officer for the entry date in writing before assuming anything is still negotiable.

faqs.question: How many usable teaching weeks does an Al Ain Year 11 student actually have?
faqs.answer: Fewer than the calendar suggests. Count school weeks to the study-leave date, then subtract holidays, the mock weeks themselves, any school event and the Ramadan period if it falls inside the window. Families here commonly find an apparent twelve weeks becomes seven or eight. That number decides whether a tutor can teach content or only recover technique, and it should be established before sessions are bought rather than discovered in the middle of a block.

faqs.question: Will an Al Towayya candidate ever sit a Cambridge exam sitting in the spring?
faqs.answer: No. Cambridge offers its February and March sitting to India only, so a UAE candidate sits the June series with November available as the resit route. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. Several tutoring pages aimed at Gulf families quote the Indian dates, and an entry deadline acted on for the wrong country is a serious mistake. Cambridge also allocates each centre to one of six timetable zones, so confirm which version applies with your school's examinations officer.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send an IGCSE tutor to a house in Al Towayya?
faqs.answer: No. We make no home visits anywhere in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Teaching for Al Ain families is one-to-one over live video at a fixed slot in Gulf Standard Time, with a shared screen for working through paper questions. In this city the gain is less about the drive, which is short, than about supply: the number of people locally who have marked a given specification is small, and a screen removes that limit.

faqs.question: When is the last moment to argue for a different tier?
faqs.answer: Before the school submits final entries, which happens months ahead of the papers. The decision belongs to the school and rests on evidence — set placement, internal examinations, the mock — so a family wanting a change needs marked work rather than an opinion. Two timed sections and a diagnostic session usually produce it. After the entry deadline the question is simply closed, and the honest plan becomes using the available ceiling fully and considering the November series where it helps.

faqs.question: What is a review of marking and should we ask for one?
faqs.answer: It is a request made through the examination centre, not by a family directly, within a short published window after results. It carries a fee and a risk, since a review can confirm a mark and in some arrangements a mark can move downwards as well as up. The decision should be made with the subject teacher, who has seen the script and knows how the cohort performed. A tutor cannot request one and should not encourage it on the strength of a disappointing number alone.

faqs.question: How does a November resit plan actually work?
faqs.answer: It is planned around the entry deadline rather than the paper date, and the deadline arrives soon after summer results — which is exactly when a family is least ready to decide. The sensible approach is to work out the position before results. For Pearson Edexcel International GCSE the November window has run from late October into November, with results reaching students in January; November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Ask your school whether it enters November candidates and at what cost.

faqs.question: Is a summer block worth buying for a student going into Year 11 in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Often, and it is among the best-value purchases available because nothing else competes for the time. Four to six sessions across the break closing specific coverage gaps — topics missed through absence, a change of teacher or a school move — removes work that would otherwise consume autumn teaching time. The same weeks are also the only teaching window available before a November entry deadline for a student resitting, which makes them unusually valuable and easy to waste.

faqs.question: How should revision be planned around the Ramadan period here?
faqs.answer: As deliberate maintenance rather than as a push. Shortened school days mean earlier arrivals with less energy, not extra usable hours. What works is shorter sessions fixed in advance for the early evening or after Iftar rather than renegotiated each week, with light retrieval practice instead of new content, and the weeks either side planned to carry the heavier work. Telling the student the period is lighter by design matters, because an abandoned plan does more damage than a few lost hours.

faqs.question: Can my child sit a subject the Al Ain school does not enter?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, as a private candidate at a centre that accepts them. The constraints are real: not every centre does, deadlines and fees are set by the centre and fall earlier than a school timetable suggests, and practical or coursework components can be difficult or impossible to sit privately depending on the specification. Where the route is open, teaching can be arranged independently, which is a case where online delivery is the whole solution. It is worth the administration when a university prerequisite depends on the subject.

faqs.question: What can still be fixed four weeks before the first paper?
faqs.answer: Technique, timing, question order, command-term discipline and the claiming of method marks — which for a student who understands the content can be worth a meaningful number of marks. A mechanical topic avoided for two years can often be banked in two sessions, which makes it the rational first purchase when time is short. What cannot be fixed is a specification never taught, a closed tier or a missed coursework deadline, and a plan that pretends otherwise wastes the weeks that remain.

faqs.question: Which authority regulates schools in Al Towayya?
faqs.answer: Al Ain sits within the emirate of Abu Dhabi, so private schools here are regulated by the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises licensing and accreditation and publishes inspection outcomes. The framework is the same one used in Abu Dhabi city, so reports are directly comparable. No tutoring provider, including IB Gram, holds approval from ADEK or from any examination board, and a page claiming such approval is making the most dangerous claim available in this market.

faqs.question: Does a tutor working with a student in Al Towayya need a permit?
faqs.answer: Yes. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued through the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged fifteen to eighteen. Tutoring without one carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so treat any page naming an amount with suspicion.

faqs.question: Why does this page avoid printing exact exam dates?
faqs.answer: Because a date restated on a page goes stale without anybody touching it, and a wrong examination date is the one error a parent will act on. We name a series by its month — the June series, the November series — which stays true every year, and we keep past dates where they are cited because that is what makes them checkable. For current timings, use the official Cambridge or Pearson timetable for your centre's zone, and ask your examinations officer which version applies.

intro.heading: A short evening is a planning problem, not an excuse
paragraphs: Al Yahar lies on the outlying western side of Al Ain, agricultural in character and some distance from the private schools most of its students attend. The school run is long in both directions, and the return leg does not get quicker in the late afternoon. For a Year 11 student that produces a short, late evening, and a tutoring plan designed for a family living beside the school will not survive a term here.

The useful response is not to wish for more time but to match the work to the time available. A forty-five minute session can do several things properly: a calculation drill, a command-term exercise, marking a section the student completed earlier, rehearsing a speaking component. It cannot do a full past paper, and a tutor who tries will produce an hour of partial work and a student who feels behind.

This matters more at IGCSE than at any other stage, because IGCSE improvement is largely a function of timed practice. Papers are long, and Year 11 students need to experience them whole. From Al Yahar the only places a whole paper fits are a weekend morning and a school holiday, which means those slots have to be used for that purpose and not frittered on review.

There is a second local fact. Al Ain's private-school set is considerably smaller than Abu Dhabi island's, which makes some IGCSE subjects thin across the whole city, notably Additional Mathematics, Computer Science, ICT and second modern languages. An outlying address compounds that for any in-home arrangement, since the willing pool shrinks with every extra kilometre of unpaid driving.

Al Yahar is in Al Ain, part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so the regulator is ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. ADEK's own listing is where to confirm which curriculum a school is licensed to deliver, which is a sensible first check given that the schools serving this area use both of the main exam boards.

IB Gram teaches Al Yahar students one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time. We do not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visiting is a service we run only in India. For a family at the edge of the city the practical benefit is specific: the session starts when the student walks in, it can be forty-five minutes rather than a notional hour, and it can move when the week moves.

None of what follows depends on hiring us. The session-length table, the paper-splitting routine and the post-mock analysis method all work on any tutor a family here finds, and the questions at the end work on anyone. The format we sell is online; the planning is simply what this journey requires.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: Four-digit syllabus codes with many subjects tiered into Core and Extended and a grade ceiling on Core. Sciences carry a separate practical component, either a laboratory test paper or an alternative-to-practical written paper, and the school chooses which. The qualification runs in a June series and a November series, with Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October.
programmes.countryNote: The detail that catches UAE families, and that matters more to an outlying family who cannot easily pop into school, is zoning. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after the wrong timetable was used. Get the zone from the exams officer in writing early in Year 11.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Codes run 4MA1, 4PH1, 4CH1, 4BI1 and 4EA1. Mathematics A tiers into Foundation and Higher; the international sciences are untiered and assess practical skills inside the written papers rather than in a separate practical exam. Modular availability in some subjects changes when a result can be banked and when a resit is possible.
programmes.countryNote: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE exams run in May/June and November each year. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026; June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026; November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series and revises them, so plan from the live official timetable rather than a restated date.

programmes.name: AS and A Level progression
programmes.description: The tier and grade a student finishes IGCSE with decides which AS subjects stay open. Core tier generally closes AS Mathematics and the separate sciences, and the decision is taken in Year 10 but felt in Year 12. For a student whose week is already short, deciding this on evidence rather than on hope saves an expensive recovery later.
programmes.countryNote: For UAE university entry the Ministry of Education equivalency rule on the British track asks for five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than grade E or 3, plus one accredited Advanced Level subject at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are excluded from the five. Five comfortable passes therefore matter more than two outstanding ones alongside three marginal results.

al-ain/igcse-home-tutor-in-al-yahar.subjectsIntro: What a session can achieve depends on the subject as much as on the clock, because some IGCSE work splits neatly into short blocks and some does not. Each entry says which.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.levels: Cambridge 0580 Core and Extended; Pearson 4MA1 Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: Splits well. Topic drills, method-line discipline and single question sections all fit a short weeknight. Full papers do not, so they belong on the weekend. The most requested subject from this area and the one where short sessions work best.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics
subjects.description: Splits poorly. Calculus and series need sustained attention, so this subject wants a longer block. It is also scarce across Al Ain because few schools offer it, which makes an early booking and a weekend slot the realistic combination.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Splits very well. Uncertainty treatment, significant figures, unit handling and reading results tables are all short, high-yield drills. The practical component also depends on which board, so confirm whether a practical test or an alternative paper applies.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Splits well for calculations and badly for organic chemistry. Moles arithmetic is ideal short-session material; reaction pathways want a longer run. Plan the weeknights for the first and the weekend for the second.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Splits well. Command-term work and short structured-question practice suit a forty-five minute slot, and the gains transfer across the whole paper. Well supplied online, so the slot can be chosen to suit the journey.

subjects.name: Co-ordinated and Combined Science
subjects.description: Needs care rather than length. The content map differs from the separate sciences, so the risk is a tutor teaching off-specification material competently. Confirm the code first; after that, it splits much like the separate sciences.

subjects.name: English Language
subjects.levels: Cambridge 0500 first language, 0510/0511 second language; Pearson 4EA1
subjects.description: Splits moderately. Directed-writing technique and reading-response structure fit short sessions; full timed compositions need a longer block. Check first against second language before anything else, because the mark schemes differ.

subjects.name: Economics and Business
subjects.description: Splits well. Definitions, diagram accuracy and short data-response practice are ideal weeknight work, and the usual failure of describing rather than analysing is structural, so a correction transfers across the paper.

subjects.name: Computer Science and ICT
subjects.description: Pseudocode and trace tables split well; ICT practical tasks do not, because the software work needs a continuous run. Both are scarce in Al Ain, so expect a wait and consider a weekend slot from the start.

subjects.name: Geography and History
subjects.description: Splits well for source skills and badly for full essays. Source technique and case-study recall suit short sessions; extended answers under timed conditions need the weekend. Both subjects improve quickly once structure is taught.

sections.heading: What each session length can actually achieve
paragraphs: This is the table nobody publishes and the one an Al Yahar family needs most. Tutoring is sold in notional hours, but the work an IGCSE student needs comes in different sizes, and matching them is the difference between a productive short session and a frustrating one. The rows below are ordered by length rather than by subject.

The honest claim is that a forty-five minute session is genuinely useful, provided it is given one job. Marking a section the student completed earlier in the week, drilling a calculation type, running command-term practice or rehearsing a speaking component all fit and all move marks. Attempting a full paper does not, and a tutor who starts one at half past seven has set the student up to fail at it.

The reverse error is equally common. A ninety-minute weekend slot spent on general review wastes the only block in the week where timed practice is possible. Families should guard that slot for whole papers and for the subjects that do not split, which is where the biggest gains live for a Year 11 student.

Use the final column as a filter when agreeing a plan. If a proposed session's task does not match its length, say so. A good tutor will adjust immediately, because they already know this; a tutor who insists on the same lesson regardless of the clock has one lesson.

One more note on the shortest row. Thirty minutes is listed because it exists and occasionally earns its place, usually as maintenance between longer sessions in a subject that has been fixed. It is not a format to build a plan on, and a provider offering a term of half-hours is selling convenience rather than progress.

sections.heading: Splitting a past paper when the evening is short
paragraphs: Year 11 improvement comes mostly from timed practice, and a long paper does not fit a short evening. The answer is not to skip timed work but to split it deliberately, and the splits that work are not arbitrary. The table sets out how to divide practice so the timing discipline survives the division.

The principle is that timing must be preserved inside each fragment. A student who does half a paper in half the allotted time has practised timing correctly. A student who does half a paper slowly because there is no clock has practised something else entirely, and will still run out of time in the real thing. Give each fragment its proportional minutes and hold to them.

The second principle is that marking is part of the practice, not an administrative afterthought. A section attempted and never marked teaches nothing. If a session is short, it is better to attempt a smaller fragment and mark it inside the session than to attempt more and mark none, which is the most common waste in short-session tutoring.

For an Al Yahar family the workable rhythm is this: the student attempts a fragment independently on a weeknight with a timer, the next session marks and corrects it, and the weekend morning is used for a whole section or paper under proper conditions. That produces real timed practice from a week that appears not to have room for any.

A final caution about who times the practice. Younger Year 10 students are poor at timing themselves honestly, so the first few fragments should be timed in session with the tutor watching the clock. Once a student has felt what the right pace is, they can be trusted to run fragments alone, and that handover is itself part of what the tutoring is for.

sections.heading: Mock season, and the fortnight that decides everything
paragraphs: Mocks are the only full-length diagnostic most IGCSE students get before the real series, and their value is almost entirely in what happens afterwards. For an Al Yahar family with limited weekly capacity, the fortnight after mocks is the highest-return tutoring purchase of the year, because it is the only point at which the whole plan can be redirected on evidence.

The analysis itself is mechanical and can be done in one long session. Sort every lost mark into one of four kinds: blank questions, method errors, timing failures and mark-scheme phrasing. Blanks mean content was never learnt and need a term or a holiday block. Method errors and phrasing mean technique and need hours. Timing failures mean practice under the clock, which is the split-paper routine above.

What families do instead is react to the grade. A grade of 5 produces either relief or panic, neither of which contains information. The same grade can come from a student who left a third of the paper blank and one who attempted everything and lost marks on phrasing, and those two students need entirely different plans and different amounts of money spent on them.

Book the post-mock session before mocks happen, and book it long. Ninety minutes on a weekend morning with the scripts on the table is worth more than four weeknight hours afterwards spent guessing. This is the single clearest piece of scheduling advice on the page and it costs nothing extra to follow.

sections.heading: Online one-to-one against a visiting tutor in Al Yahar
paragraphs: The search phrase says home tutor, so the comparison belongs here rather than in a footnote. IB Gram provides no home visits anywhere in the UAE, and the table's final row says so plainly rather than reframing the question.

The row that decides it for an outlying family is session length. A visiting tutor cannot sensibly travel a long distance for forty-five minutes, so in practice they sell a full hour or ninety minutes and arrive later to make the journey worthwhile. That removes exactly the option an Al Yahar weeknight needs, which is a short, early, focused session.

The second is flexibility of length week to week. Some weeks a student needs forty-five minutes of marking and some weeks they need ninety minutes of timed practice, and an arrangement pinned to a driving route cannot vary. Online delivery can, which turns the session length into a planning tool rather than a fixed cost.

Cost appears in the table and is not the deciding factor. The UAE in-home band runs AED 180 to AED 500 an hour with travel included, against AED 150 to AED 300 for a qualified online subject tutor; the premium pays for the car and the unpaid driving, which from Al Yahar is substantial. What it does not buy is a wider choice of tutor or a shorter session when that is what the evening allows.

The caveat belongs here as well. Some students work far better with an adult physically beside them, and for those families the premium and the inflexible length may be worth accepting. The table argues about session length and reliability rather than about every child, and that judgement is the parent's to make.

sections.heading: Zones, deadlines and the series UAE candidates sit
paragraphs: One correction first, because acting on it would make a family miss an entry. Cambridge International's February/March series is offered to India only. UAE candidates sit the June series and the November series. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. A page quoting a UAE family a February/March entry deadline has published another country's calendar.

The zoning point matters particularly for an outlying family who cannot easily call into school. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after the wrong zone timetable was used. Ask the exams officer for the zone in writing in the first term of Year 11 and keep it.

Pearson's documented pattern is useful for anyone weighing a resit. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. So a November entry historically means a January result, which matters if a sixth-form or university deadline falls between.

The forward-looking rule is to name a series by its month and check the live official timetable, because Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series and revises them. No future date on this page carries a year for that reason, and any page that gives you one should be verified against the board before you build a revision plan on it.

sections.heading: ADEK, permits and what a parent can check
paragraphs: Al Yahar is in Al Ain, part of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi, so the regulator is ADEK, the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools in the emirate. ADEK is named by none of the competitor pages reviewed for this project, which is a reasonable signal about how locally grounded a tutoring site is.

Private tutoring in the UAE runs on a permit. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students, applied for through MoHRE's own private tutor licensing service with a stated two-working-day completion.

One restriction applies specifically because of the emirate. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school. A tutor whose pitch rests on teaching at your child's school is offering an arrangement to decline, and the current wording should be checked against ADEK's own policy document.

Those tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, with no published fine schedule, so any quoted amount is unverified. For completeness, IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from ADEK, KHDA, SPEA, the Ministry of Education, MoHRE, Cambridge International or Pearson. A tuition centre with premises in Dubai would need a KHDA Educational Services Permit, which is a different and specific thing.

sections.heading: Practical papers and the line a tutor will not cross
paragraphs: IGCSE carries less assessed coursework than the Diploma, but the practical component and any school-supervised work still have a boundary, and it is worth knowing where it sits before buying anything.

Inside the boundary, and entirely teachable in a short session: apparatus conventions, how to draw and read a results table, uncertainty and significant figures, choosing a sensible scale for a graph, and the standard phrasing a mark scheme rewards for describing a method or a source of error. None of that needs a laboratory, and all of it carries marks.

Outside the boundary: producing data, writing up an investigation, supplying answers for work that will be submitted, or preparing material a student presents as their own. We also will not reproduce or supply board syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes or grade-boundary tables as downloads; the correct route is to cite the official page and link to it.

One question settles which kind of provider you are dealing with. Ask what they would do if a student brought submitted work the night before it was due. An answer about reading and marking it against criteria is correct. An answer that involves fixing it tells you what else is for sale, and the research behind this page found completed assessments on offer to UAE students at around AED 3,750, so it is not a hypothetical concern.

There is one more thing worth asking about materials. A provider that advertises a library of past papers and mark schemes for download has already answered a question about how it treats board copyright, and by extension about how carefully it treats everything else. Citing and linking the official page is the correct route and costs nothing.

sections.heading: What we can cover from here, and the slots that fill first
paragraphs: Availability transparency is missing from every competitor page reviewed for this project, so here is ours as a limit. Mathematics, the separate sciences, English and the humanities are well supplied and usually matched within a week. Co-ordinated science needs the code confirmed first. Additional Mathematics 0606, Computer Science 0478 and ICT 0417 are limited. Second modern languages are thin and often declined.

The slot matters as much as the subject. The weekend morning band and the six to eight weekday band are what every family in the emirate wants, so they go first. An Al Yahar family able to use an earlier Friday slot, a later weekend morning or a forty-five minute weeknight sees a materially wider choice immediately, because short slots are easier to place than long ones.

When we cannot cover a request we give a named date or decline. We do not substitute across specifications, because a separate-science tutor filling a co-ordinated science request or a 0580 specialist filling a 0606 request will teach competently and off-specification, and that failure is invisible until the paper.

Put the same questions to anyone, including a local in-home tutor. Can you cover this code and tier, in this slot, starting when. Will you work in a forty-five minute session if that is what the evening allows. What happens if the first tutor is wrong. Three specific answers make a provider comparable; an unqualified yes to everything does not.

One further thing a family can control. Giving two possible slots rather than one roughly doubles the field, because a specialist with a Wednesday gap and no Tuesday gap becomes available. In the scarcer subjects that flexibility is worth more than any other concession a family can make.

Book a ninety-minute weekend session for the fortnight after mocks before the mocks happen, because that is the highest-return hour of the year for a family with limited weekly capacity.

process.title: Agree which task belongs in which length
process.description: Short weeknight sessions take drills, marking and oral rehearsal. The weekend morning takes timed practice and the subjects that do not split. If a proposed session's task does not match its length, say so; a good tutor adjusts immediately because they already know this.

process.title: Put the volume in the holidays
process.description: Breaks remove the journey and make daily morning sessions possible, which is the only way an outlying family can accumulate hours quickly. Those blocks are aimed at content repair rather than exam technique, because technique work needs the term's marked papers to react to.

whyPoints.title: Sessions sized to the evening
whyPoints.description: Forty-five minutes is a real slot here, planned with one named task, rather than a shortened hour. A visiting tutor cannot sensibly travel a long distance for forty-five minutes, which removes exactly the option an Al Yahar weeknight needs.

whyPoints.title: Timed practice that survives a short week
whyPoints.description: Paper practice is split deliberately, with proportional minutes held inside each fragment, so the timing discipline is still being trained. Marking happens inside the session rather than being left undone, which is the commonest waste in short-session tutoring.

whyPoints.title: Matched on the code, not the subject name
whyPoints.description: The schools serving this area use both boards, and Cambridge 0625 and Pearson 4PH1 examine practical skills differently. A tutor is proposed only for the specification and tier your child actually sits.

whyPoints.title: Coverage stated before you book
whyPoints.description: Additional Mathematics 0606, Computer Science and ICT are limited and second languages are thin across the whole city. We give a named date or decline rather than substituting a tutor from a different specification.

whyPoints.title: Delivery stated at the top
whyPoints.description: One-to-one live video on Gulf Standard Time, with no home visits anywhere in the UAE because that service exists only in India. On the in-home axis we are not an option, and that belongs before a booking rather than after.

whyPoints.title: Dates with sources, or no dates
whyPoints.description: Cambridge and Pearson calendar facts are given with their sources and future series are named by month only. We do not publish IB session dates at all, because the IB's own site is the only source and none has been confirmed in this project.

faqs.question: Is a 45-minute session long enough to be worth paying for in Al Yahar?
faqs.answer: Yes, provided it has one job. Forty-five minutes handles a calculation drill, a command-term exercise, marking a section your child completed earlier in the week, or rehearsing a speaking component, and all of those move marks. What it cannot do is a full past paper or new Extended-tier content late in the course. The failure mode is a tutor running their standard hour-long lesson in less time, which produces partial work and a student who feels behind. Agree the task before the session, not during it.

faqs.question: How do we fit timed paper practice into a short Al Yahar evening?
faqs.answer: Split it and keep the clock. Give each fragment its proportional minutes: the first ten marks of a paper, one structured question, or one extended-response question, each strictly timed. A student who does half a paper in half the allotted time has practised timing properly; one who does half a paper slowly has practised something else. Marking matters as much as attempting, so a smaller fragment marked inside the session beats a larger one left unmarked. Whole papers belong on the weekend morning.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send an IGCSE tutor out to Al Yahar?
faqs.answer: No, and not anywhere else in the UAE. In-person home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Al Yahar students are taught one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time. We state that before any booking because the phrase families search is 'home tutor' and the format should never be a surprise. If physical presence is a requirement, hire locally, ask which MoHRE permit category the tutor holds, and expect the rate at the top of the in-home band because of the distance.

faqs.question: Why is the fortnight after mocks the most valuable tutoring purchase?
faqs.answer: Because mocks are the only full-length diagnostic most IGCSE students get, and the information is in the scripts rather than the grade. Sort every lost mark into blanks, method errors, timing failures and mark-scheme phrasing. Blanks mean content was never learnt and need a holiday block. Method and phrasing mean technique and need a few hours. Timing failures need split-paper practice. The same grade can come from two students needing entirely different plans, which is why reacting to the number instead of the script wastes money.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE subjects split well into short sessions?
faqs.answer: Mathematics, Physics, Biology, Economics and Business split very well, because the high-yield work is drills, command terms, definitions, diagram accuracy and short structured questions. Chemistry splits for calculations and not for organic pathways. English splits for technique and not for full timed compositions. Additional Mathematics 0606 and ICT practical work split poorly and want a longer block. Plan the weeknights around the first group and protect the weekend morning for the second, which is the whole scheduling argument for this area.

faqs.question: How do I find out which Cambridge zone my child's school is in?
faqs.answer: Ask the exams officer, in writing, in the first term of Year 11, and keep the reply. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, and says it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after the wrong zone timetable was used. For an outlying family who cannot easily call into school, having that in an email matters more than for a family living next to it. Then work from that zone's timetable only.

faqs.question: Do Al Ain students ever sit the Cambridge February/March series?
faqs.answer: No. The February/March series is offered to India only. UAE candidates sit the June series and the November series, with Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. If a tutoring page quotes you a February/March entry deadline, it has published another country's calendar and acting on it would mean missing an entry. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. Always confirm dates on the board's own live timetable rather than from a restated version on any site, including this one.

faqs.question: What does a November Pearson entry mean for when results arrive?
faqs.answer: Historically, a January result. The documented pattern is that the November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. That lag matters if a sixth-form or university deadline falls between the paper and the result. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series and revises them, so check the live official timetable before planning around any future series.

faqs.question: Should we use the school holidays to catch up on content?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the only realistic way for an outlying family to accumulate hours. During a break the journey disappears, which makes daily morning sessions possible, and morning work is far better than evening work for anything requiring consolidation across consecutive days. Aim holiday blocks at content repair rather than exam technique, because technique work needs the term's marked papers and a live mock to react to. Six to twelve sessions in a break does more real learning than the same hours spread thinly through a term.

faqs.question: Can a tutor prepare my child for a Cambridge practical paper online?
faqs.answer: For the examinable skills, yes, and those are most of the marks. Apparatus conventions, drawing and reading results tables, uncertainty and significant figures, choosing a sensible graph scale, and the standard phrasing a mark scheme rewards for describing a method or a source of error can all be taught and drilled remotely from past practical papers. What matters first is which paper your child actually sits: Cambridge offers a practical test or an alternative-to-practical written paper, while Pearson examines practical skills inside the written papers. Confirm with the school before any plan is built.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE subjects are hard to find a tutor for in Al Ain?
faqs.answer: Additional Mathematics 0606, Computer Science 0478 and ICT 0417 are limited, and second modern languages are thin and often declined. The cause is structural: Al Ain's private-school set is considerably smaller than Abu Dhabi island's, so few schools offer these subjects and few teachers have taken a cohort through them. An outlying address compounds it for any in-home arrangement. Mathematics, the separate sciences, English, Geography and History are well supplied and should be matched within a week at a mid-band rate.

faqs.question: Why are short slots easier to book than long ones?
faqs.answer: Because a forty-five minute session fits into gaps that a ninety-minute one cannot, so there are simply more of them available. The weekend morning band and the six to eight weekday evening band are what every family in the emirate wants and they fill first. A family willing to take an earlier Friday slot, a later weekend morning or a short weeknight sees a materially wider choice of tutor, and in the scarcer subjects that choice is the difference between a specialist and a fortnight's wait.

faqs.question: What practice should be set between sessions for a Year 11 student here?
faqs.answer: A single question section with a timer, not a full paper. A tutor who sets two hours of work for a weeknight after a long journey has set something that will not be done, and the next session gets spent discussing why rather than on the subject. The loop that works is: the student attempts a timed fragment alone on a weeknight, the next session marks and corrects it, and the weekend morning takes a whole section under proper conditions. That produces real timed practice from a week that looks too short for any.

faqs.question: Can a teacher at my child's Al Ain school tutor them privately?
faqs.answer: Not for payment. ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE private tuition work permit carries a code of conduct barring the same thing. Teachers who tutor outside school hours must hold the permit, which is free and valid for two years. If a tutor's pitch rests on teaching at your child's school, treat it as a reason to decline rather than a credential, and check the current wording against ADEK's own published policy.

intro.heading: Scheduling is the problem, not supply
paragraphs: Falaj Hazza is one of the better-connected districts of Al Ain: a dense residential grid in the western half of the city with a short run to the central school cluster. A family here can usually find somebody willing to teach IGCSE. What a family here struggles to find is an hour in the week that genuinely stays free, and that is a different problem with a different solution.

Work through a normal Tuesday. School finishes somewhere between quarter past two and half past three depending on the setting and the key stage. Pick-up queues absorb fifteen to twenty-five minutes. The drive back into Falaj Hazza from the central or western school belt adds another fifteen on a clear day and more when a road is dug up. A child then needs to eat, change and decompress. A four o'clock start, which is what most tutoring timetables assume, is usually fiction. Half past four is the earliest honest answer and five is more common.

Now layer on everything else a Year 10 or Year 11 evening carries: a sibling's pick-up on a different timetable, Quran or Arabic classes, sport two evenings a week, and in many Al Ain households a parent who commutes to Abu Dhabi and is not home until seven. Two or three candidate slots exist in a week, not ten. An in-home tutor needs one of those slots to coincide with their own availability and their own travel, which is why so many families end up with a Thursday arrangement nobody wanted.

Online delivery changes the arithmetic rather than the pedagogy. Because nobody is driving, a lesson can sit at 5.15pm or at 8pm, can move by half an hour on a week when school finishes early, and does not collapse when the student is in Abu Dhabi for two days. IB Gram teaches Falaj Hazza students one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. Home visits are an India-only service for us and we do not run them in the UAE, which we say plainly rather than leaving a parent to discover it at booking.

The rest of this page is practical. It maps school finish times onto realistic session windows. It prices IGCSE support by the month rather than the hour, because that is how a household budget works, using figures published by others and attributed to them. It compares Falaj Hazza with the districts either side. It covers the Arabic and Islamic Education obligations that run alongside an international curriculum, Ramadan and holiday scheduling, how progress actually gets measured across a year, and the boundary a tutor must not cross on assessed work. None of it assumes you have already decided to buy anything.

al-ain/igcse-home-tutor-in-falaj-hazza.programmesIntro: Al Ain students reach IGCSE by a few different routes, and each route changes what an after-school hour should be spent on. These are the programmes our IGCSE tutoring touches.

programmes.description: The three years feeding IGCSE, with optional Checkpoint tests in English, mathematics and science sat in March, May and October. Reports give diagnostic bands rather than grades, which is where parents lose the thread.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: Subject-by-subject examinations with Core and Extended tiering in most sciences and mathematics. Core maths caps below the top grades; Extended reaches the top. Sciences use either a practical test or the written alternative-to-practical paper.

Cambridge allocates each centre to one of six administrative zones with its own timetable version and states it cannot accept responsibility for a candidate who misses an exam after using the wrong zone. Ask the exams officer for the zone in September, not in April.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Codes such as 4MA1 and 4PH1, with Mathematics A tiered Foundation and Higher and several subjects available modularly so units can be sat across sessions rather than banked to the end.

programmes.name: Cambridge International AS & A Level
programmes.description: The two years most Al Ain British-curriculum students move into. Content steps up sharply from Extended tier, particularly in mathematics, where the top third of the IGCSE syllabus is assumed as fluency rather than taught again.

A student intending to continue a subject should not sit it at Core tier, and the evening hour in Year 10 is cheaper than the catch-up hour in Year 12. al-ain/igcse-home-tutor-in-falaj-hazza.subjectsIntro: The IGCSE subjects Al Ain families most often book, with syllabus codes attached. Codes matter more than subject names, and the exams officer can confirm yours in a single message.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580)
subjects.description: Two papers, one without a calculator. The recurring loss is unwritten method on multi-step questions, plus the Extended-only vectors, functions and transformations content met late in Year 11.

subjects.name: Mathematics A (Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: Different question architecture from Cambridge even where topics overlap, with its own formula provision. Practice must be board-matched; drilling the wrong board's papers is a common and expensive mistake.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625)
subjects.description: Electricity and motion graphs cost the most marks. Paper 6, the written alternative to practical, rewards disciplined description of method - what was controlled and how - rather than knowledge of physics.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620)
subjects.description: Moles, ionic equations and organic chemistry carry the weight. Most lost marks are presentational: early rounding, absent units, missing state symbols in equations that require them.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610)
subjects.description: Heavy content with strict command-term marking. Transport in plants, homeostasis and inheritance are where sound answers routinely score half because describe was used where explain was asked.

subjects.name: Co-ordinated Sciences (Cambridge 0654)
subjects.description: Three sciences compressed into a double award, which many Al Ain students sit instead of three separate subjects. Physics content is trimmed hardest, so A Level physics later arrives with real gaps.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510/0511)
subjects.description: Reading, directed writing and a speaking component depending on the code. The directed task is marked on register and audience, so a strong essay in the wrong form loses the task marks outright.

subjects.name: First Language English (Cambridge 0500)
subjects.description: Reading passages, directed writing and composition. The summary question splits its marks between content points and writing quality, and listing points rather than composing prose throws half of them away.

subjects.name: Business Studies (Cambridge 0450)
subjects.description: Case-study led, and the grade separation sits in application marks awarded only for answers referring to the business in the insert. Generic theory answers plateau well below ability.

subjects.name: Arabic as a First Language (Cambridge 0508)
subjects.description: Comprehension and summary writing dominate. The extended writing task expects formal Standard Arabic, which is a register many students in Al Ain read fluently and write less fluently.

sections.heading: Mapping the Falaj Hazza school run onto a lesson slot
paragraphs: The gap between a school's published finish time and the moment a student is actually able to concentrate is where most tutoring arrangements in Al Ain quietly fail. A slot agreed in September against the timetable rather than against reality gets missed, then moved, then missed again, and by November the family concludes tutoring does not work for them. The slot was wrong, not the tutoring.

The variables are measurable. Finish times across Al Ain's private schools spread over roughly an hour depending on setting and key stage. Pick-up queues absorb fifteen to twenty-five minutes, more at the larger schools where buses and cars share one approach road. The drive into Falaj Hazza from the central belt is short but not instant. Then there is the part parents forget to count: a student who has been in a classroom since half past seven needs food and twenty minutes of nothing before they can usefully think.

The table turns that into a planning tool. It is not a promise about any particular school - finish times change and should be checked against your own school's current calendar - but the shape holds. Read the last column, which is the one that actually decides whether the arrangement survives to February.

The reason online delivery matters here is not that it is clever. It is that it removes travel from both sides of the equation. A tutor who is not driving can start at 4.45pm one week and 5.30pm the next during a short-day week. A student who is in Abu Dhabi on a Wednesday keeps the slot. A family that would otherwise have been offered the one evening their local tutor had free gets the evening that suits their household. IB Gram does not provide in-home visits in the UAE, so what is on offer here is the online version, stated as such.

sections.heading: What an IGCSE hour costs a Falaj Hazza household each month
paragraphs: Hourly rates are how tutoring is sold and monthly totals are how families decide. Converting one to the other changes the conversation, because a rate that sounds reasonable per hour can be an uncomfortable figure across a school year, and a rate that sounds high can be fine if it is only needed for ten weeks.

Start from the published monthly figures rather than the hourly ones. Bestimate's 2026 estimates for a weekly one-hour session put budget tutoring at roughly AED 240 to 600 a month, mid-range at AED 600 to 1,200, and specialist exam-year support at AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above. Advertised monthly packages in the market include around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. Those are other people's published numbers, quoted here as the market rather than as an IB Gram price list.

The monthly view exposes two things an hourly rate hides. First, the in-home premium compounds: four two-hour in-home sessions at the advertised package price costs roughly double eight online sessions, and a meaningful share of the difference is transport into Falaj Hazza rather than teaching. Second, duration matters more than rate. A specialist at the upper end for ten weeks before a June sitting usually costs less across the year than a cheaper tutor retained from September for insurance.

The table below is built the way a household budget is built - by the month, with the number of sessions stated - so you can compare an arrangement you are being offered against what the market publishes. Ask any provider in Al Ain, including us, which of those columns their quote sits in and what happens to the figure in exam term.

sections.heading: Falaj Hazza compared with Al Muwaiji and Al Jimi
paragraphs: Families moving within Al Ain, or choosing between compounds, ask whether the district changes the tutoring picture. For in-home arrangements it does, a little. For online ones it does not at all, which is itself a useful finding and worth setting out with the numbers behind it rather than asserting.

What changes between these three districts is journey time, the density of the local tutor pool and how early evening slots get taken. Al Khabisi and Al Jimi, being central, have the shortest distances and consequently the earliest-filling local tutors. Falaj Hazza and Al Muwaiji sit a little further out with slightly longer runs and a correspondingly thinner pool of people willing to drive at six o'clock. Zakher and Al Maqam are further again, and that is where in-home quotes drift towards the top of the published market band.

What does not change between districts is the thing that most affects a grade: whether somebody has taught your child's syllabus code. Extended-tier sciences, Additional Mathematics and Computer Science are hard to staff in every district of Al Ain, because the constraint is the size of the city's teaching population rather than the length of a drive. A family in central Al Jimi has the same problem as a family in Zakher; they simply have more unsuitable options close by.

So the comparison resolves the same way across the city, which is the honest finding rather than a sales point. If presence in the room is the priority, choose locally and accept the subject pool you have. If the syllabus match is the priority, the district stops mattering, and a Falaj Hazza family is choosing from the same specialists as a family in Al Towayya. Our own answer is the second one, because we deliver online across the UAE and do not run home visits here at all.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and social studies alongside IGCSE
paragraphs: Almost no tutoring page in this market mentions the mandatory UAE subjects, which is odd, because they occupy real hours in a Year 10 week and they affect how much room is left for anything else. Private schools in the UAE are not obliged to follow a specific national curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, and must otherwise follow the Ministry's general regulations. That federal baseline is what sits behind each emirate's own requirement.

Dubai's requirements are the most fully published and are a useful reference even for an Al Ain family, because the structure is similar. KHDA requires Arabic, Islamic Education and social and moral studies in all private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum. Separate classes must be organised for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and social studies, and combined classes for the two groups are prohibited because the curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ. Instructional time is calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit, with schools permitted to vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met and a minimum of twenty-five minutes advised per lesson.

Two practical consequences follow for a Falaj Hazza family planning tutoring. The first is arithmetic: these subjects are already consuming timetable hours, so the realistic ceiling on additional weekly tuition is lower than parents assume, and one well-used hour beats three badly attended ones. The second is content. For the mandatory subjects, use of different or additional material without prior Ministry permission is prohibited, so a tutor working in this space supports the school's own material rather than substituting their own scheme.

The equivalency angle is worth knowing too. On the British track, the sourced Ministry requirement counts five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at a grade no lower than E or grade 3 - and Arabic and Islamic education are not among those five. So a student can be doing everything right in their mandatory subjects and still need five other passes. Verify your own child's position with the Ministry rather than through any tutoring provider.

sections.heading: Ramadan, holidays and when revision actually happens
paragraphs: The UAE academic calendar has a shape that revision plans drawn up elsewhere do not account for. Ramadan brings shortened school days and a household rhythm that makes late afternoon the worst teaching hour of the day. Eid breaks arrive at a point in the spring term when IGCSE candidates would otherwise be building paper stamina. Summer sits between the June series and the start of Year 11 for the cohort behind.

During Ramadan the workable hours move rather than disappear. Post-Iftar sessions, roughly from mid-evening, are the ones that work, and students are often sharper then than in a normal 5pm slot because the house is calm and nothing else is scheduled. At IB Gram sessions move to post-Iftar timing at no additional cost and without renegotiating the arrangement, which is only possible because nobody has to drive anywhere to deliver them.

Holiday weeks are the most underused asset in an IGCSE year. A student who does nothing across a two-week break loses recall; a student who sits two timed papers and reviews them arrives back ahead. The useful holiday work is not new content - that is what term time is for - but paper technique, the error log and the one topic that has been avoided since October. Three sessions across a break are usually worth more than six in a busy term fortnight.

Then there is the long view. Cambridge candidates in the UAE sit June and November; Pearson runs May/June and November. That gives a genuine resit route, and the planning point is that the decision should be made before results day rather than after it. A student who knows in April that a November entry is the fallback behaves differently in May from one who is told in August that they have six weeks to turn a grade around.

sections.heading: How progress gets measured between September and June
paragraphs: A parent paying for a weekly hour deserves something better than a feeling about whether it is working. The problem is that school reports arrive two or three times a year and a child's own account of a lesson is unreliable in both directions. So the measurement has to come from the tutoring itself, and it has to be built in from the first session rather than invented in February.

The method we use is unglamorous. The first paid session is a diagnostic on a real marked script, producing a list of where marks were lost by category - unwritten method, command-term error, rounding and units, topic gap. That list becomes the baseline. Every subsequent timed paper is marked against the official scheme and the losses are coded against the same categories, so by the third or fourth paper you can see which categories are shrinking and which are not. A category that has not moved in six weeks is a signal to change approach rather than to do more of it.

Each session leaves a short written note: what was covered, what the student could not do, what they are to practise before next week. Three lines, not an essay. The value is cumulative - eight notes across a term show a trajectory that no single conversation does, and they give a parent who was not in the room something concrete to ask about.

At half term the honest question gets asked: does this subject still need the hour? Sometimes the answer is no, and saying so costs us a booking and keeps a family for the subject that does need it. Sometimes the answer is that the hour should move to a different subject. A provider who never recommends reducing is not measuring anything.

sections.heading: Controlled assessment, coursework and the line a tutor must not cross
paragraphs: IGCSE carries less internally assessed work than the Diploma, but several subjects still include coursework, controlled assessment or a speaking endorsement, and schools set internal deadlines around them. Those deadlines are when families ask for the most help and when the boundary is most likely to be crossed, so it is worth knowing where it sits before the week it matters.

A tutor may teach the skill the task assesses, explain the assessment criteria plainly, look at the student's own draft and identify which criterion is under-served, teach a referencing convention, and run timed practice on a comparable task that is not the assessed one. That is teaching, and a moderator who asked would have no issue with any of it.

A tutor may not write any part of the submission, dictate sentences for the student to copy, rewrite a paragraph into their own prose, provide a skeleton for the student to fill, or edit a draft until the text is substantially the tutor's. The test is whether the submitted work represents this candidate's own thinking and expression. Help that improves the text while making it less the student's fails that test even when every sentence is original.

At IB Gram the practical rule is that the document stays with the student. Tutors annotate, question and point rather than typing. If asked to cross the line we decline and record the request. In a market where at least one site openly advertises completed assessments for sale, stating this on the page rather than in a buried policy is a reasonable thing for a Falaj Hazza parent to expect.

sections.heading: Choosing a slot that survives a normal week
paragraphs: Everything above comes down to one decision: which hour. Families who get this right in September rarely change tutors; families who get it wrong often conclude the tutor was the problem. So it is worth ten minutes with a calendar before anything is booked.

Work from the constraints rather than the preferences. Write down the fixed items: school finish for each child, both pick-ups, sport, Arabic or Quran classes, the commuting parent's realistic arrival time, and the hour at which your child becomes unteachable. What is left is usually two or three candidate slots, not ten. Choose the one that also exists in a bad week - the week with a late pick-up and a dentist appointment - because that is the week that decides whether the arrangement holds.

Then make the slot slightly harder to lose than to keep. A fixed hour with the same tutor every week builds its own momentum; a floating arrangement negotiated by message each Sunday does not survive December. Where the evening is genuinely full, two shorter sessions often work better than one long one, and a weekend block is better than a weekday hour that is attended with half a brain.

Finally, be honest about what you are buying. If physical presence with a younger or easily distracted child is the point, hire locally in Falaj Hazza and ask for the MoHRE private tuition work permit and the syllabus code. If the syllabus match and a slot that moves with your week are the point, online is the better instrument. IB Gram sells the second of those; we do not offer home visits in the UAE, and a family that needs the first should know that from the top of the page rather than the bottom.
